For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, snd the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroboratee opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital: "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that Is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get Into a place, the lady of the house will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup 01 tea.' I say 'thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivemuelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is ' being cultivated has become so pewertul in its effects upon the nervms system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresis, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspooaful for each person and one for the blessed pot. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for- gotten what this old fashioned tea is like. '94, Commercial Road, Peckham, July 12, 1889. "Dear Sir,—l am a poor hand at expressing my feelings, but I should like to thank you. Your lozenges have done wonders in relieving my terrible cough. Since I had the operation of' Tracheotomy' (the same as the late Emperor of Germany, and unlike him, thank God, I am still alive) per- formed at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, no one could possibly have had a more violent cough ; it was so bad at times that It quite exhausted me. The MUM, which was very copious and hard, has been softened, and I have been able to get rid of it without difficulty.—l am, sir, yours truly, a. HILL.''

UTTERLY UNRIVALLED. The above speaks for itself. From strict inquiry it appears that the benefit from using Keating's Cough Lozenges is understated. The operation was a specially severe one, and was performed by the specialist, Dr. if. T. Butlin, of St. Bartholomew's Hospital. Since the operation the only means o frelief is the use of these Lozenges. So successful are they that one affords immediate benefit, although from the nature of the ease the throat irritation is intense.

Dr. Phillips Brooks, the Bishop of Massachusetts, whose death is announced, was so rapid a speaker that only the most expert shorthand writer could keep pace with him, and then not for very long. Dr. Brooks's most intimate friend here was Arch- deacon Farrar, who, at his invitation, preached two or three times at Boston. Dr. Brooks, when in this country, also preached in Westminster Abbey and of course many went to hear him.

A COQUETTE is said to be a perfect incarnation of Cupid, as she keeps her beau in a quiver. THE STAMP OF INIQUITY. —The Government stamp on a box of quack pills.—Punch. PLEASANT.—To open your wife's jewel-box and discover a strange man's hair done up as a keep- sake.

If Princess May is a believer in palmistry, as has been asserted, Prince George ought to be a firm believer in astrology, for some prophecies published in 1868, by one who had cast the Prince's horoscope seem on the fair way to be verified. One was that the Duke of York would ascend the throne of Eng- land, and another that he would marry in his twenty-eighth year. Prince George was born at eighteen minutes past one a.m. on 3 June. 1865, and Princess May at midnight on 26 May, 1867. With this exact information all the astrologists in the country ought to set to work and trace out the future of the young couple.

Dr. W. H. Dallinger, F.R.S., whose lecture on "The Spider" so delighted his audience at the Victoria Hall on Tuesday night, has passed his fiftieth year. The early years of his life were passed as a Wesleyan minister and he held for some time the governorship of Wesley College, Sheffield. Resigning this post in order to give up his whole time to minute biological research, he built himself a microscopical laboratory near London, and his name has become famous as the recorder of the life histories of those minute forms of life concerning whose origin there was so much discussion. Learned societies at home and abroad count Dr. Dallinger as an honored member, and his fame as a lectures is world-wide.

Caltious MucrArion..—We have always been aware that, on our canals Paddies generally raise riots, but what was our astonishment to learn from a recent agricultural work, that in certain districts of India, labourers, termed ryots, raise a sort of rice known as paddy! COURT CIRCULAR OF ANCIENT BRITAIN,—An antiquary has forwarded us a specimen of a joke— which, coming from such a source, may perhaps be a relic of the olden time—to the effect that the first court circular was Arthur's Round Table.— Pnnch.

Miss Annie Lethbridge at her wedding on Wed- nesday wore a white satin costume of the 1830 period, edged with orange blossoms, the long train being fastened from the shoulders. There were six bridesmaids—Lady Mabel Egerton (daughter of the Earl and Countess of Ellesmere), the Hon. Frances Wolesley (daughter of Viscount and Viscountess Wols.eley), Miss Cory, Miss Maud Morris, (daughter of Lady Morris), Miss Constance Peel, and Miss Maud Joicey. Their dresses are of white satin, with bright green velvet bats, and their black picture hats were trimmed with feathers. The bridegroom's gift to each is a large white ostrich feather fan and a bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley.

IN Victor Hugo's younger days, during a per- formance of his play "The Burgraves," Alexandre Dumas, seeing a man asleep in the stalls, said to his friend : "There, Hugo, watch the effect of your verses." A little nettled, Hugo waited for his opportunity, and a week later, while Dumas's play of "Henri III." was being played, caught a spectator napping, and called Dumas's attention to him. "Yes," said Dumas, "but that's the same man who went to sleep the other night; it has been impossible to awake him !" KITTY was studying her Sunday-school lesson, and one of the mottoes she had to learn was: " Walk in the way of good men." "Mamma," she said. thoughtfully, "papa is a good man, isn't he?" "Certainly, my dear." " Well, I don't see what it means. You always tell me not to get in papa's way, but he is a good man, and this says, Walk in the way of good men. I think it is pretty queer." AT a hotel in Scotland—where the Episcopal Church is called " The Establishment "—a gentle- man finding that the person who acted as waiter could not give him certain information which he wanted, put the question: "Do you belong to the establishment ?" meaning the hotel. To which the waiter replied: "No, sir. I belong to the Free Kirk."

The announcement of the engagement of Justice Handy M'Carthy, to Miss Aida Jenoure, occasioned no surprise to those who knew how profoundly the young dramatic critic had been impressed by the talent of the young actress whom "The Mounte- banks" revealed to the metropolis. It is just about a twelvemonth since he addressed to her" A Bal- lade of Columbine," which appeared over his signa- ture in the columns of the late lamented "Arid." "Columbine has come again" was its joyous refrain and the " Envoy "ran. Aida of the winged slio.an. London in her Lyric fane Hails a frolic Muse's boon— " Columbine has come again."

Mr. Francis Guise, the Itecorder of Hereford, who died on Saturday at his residence. Dear, Hall, Newn- h am, Gloucestershire, was the member of a very old Gloucestershire family, who acquired the Manor of Elmore, the seat of Mr. Guise's nephew, Sir William Guise, Bart., in the thirteenth century. by an alli- ance with the powerful De Burghs, Mr. Guise, who was nearly seventy-three,Tas formerly a stipendiary magistrate at Chatham, but resigned that office on attaining the excelhant appointment of Clerk of the Peace for his native county, which he held a, well as the Recordership of Hereford. He was a ba:ris- ter by prolession, and was one of the very few who have been made clerks of the peace, for that lucra- tive post is almost invariably given to a solicitor.

EASY TO TAT': E.-Dr. G-ildsmith having been requested by a wife to visit her husband, wo was melancholy, called upon the patient, and, seeing that the case was poverty, told him he would send him some pills, which he had no doubt would prove efficacious. He immediately went home, put ten guineas in a pill-box, and sent them to him. The remedy had its desired effect. A SMART LAD.—A boy from the country was recently taken into a gentleman's family. One evening, after having been called up to the draw- ing-room, he came down into the kitchen, laughing immoderately. " What's the matter ?" cried the cook. "Why, dang it 1" said he, "there are twelve on 'em up there, who couldn't snuff the candle, and they had to ring for me to do it." A PRECOCIOUS CHIEL.—A few days since a juvenile offender was brought before one of the Glasgow baillies, who after reading a lecture to the lad, put the following interrogatory :—" Where did you learn so much wickedness ?" The youth personifying innocence, with an inquiring look, replied, "Do you ken the pump-well in Olassford- street ?"—" No," said the Wilk. " Weel, then, do you ken the pump-well in Briggate ?"—" Oh, yes," answered the man in office quickly. " Weel, then," rejoined the accused, "ye may gang there, and pump as lang as ye like, for I'm hanged if ye pump me."—Dumfries Courier. Tint curate of Nevermind where, was lately called up in the middle of the night to see a sick woman. "Well, my good woman," said he, "so you are very ill, and require the consolations of religion? What can I do for you ?"—" No," replied the old lady, "I am not very ill, I am only nervous, and can't sleep."—" How can I help that?" asked the curate.—" Oh, sir, you always put me to sleep so nicely when I go to church, that I thought if you would only preach a little for me !." The curate muttered something, and became invisible "in less than no time."

Mr. George Lewis Garcia, who succeeds to the vacant Attorney-Generalship at Trinidad, is in the prime of life, and has been long and favourably known in his native land as a friend of the people in their struggle for the extension of the electoral franchise, Like his father before him, he has held the Solicitor-Generalship to the advantage of the community. Educated at Stonyhurst, and marticu- lating at London University. Mr. Garcia became a member of the Legislative Council in 1882, and has practised at the Island Bar since with considerable success, and proved himself to be a man of sound judgment, and possessed of legal acumen. He has long been regarded as a leading Roman Catholic layman at Port of Spain.

Mr. George Lambert, who is to move, and Mr. Mark Beaufoy, who is to second, the Address in the House of Commons in reply to the Queen's Speech, both entered the last Parliament at bye-electicns, both captured their seats from the Tory party, and both retained the seats thus won at the last General Election.

Mr. George Lambert, who represents the South Molton Division of Derbyshire,which he won upon Lord Lymington's succession to the peerage, in November, 1891, converted on that occasion the Liberal Unionist majority of 1,689 in 1886 into a Radical majority of 1,212, which was further in- creased last July to 1,339. Mr. Lambert is a young , man of twenty-seven, with a profusion of flaxen hair, and blue eyes, high complexion, and aquiline nose. He is a country gentleman and much devoted to field sports. He is also an ardent Radical, and the one speech he has as yet delivered in Parliament has created a highly favourable impression. Mr. Lambert, is on terms of close friendship with Mr. Seale Ilayne, the new Paymaster-General—the one Radical returned by Devonshire in 1886 and popu- larly known as "the star of Devon."

A SURGEON to one of the pnblic institutions in Nottingham, on visiting a club patient the other day, was surprised to rind a professional brother from another club in attendance upon her "How long have you been called in ?"—" Five days since," was the reply. " The same time as myself." On naming it to the patient, she said, " Why gentle- men, big people li,ve two doctors, and as my husband is in two clubs I thought so would I."— Well, my good woman, continued the speaker, "but you have two orders, what do you do with them."—Oh l" responded she, "I fetch the medi- cines and take 'ern both."—Xotanglictra Guardian. CAMP MEETING ANECDOTE. —At a camp meeting,. a number of ladies eoa,ibued standing on the benches, notwithstanding frequent hints from the ministers to sit down. A revtrend old gentleman, noted for his good humour, arose and said—" think if those ladies standing on the benches knew they had holes in their stockings, they would sit down." This had the desired effect—there was an immediate sinking into the seats. A young minister standing behind him, and blushing to the temples, said, "Oh, brother, how could you say that?"—" Say that !" said the old gentleman; "it's a fact—if they hadn't holes in their stockings, I'd like ro know how they could get them on 1' IN a certain village a well known bishop, during the exercise of his official duties, was quartered with tee chief inhabitant, whose wife was absent on a visit, and the guest was given the spare bed- room. The wife, on her return, inquired who had been at the house in her abs lice. "Bishop X," said the husband. "Bishop XI" exclaimed the good worn an. "And where did you put him to sleep "In the spare bed, ,11 course.', "In the ?" spare bed!" shrieked the horrified matron. "Why I put all the silver under the mattress before I went away l" And she rus 'led up stairs to the Beare bed room to see if the silver was safe. A FAMILY .FUZZLED.—A ooy at Diorwich literally his own grandfather ! It is in this wise There is a widow (Anne) and her daug ter-in-law (Jane), and a man (George) and his son (Henry). The widow married the son, and the daughter married the father. The widow was therefore mother (in-law) to her husband's father, and con. sequently grandmother to her own husband (Henry) By this husband she had a son (David), to whom She was great-grandmother. Now, as the son of a great-grandmother must be either a grand- father or great-uncle, this boy (David) was one or Ho in his own grendlether I

-- Mr. Mark Beaufoy won in 1889 the seat in Ken- nington from the Tories. This was almost the first of a series of Radical victories in the metropolis, and wns emphasised by the fact that Kennington was a Tory constituency in 1885, when the fortunes of Radicalism were at the highest. Mr. Beaufoy, who is still in the prime of life—he is well under forty—is of medium size, with auburn hair divided down the middle e,f the head, broad forehead, blue eyes, and very pleasing expression. He is by trade an extensive wine merchant. He is also a graduate of Cambridge and a gentleman of highly cultivated literary tastes. His library is a miniature museum, replete with relics of Shakespeare, Johnson, Thom- son, and the great Duke of Wellington. Mr. Beau- foy is a good electioneerer, but Mrs. Beaufoy far surpasses him as a persuasive canvasser, and his victories at the poll are largely due to her exer- tions.

Lady EmilyrrCadogan, Earl Cadogan's daughter, who is to be married to Lord Lurgan on 7 Feb., will have a very smart wedding. The bridesmaids will be Lady Sophie Cadogan, her sister, the Hon- ourable E. Brownlow, sister of the bridegroom, Lady Barbara Coventry, cousin of the bride. Miss Abarcromby, cousin of the bridegroom, Lady Edith Ward, Lady RosetMolyneux, Lady Evelyn Gordon Lennox and Miss Williams Bulkeley. The cere- mony wll be performed by the Rev. W. Brownlow the Rev. R. Eyton, the Rev. J. Roumien (vicar of Culford, Suffolk), and the Rev. E. Symmonds (formely chaplain to Earl Cadogan), and will take place at the church of Holy Trinity, Sloane-street. Lord Herbert Vane Tempest will act as best man, and after the reception, which naturally will be held at Chelsea House, Cadogan-place, the bride and bridegroom will start for Culford Hall, Bury St. .Edmund's, Earl Cadogau's seat, where the honeymoon will be spent.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1893. THE FRENZY OF THE DESERT. GLASS BOTTLE MAKERS AND THEIR: DARKWOOD• WAGES.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1893. THE FRENZY OF THE DESERT. GLASS BOTTLE MAKERS AND THEIR: DARKWOOD• WAGES.

It is afternoon of the third day since we left the Canadian river and headed to the south-west across the great staked plains of Texas on our way to Fort Stanton. Sand ! sand! sand! Here and there a bush.dying or dead. Here and there an ugly cactus with three or four rattlesnakes coiled up at its root. Always the same monotonous landscape, always the hot and burning sand under foot. For an hour past I have observed that certain of the troopers are acting queerly. Their lips are blue and their faces pale, and they look about in a nervous way. Twice when I have spoken to Corporal Johnson he has seemed to be overcome with emotion. We are carryiog plenty of water, and there is no danger from the In- dians? What can be the matter with these men?

The captain and lieutenant have been riding in advance. They now gradually drop back until the second officer is at the rear of the column. I notice the captain exchanging signs with some of the sergeants and corporals, and the mystery deepens. We jog along at a walk. The August sun blisters the troopers, and the hot sands bake the feet of the horses. The column straggles out like an Indian village on the move. " Halt that man ! Somebody grab him ! Here, you —Corporal Johnson !" All of a sudden the corporal had flung his carbine to the ground, unbuckled his sabre, and started to dash away. Luckily for him he was overtaken almost at once. Every vestige of colour has fled from his face as the captain rides up. His chin quivers, he trembles all over, and there is a look of terror in his eyes. " Get back in the ranks or I'll cut you down !" shouts the captain as he flourishes his sword about. "Don't you hear me ! Get back, I say ! Take that !" There was a blow with the flat of the sword, and the corporal turned his horse in the column, and received the carbine and sabre haaded up to him by a comrade. Then he began to weep to sob and lament, and a grim old trooper whispered to me : "That's good ! He will be all right now !" " But what ails him ?"

"Taken with the frenzy. It always comes to some of them when crossing the desert. If he'd got away, we should never have seen him again. Hello! There goes another !" It was a sergeant this time—a man who had grown gray in the ranks. He had been glancing about him in a furtive way for some time, and the men beside him were ready for his move. He suddenly uttered a scream, drove the spurs into his horse, and was pulled out of the saddle in trying to get away. He stood for a moment and then sank down in a heap. His face was fairly blue, his hair stood up litce bristles, and he held up his hands as if to protect his face. "Now, then, Small," said the captain as he rode up to him with a cocked revolver. "I'll give you one minuto to get up and reach your horse! You coward! You disgrace ! If I don't shoot you now, you'll be court mar- tialed and the regiment forever disgraced! If I had a whip, I'd lash you for a poltroon ! " The sergeant broke down as the corporal had done and began weeping and in three minutes he was back in the saddle and riding in his place. " Would the captain have done it ? " I queried. "No. He felt pity for him, but he had to be harsh. The object is to make them weep. That relieves the mental strain and brings them back to reason. It is the terrible monotony, the feeling of loneliness, the fear of being lost out here, that overcomes them. The officers always lcok for it when they cross, and they always do as you have seen them." "But do men ever get away?" "Look there to the right —and there to the left !" There were ribs of human skeletons showing above the sands—skeletons of men who had dashed out of march- ing columns when the frenzy was upon them, had dis- tanced pursuit, and had wandered about for who can say how many days and nights before they finally sank down and died of hunger and thirst, or perhaps fired a bullet threugh their own heads. There was another break and yet another before sun- set came, and we went into camp. The frenzy came to I all the same way—passed away after an hoar in each case, leaving no remembrance. It was the madness which has dotted every mile of that great sea of sand with human skeletons and woven a thousand mysteries around the fate of emigrants who have disappeared never to be heard of again.
THE NATIONAL CONFERENCE AT ST. HELENS.
DELEGATES URGING LANCASHIRE TO STRIKE.

The national conference of delegates representing the whole of the districts in Great Britain and Ireland in which glass bottles are manufactured, including St. Helens, Newton-le-Willows, and Manchester, in Lan- cashire ; Castleford and other places in Yorkshire ; Sunderland, Seahain Harbour, Brierley Hill (Stafford- shire), Scotland, Bristol and Dublin, resumed their sittings in St. Helens on Saturday morning. The special business was to consider the present position of the trade, and the reductions which are being made generally in the wages of bottle hands. The present to regarded as a very critical period in the history of this manufacture. Heavy reductions have been made in Lancashire, while in Yorkshire a strike is going on to resist the decreased wages. The Yorkshire men have regarded the acceptance of the reduction by the Lan- cashire men with much disfavour, and even among Lancashire men themselves much dissatisfaction has been expressed. Four delegates were present from Yorkshire, including Mr. Greenwood, of Castleford, secretary to the National Federation of Glass Bottle Makers, who stated to a press representative that it was

A SPECIAL NATIONAL CONFERENCE, and was warranted by the present exceptional state of affairs. Some preliminary business was transacted on, Friday night, but the real business commenced by a meeting 01 the delegates at the Royal Hotel on Satur- day morning, at ten o'clock. This continued until two o'clock, although a general meeting of the workmen in, St. Helens had been called for one o'clock in the old I theatre (now the Salvation Army Barracks). This I meeting continued from two o'clock until after six o'clock, and as the building was required for the Salva- tion Army at seven o'clock, an adjournment was made to the circus, in North-road, and here the conference was continued until eleven o'clock, in fact, it was • TWELVE Roues' CONTINUOUS SITTING. The proceedings were conducted privately, but it was evident, both at the old theatre and in the circus, that things were very lively. Delegates, from Yorkshire especially, urged the Lancashire bottle hands to seriously consider all the questions at stake, and ask themselves whether it was fair to the trade as a whole that they should accept such reductions. One delegate stated that if the men accepted the reduction, the condition of the trade at the end of 1893 would be worse than it was at the end of 1892. Another delegate said that if the Federation of Bottle Makers made a determined stand, the masters must keep up wages. Foreign competi- tion was not the most serious reason of the reduction —English competition, manufacturer against manu- facturer, had a good deal to do with it. If every- thing was weighed up, and the men found the masters had no just cause for these reductions, then they would be perfectly justified in not submitting, and it would injure the -trade if they did submit. One Yorkshire delegate said it was utterly impossible for the Yorkshire men to resist the reduction while the Lancashire bottle hands—their own flesh and blood—had surrendered, and were working and supplying Yorkshire with bottles. The Yorkshire manufacturers clapped their hands for . .

joy when they knew that Lancashire had surrendered. They (the Yorkshire workmen) did not fear to fight their own manufacturers; but it was very bitter when they had to fight the Yorkshire and Lancashire manufac-

turPrs and the Lancashire workmen. There was only one way of escape for the present, and one hope for the future, and that was in the Lancashire men standin2 by their Yorkshire brethren and resisting the reduction. (At this sentence there were many cries of " We will"). It would be far better for them TO SPEND EVERY SHI LLING OP THE £25,000

they had in hand than be crushed down by the masters. The Yorkshire men had been promised support from all parts of the United Kingdom, and the Continent as well, with the exception of Lancashire ; and now they asked the Lancashire men, if they had a spark of sympathy in their hearts to sympathise with them ; and the only practical sympathy they could give would he to stand out against the reductions. The addresses were received with loud applause, and it was apparent from the tone of the meeting that large numbers of St. Helens men were averse to working under the reductions. During the day the men discussed the situation in little groups, and a good deal of discontent was heard from men who have been out of work for several month, and who with wives and families, have had to eke out an existance on the I.os. a week club allowance while others have remained in their situations.

The proceedings of the day terminated, we under- stand, without any decision being arrived at. The pro- bability now is that a ballot will be taken of the whole of the Lancashire glass bottle makers, to ascertain the exact feeling, as by the rules of the society in such a crisis there must be a clear two-thirds majority before a strike can be resorted to. The possibility of a strike in St. Helens, where trade is generally depressed, is looked upon with considerable anxiety.

div.head: GOOD BUT PIG-HEADED.
div.p: GOOD BUT PIG-HEADED.

A man about 50 years of age got on the train at Clarkesville and took a seat in front of me. He had a shot-gun in his hand, and soon after sitting down he pulled at a big revolver and shoved six cartridges into the cylinder. My curiosity was aroused, and I leaned forward and asked, "My friend, is game plenty in this locality ? " " Waal, not so powerful plenty, stranger, but Oar's some- thin' around now and then."" Small game,mostly?" " Tans, mostly, but sometimes it is purty near six feet high. The game I'm arter is purty near that, I reckon." "You must mean a man ? " " That's ex- actly what I mean, stranger. I liain't got no time to be huntin' around arter foxes and possums and sich ; I'n goin' down to Erin to hunt a man." " Some one you have had trouble with ?" Exactly ; he's bin onery with me for 20 years. and I can't abide him no mo'; doan' want no fussin' with nobody, but I dun can't put up with such a critter forever." "Is he expecting you ? " "Reckon he is, fur I dun sent him word yesterday; he'll most likely be at the depot when we git thar." " And will he be armed too ? " " Sartin' ; he ain't the kind to sten' round and be shot at without shootin' back; no sir !" "Why, man, you don't mean to tell me you are deliberately going down to Erin to kill or be killed ? " I exclaimed almost overcome with his cool- ness. "I ain't gwine for nuthin else !" he replied ; "as I tol' you, l've stood him as long as I kin, and somebody has got to drap; mabba it'll be me, and meb- be it'll be him.' He put up his revolver, put on his spectacles, and had been reading a newspaper for some time when he reached Erin • as the train slacked up he picked up his shot gun and went to the door; a minute later he stepped out on the platform and descended and just as he left the last step the report of a gun was heard, and he fell in a heap, shot through the head. The onery critter" had got his message and was on hand. Is the train moved on I asked the conductor for further particulars, and he replied, " They'll send the body home—that's all; I told him how to work it,but he was pig-headed. He ought to have gene out of the other door and tired under the car, but he thought he knew it all and got left ; good man he was but dreadfully pig- headed." •

div.head: SHOCKING TREATMENT OF A BIRMINGHAICI GIRL AT DOUGLAS. EXTRAORDINARY DISCLOSURES.
div.p: SHOCKING TREATMENT OF A BIRMINGHAICI GIRL AT DOUGLAS. EXTRAORDINARY DISCLOSURES.

The Under-Sheriff for Warwickshire (Mr. Heath) and a jury sat in Birminghan on Tnesday to assess dam- ages in an action for assault brought by Rose Morgan aged twenty, of 'Clifton Road, Birmingham, against Thomas Ilarris, wine merchant, residing at Douglas, Isle of Man. Plaintiff, a girl of prepossessing appearance, said she lived with her grandfather, her mother being the defend- ant's housekeeper at Douglas. In July, she visited her mother at the defendant's house, Strathalan Park, Douglas. On seeing her, defendant put his arm round liar waist and tried to kiss her. He also tried to pull her on his knee, but she resisted him. On several subse- quent occasions defendant sought to take liberties with her, and once she tcok up a carving knife to protect herself. About midnight defendant and her mother came into her room, and, in spite of her struggles, un- dressed her, and when she fell exhausted on the floor they carried her to the defendant's bedroom, where defendant assaulted her. She immediately wrote to her grandfather, and eventually returned to Birmingham in a prostrate condition.—Damages were assessed at £2OO, the Under-Sheriff strongly denouncing the conduct of the defendant and the plaintiff's mother.

div.head: TALE OF LONEMOOR
div.p: A TALE OF LONEMOOR
BE MRS. HARRIETT LEWIS, Luthor of "The Sundered Hearts," "The Bailiff's Scheme," "The Double Life," &c.
CHAPTER VI. AFTER MANY YEAR..

At an early hour upon the morning after the funeral at Penistone, directly after his breakfast, which he had not touched, Squire Markham rang the bell violently, and summoned both his house- keeper and his butler to his presence. They came in, apprehensive of dismissal from his service. They found him pacing the floor restlessly after his usual habit. He turned his face towards them, and they were startled at the great change a few hours had wrought in it. His eyes were more sunken ; his features more haggard; his expression one of utter hopelessness. His form was bowed, too, as under the weight of many added years. He looked like a stately tree over which a tornado had pas,e4l. Cold, and hard, and stern as ever, there , was now an air of desolation about him, a strange loneline,s that touched even these dependents, who secretly judged him so harshly. "He is all broken up," thought the butler. "Who , would recognise in him the genial, hospitable gentle- man of two years ago ?" Ala, who indeed? "I have summoned you both for a brief private conference," said the squire not halting in his march. "It is time we understood each other. You hold in your keeping a secret of the most 1 -vital importance to me—a secret concerning the honour of this house and. my old name. Have either of you ever by word or look betrayed that secret or even a hint of it to any human being ?" "Never !" cried. husband and wife in one breath. Squire Markham's burning eyes seemed to pierce to their souls, but he found in them no shadow of untruth. The old couple had been no less reticent than lie save in their discourse with each other. "It is well," he said. "Now, swear to me that the secret of my house—the maternity of that child —shall never escape your lips." "I swear it !" said the butler.

"I swear to keep the secret until you yourself, squire, give me leave to speak it," said the old housekeeper solemnly. Her master smiled sardonically. "Then you will die with it untold," he said. "You have sworn to keep this secret. You have both served me many years, and I never detected either of you in fault. I have proved your fidelity to me—your sense of honour—your affection. You shall not lose your reward. Lonemoor has become distasteful to me. I have decided to go abroad, to remain for years—very probably for ever. I have ordered the carriage, and shall start fox Penistone within the hour. The old servants uttered no exclamation—be- trayed no surprise. In truth it seemed to them that nothing now could ever surprise them. "1 had a long talk with my land bailiff last night," continued the squire. "It is needless to tell you that he knows nothing, suspects nothing, of this. change. He has orders to pay you each an increased salary. You two will look after the house. You will dismiss all unnecessary servants, reduce the household, close the family rooms, and exclude all visitors. You will communicate with me through say solicitor once a month, giving me the minutest iatelligenoe concerning the place., ' The butler and housekeeper bowed assent. "The stables will be reduced," said the squire. "The hunters will be sold. The land bailiff will attend to that. There is but one more thing tc

mention." He took a turn or two about the floor, and tiler said, huskily— The child--I have never seen it. Is it s boy ?" • "No, sir, a girl—a bonnie wee girl," said the old housekeeper, eagerly. "Is she healthy ?' "She is weak and frail, sir. It is a question i! she worries through," said Mr. Quillet, sorrowfully "I don't think she'll live to grow a woman." The squire's face lightened a little. "So much the better," he said, briefly. "If she : dies, you may mention the fact in your letter." " Will you not see her, sir?" ask•d the house. , keeper, tremulously. "Oh, sir, she is so sweet, and delicate, and pretty " "Hush !" commanded the squire sternly. " Yor know not what you ask. I hope she will die. Al you say that she is frail, I need make no further mention of her. I have said all that is necessary. You may go." The pair retired, and the land bailiff, who resided upon the estate, was announced. An hour later, Squire Markham and Orkney, the bailiff, departed in the carriage for Penistone. They parted company at the railway station, and Squire Markham went up alone to London. The next day he crossed to Dover, and proceeded by rapid stages to Berlin. He had one or two interviews with the straw's' man who had visited him • so mysteriously on ere ' night of poor Clara's return. He had apparently ' failed in his mission, whatever it was, for the squire on the last occasion had dismissed him in terrible anger. It is not our purpose to narrate the experiences 01 adventures of the grim old squire. It is enougl for us to say that he spent some months in Berlin that he then wandered to Italy, to Syria, and te Egypt, trying to lose amid strange scenes and uncles foreign skies the haunting memories of the past. Wherever he went he carried his skeleton wits In Rome, amid the mighty relics of the mighty past, in Greece, under the shadow of ancient arts; , upon the Nile, when floating under moonlit skies ! between palm-shaded banks in his dahabtah, in the ; sunny days or lonely nights, be saw always in his thoughts the daughter he had cursed—the daughter ; who had returned to him like a spirit of the storm, I wild and crazed, and who had fled again into the storm with his curse upon her to meet hr death. He received monthly packets from his solicitor, containing letters from his land bailiff, butler, and , housekeeper ; but in none of these letters was men. Lion made of the death of his daughter's child—nor , allusion was even made to her existence. He did I not know by what name Mrs. Quillet had called her. Ile looked for the mention of her death, and not ' finding it, gave no further thought to her. Years were consumed in these wanderings. , Strange adventures happened to him. He found no pleasure in his journeyings, but he could not return to his desolated home. The grimness and hardness that had come upon him after his first visit to Berlin had now become his true characteristic. , Ile was harsh and suspicious. All his former geni- rlity and warm-heartedness had utterly vanished. His life had been laid waste, and he looked for death as a friend, bnt death shunned him. ired of aimless wanderings, he took a house in Alexandria, and settled down into a hermit-like 3xistenee, seeing none of his countrymen, and being lttended only by black servants. Thus passed other years. Then the old spirit of unrest that had slept Co long awoke again, and he resumed his journey- tngs, still keeping, however, within a month of England. • One day a strange fit of retrospection came upon rim, and with it came a longing as irresistible as it as sudden and strange. He was riding into Jerusalem from the valley of Kedron when the impulse came upon him to seek the old home at Lonemoor—the home in which he rad been born, and where he had once expected to lie. "It is seventeen years since that awful tragedy," le thought; "seventeen years since I left England. Why should I not go back, if only for a brief risit The idea grew upon him. "I will not stay there," he thought. "I could sever endure to remain there. But I would like one ;limps° of the old house, the woods, the moor. Die child must be dead, although the Quillets have ' kgotten to mention the fact. They said she was weak and frail. Yes, she is certainly dead; I have nissed one or two packets of letters during these ieventeen years. Probably one of the missing mckets contained tidings of her death." , This seemed more than probable, and he rrsuaded himself that his they was true, that ris grandchild was dead, and that one of the miss. , ng packets of letters had contained the announce- malt of her death. Thenceforward no thought of • ;he girl entered his mind. He rode at a quickened pace to his inn and went sp to the small, ill-lighted, bare chamber he had or several weeks occupied. A °racked mirr.a. swag upon the wall. He glanced into it, beholding his reflection, and a bitter smile curled his lips. A long white beard fell upon his breast. His hair hung in long white locks upon his shoulders. His eyes, dark and fierce, burned like coals in the midst of a hard, stern, frosty visage. "They would hardly know me," he said to him. self. " They ? Who are ' they ?' The bailiff, the butler, the housekeeper? Whom have I left in Eastland I cut loose from the old friends long

before t began my wanderings. lam trienaiess, still smarting under my secret disgrace. Yet I will go back on a flying visit, and then return to Alexandria and the old house there, and so settle down for good." He tossed his Lew effects into his travelling bag and hastened to make arrangements for his de- parture. He journeyed leisurely towards England, half ashamed of the impulse which drew him thither, and half resolved to give over his project even now. He lingered at various points along the route, and spent more than a week at Marseilles, and a fort- night in Paris. He arrived in England on a foggy, dull day in January, and hastened up to London. He remained there for a week, devoured with unrest, half resolved to take ship for Australia. His beard and hair had been trimmed, his attire conformed to English custom, but still he could scarcely have been re- cognised at first glance by one who had formerly known him. "I'll run down to Penistone and see my lawyer,' he at last decided, "and visit Lonemoor and my bailiff. I'll be off again the same day. There is nothing to keep me in England." He started the next morning for Yorkshire. At Penistone he visited his solicitor, was duly recog- nised, examined into his business affairs, and found, as he had expected to find, everything in a flourishing condition. The following day he took a carriage and drove towards Lonemoor. He had asked his solicitor no question concerning the child under Mr. Quillet's charge. And the solicitor had made no mention of her, although he had spoken repeatedly of the Quillets, of Lonemoor, and of the bailiff. _ _

"If she had been living she wrsuld be now seven. teen years old," thought the squire, as he drovs rapidly over the road that traversed the moor. "He would certaiftly have spoken of her if slu were in existence. The lawyer's silence in regare to her is proof positive that she is dead." He touched up his horse which sped onwards between the banks of gorse and heather no peeping out from a thin sifting of snow, and gradually the old mansion of Lonemoor dawnec upon his vision. And now his heart, which he had thought dead to all feeling, swelled within him. "Home !" he said to himself. "Home agair after all these years. What changes have occurred since I went away. I almost think if the girl h dead I'll not go abroad again. Of course she's dead. She must be dead. A few minutes mon and I shall know."
CHAPTER Vll.l OWENDOLIN_E.
During the seventeen years- of —Squire Markham'e wanderings what had become of the child of the unfortunate Clare Markham ? _

A life begun under conditions like those undo which her life had begun if it were prolonged tx adult years could not be other than extraordinary Had it been so prolonged, and did she live to bea, hor heritage of woe? Or had she haply died in hei Infancy, as the squire hoped and believed? These questions we now purpose answering. The little waif struggled through a feeble, sickli infancy, experiencing every infantile disease; btr when sae had attained the age of three years tin doctor declared her an incarqaticm Of health, ant ventured to predict for her a bang life. And then for the first time, the old housekeepei and butler faced the prospect of the girl's growti to womanhood.

They were alone in the housekeeper's room m the evening after the doctor's departure. Thc child was asleep upstairs. "John" said Mrs. Quillet, "you heard what thi dootor said? The child will probably live to 13( an old woman. What would the squire say if ho knew?' "He would send her out of the house." said thi butler, "to some orphan asylum, or foundliN hospital, most like. He would never have let ha' remain here if he hadn't believed and expected slit would die."

"lain not over fond of the child," said Mrs Quillet, "although I own she has rare winnini ways, and is a thorough beauty; but you see, I cal never forget all the trouble she brought with hel upon us all. She came to us in mystery. She made the master a wanderer on the face of the earth But for her Miss Clare might have been alive a' this day." "But the child is not to blame, Maria." "I know it. I suppose it's unjust, John, and blame myself for it ; yet I lay to the child's door al the trouble and shame of Miss Clare's awful fate And I can't love her—l can't. For poor Miss Clare's sake—because the child was her's—l gave her f nurse's care ; but my heart is not in it. Bui although l'cl be glad to have her die I could neve) send her to an orphan asylum. For Miss Clare'l sake, she shall be brought up a lady." . "We've no children of our own," said the butler "We have laid up a pretty penny, and all we have came to us from the.Markhara's. Let a portion gc ' back to them through the child 1" "Who was her father ?" said the housekeeper, musingly. " What was his name and station And that reminds me, John, since the child ,will live, we ought'to give her I. name. Think of 'lt! Three years old, and she has no name l" "Time she was christened," said the butler. "It won't do to go on calling her by the pet name Princess any longer. Why not name her after hex nether ?" " Clare ? Aid set the servants wondering? And make gossip? And infuriate the master? John, you stuprise me. I thought you had more sense.' "Chen why not name her Maria after yourself V' suggested the butler. "I don't love her enough. Besides it might be proved some day that she was well born—such a thing is just possible—and then the master would be angry at my presumption. She shan't be Maria, nor yet Quillet," declared the old woman de- cisively. "She looks something like the picture of the earls daughter who married Squire Markham, the master's grandfather," said the butler meditatively. "She was haughty and proud, I've heard tell, aDd the greatest beauty in Yorkshire—the lady Gwen- dolitv-, you know.' " Gwendoline 1" repeated the housekeeper. "Let us call her Gwendoline. But Gwendoline what ?"

" it was frightfully wintry weather that Novem- ber night When she came," said the butler. "Why not call her Winter ?" "That will do. The name will probably typify her lifk:," said Mrs. Quillet, sighing. " She's Gwen- doline Winter henceforth. And being what she is, we must not call her Princess any longer." And this was the way in which the little nameless waif received her name of Gwendoline Winter. The child grew in years, in strength, and beauty. The pretty imperious ways that had from the first won her the name of " Priacess " grew with her growth. She was active, quick-witted, impulsive, bright, 'sweet, and wilful as any spoiled darling in he land. But she was no spoiled darling. No one wer caressed her ; she was lonely in her babyhood. kny temperament less warm and sunny than hers would inevitably have soured under such neglect ind coldness.

Mrs. QuiHet had no real love for her, and at times 3ould not bear to have her insight. The little one, varm hearted and loving' clung to her until constant 7epulses and chislings had chilled even her baby lead, and then she turned to her dolls and her dogs or the toleration elsewhere denied her. It was a lard lot for any child, especially hard for one like ittle Gwen, with her vivid imagination, her impul- siveness, her bright impetuosity. "You* will harm the child by your unkindness, Nlaria," expostulated the butler one day. "She is L lovely little creature. Why can't you love her for ler mother's sake and for her own 9" "I can't, John. Sometimes I loathe her, and I ;annot help it." Yet the housekeeper, bearing in mind always a vague hope that the squire might some day adopt ittle Gwen, bestowed great thought upon her future ;raining. For some years the child played in the lonely gardens and upon the moor with her dolls and her dogs; but when she was seven years old, Mrs. Quillet succeeded in engaging for the little waif an experienced and accomplished governess, a gentle- woman by birth and education, who came to Lone. moor to reside. The child was introduced to Miss Granger as the daughter of a poor lady who 114 died at Lonemoor soon after Gwen's birth. It was not until a year or two later, by which time the governess had become deeply attached to her young charge, that Miss Granger heard from one of the maid servants, whom Mrs. Quillet still employed, that little Gwen was the offspring of a vagrant woman, who had given birth to the child at LoLemoor, and who had subse- quently perished in a snowstorm on the moors. Had Miss Granger been informed of her pupil's origin at the outset, she would probably have declined the engagement ; but now, however, pity was added to her love for the child, and she gave to little Gwen a tenderness' and affection that were almost maternal. In the warmth and sunshine of her care, the child found the first happiness her poor chilled soul had ever kaown,

Miss Granger remained at Lonemoor seven years, ' instructing Gwen in all womanly accomplishments as well as the solid branches of learning. Then, when the girl most needed her, the governess departed to marry a curate, to whom she had been twenty years betrothed. The Quillets, after due deliberation, and still cherishing their vague hope that Squire Markham might some day look with favour upon his grand- child, and adopt her legally, sent their charge to a finishing school in Pays—not to a cheap insitution, but to an expensive first class ensionnot. In this establishment were gathered the daughters of English and Russian nob.es. A few French girls, a few Americans, and one or two ItaUns, assisted • to make up the limited number of pupils received at the Pensionnat de Loraine. Miss Gwendoline Winter would by no means have been admitted into this aristocratic circle, but for letters which she had brought from Miss Granger—now Mrs. Myner—and from the good rector at Penistone, who took a lively i interest n our young heroine. Miss Winter remained at the Paris pensionnat three years, going through the highest course of study, and carrying off the highest honours over all competitors. Nature had given her genius, a keen, bright intellect, a noble soul—splendid gifts—as if to compensate her for what had been denied. "Ma toil' said Madame de Loraine to herself upon the day when this her favourite pupil was to leave Paris for England, "she will create a jurore in English society. She will marry a peer. With her beauty, her genius, there is nothing short of Royalty to which she might not aspire. I shall search the English Court journals for news of her." And this girl whotamadame thus eulogised was a social outcast—a nameless creature, whose very origin was a mystery. During Gwendoline's three years at the pensiormat De Loraine she had not visited England. She knew nothing of her own history, but supposed that she was well born, and an orphan. She vageely supposed herself a poor and distant relative of Squire Markham, and that she had been educated by his kindness, and that she was to become the mistress of his home. There had been much to foster this belief. She had spent her early years at Lonemoor, where her position had been something better than that of mere dependent. Mrs. Quillet, ever bear- ing in mind her maternity, had treated her with scrupulous respect, had appeared to regard her as a. superior, and had served her, it with little affection, with the more attentiveness. And then her three years at the pewionnat had been very expensive, and the girl could not in her heart believe that the Quiliets had done so much for her, since they had told her long ago that she was not of their blood.

She'linew that Squire Markham was travelling during all these years. To her he was a sort of hero —a princely kiwi of uncle, or elderly relative, who had lavished money without stint upon her, and who would return by and by to his old home, when she would cheer his age with the exercise of her accomplishments, and give to him the tender love of a daughter. And with these romantic dreams in her seven- teen years old head, Gwendoline Winter looked forward to her return to Lonemoor with impatience and delight. The day that had been appointed for her journey to England came, as we have indicated, a faultless day in June—the June preceding the December in which Squire Markham took his sudden resolve to revisit Lonemoor. In the months that were to intervene between that pleasant June and the squire's return in the ensuing February, through what strange experi- ences was poor young Gwendoline to pass. How crowded were those months to be to her with events? What tragedy they held in their brief scope for her young life I At an early hour, after the pensionnat break- ' fast, Gwendoline bade adieu to her schoolfellows, with whom she had been intensely popular. Then she visited the governesses one by one, and finally appeared in the private apartment of Madame De Loraine in full travelling costume. A minute later a servant entered with the announcement that Madame Quillet waited in the reception room. "Madame Quillet" being only a housekeeper—an upper servant—Madame De Loraine did not go down to her. Gwendoline was pressed to madame's heart in a tender embrace, and the girl turned , away, blinded by her sudden tears, and seed down the stairs and hurried into the reception ream
(To be continued.)

div.head: CENTENARY OF FARNWORTH SUNDAY
div.p: CENTENARY OF FARNWORTH SUNDAY
SCHOOL.

Special services were hold at Farnwertli Parish Church on Sunday, in commemoration of the cen- tenary of the Sunday School. In the morning the Vicar, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, delivered an eloquent and interesting discourse, based upon the text "For I know that he will command his child- ren and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord to do justice and judg- ment," Gen. xviii. 19. In the course of his sermon the rev, gentleman said it would be in the memory of all that a little time ago the centenary of Sunday schools was celebrated in England ; a movement which spread throughout the country for the purpose of giving religious instruction to the children, whatever might have existed before. The preacher said from records which were preserved to them he found that in 1792 the most careful, thorough, and evidently successful lines were laid down for the inauguration of the Sunday school which is now in existence at Farnworth. On the 4th of November, 1792, a preliminary meet- ing of the parishioners was held, when it was decided to commence a Sunday school, which was eventually opened on November 25th. A glance at the regula- tions, written by one long since dead, impressed him with the thoroughness and the earnestness of the founders, whose liberality was unbounded, as proved by a list of subscribers entered in the record book, which had been very carefully kept. It also showed that there were collections in church in behalf ef the schools on "Wake Sunday," when the sum of £3O was sometimes raised. It was customary at this period for the teachers to receive a remuneration, but it was pleasing to find that at the present time there were so many who were willing to dovote their time and talents to the work of training the young without receiving any remuneration whatever. A part of what was now the old school in Fern- worth was built when the Rev. Mr. Jeff was vicar, and the upper storey was added in 1832. It was an import- ant fact to remember that when the school was formed the whole country was being torn and upset by the French revolution, but still this spiritual work was being carried quietly on in Farnworth. To have a school founded upon such lines was indeed a precious and glori- ous heritage, and surely it would be an incentive to those who were now connected with the schools to press forward in the work, with increased earnestness and renewed vigour, at the commencement of the second century of the school's existence. Referring to the church, the rev, gentleman said that at the time under consideration it was very much different in- side to the present one; a large portion of the gallery did not exist, as that was quite a modern in- trusion ; there had also been several other additions since then. A very interesting feature was an entry in the book already referred to respecting the proceeds of a bazaar in May, 1834, which amounted to £2OO 18s. so that bazaars were not unknown in early times. The preacher took the opportunity to mention that it was intended to hold a bazaar in 1894 (sixty years after the one referred to), in aid of the renovation of the ' church, and he hoped they would receive the assistance of all connected with the old church and her daughter churches. In 1838 there was another large item of expenditure for the building of a school on the Marsh, which was the first step in the ecclesiastical arrangements of the pre- sent important and populous parish of Widnes. In conclusion, the rev, gentleman said it must be plain to thoughtful minds that they were opposed by many subtle forces of this world which were quietly, but surely, preparing for an onslaught, not upon individual Christian churches, but upon the vital truths of the Christian faith ; he therefore urged all to be well grounded in that faith, which was so dear to them in order to be prepared to withstand attempts that might be made to assail and destroy those principles and truths which were taught in their Sunday schools and churches. Special services were also held in the afternoon and evening, when the Rev. W. Edmondson, vicar of Parr, occupied the pulpit.

div.head: THINGS TO REMEMBER BY.
div.p: THINGS TO REMEMBER BY.

If a great fortune were unexpectedly left me (and it tank/ be unexpected) I'll wager anything that I should never forget the time or place where I first heard of it. Or if I should go home to-night and find (which God forbid) my house burned up, and everything in it, I'm equally certain that the main circumstances connected with the event would stick in my memory until all the Past's pictures fade out in the light of the life that is to be. 'T would be the same with you, I fancy? Yes. And here comes a woman who will not soon forget the month of December, 1890. It is not because Christ- mas comes in that month, for it is what she lost, not what was given her, that makes, that particular time stand out above other ti m es. And what she lost was her health, a matter worth talking about, as cne never can tell when he may be more interested in that subjeet than in politics or the price of provisions.

She says her illness began with nausea. She could keep nothing in her stomach, and threw up what she calls " a dirty green fluid." Now this dirty green fluid is not a thing to be disgusted at, but to be studied and under- stood. It is bile, and bile is one of the most important agents in the getting rid of the contents of the bowels. It oils the way so to speak, and helps to make the mass of stuff inside there more liquid and easily moved. The liver gets it from the blood, and when our machinery is all right we don't know there is such a thing in our bodies. But when the liver is torpid and lazy, then the bile stays in the blood and poisons us all over. It makes the head acho, the skin yellow and dry, and finally is expelled from the mouth, as this woman says. Nature can't use it the right way, so she throws it overboard the best way she can, which is a bad and sickening way indeed.

Our lady friend goes on to mention that her tongue was covered with a thick slime, her appetite was poor, she had a foul taste in the mouth, nd what she ate gave her great pain in the chest and back. All these symptoms were signs of one trouble and liable to do an immense amount of mischief, just as a wild animal loose in the streets may do a variety of mischief before he is captured and shut up again.

" I felt cold chills all over me," she says, ', and would it over the fire for hours, for I felt so chilled and starved. I lost a deal of sleep at night, and often had to get up and walk about the floor." This was a miserable state to be in, and nobody ever

experienced it without looking back to it with horror and dismay. That is, if he ever got over it ; for some never do., They get worse and worse until the doctorg shake their heads, and old friends wipe their specs, and think about certain funerals that are going to come off before long. For this disease is the essence and sub- stance of almost all the rest, no matter what names they are called by. It scatters death with both hands, and fills you so full of pain and misery—mind and body —that you soon don't care much whether you live or not. Well, Let us hear more from our friend. "1 had so much pain," she says, that it took all the power out of my body. At times my breathing almost stopped. I would gasp for breath, and for hours I was in agony. After any simple food I was so bad I had to lie on the couch, and one night I thought I was dying. "Last April my husband persuaded me to try Mother Seigel's Syrup, that had cured him of liver complaint. I got a bottle from Mr. Jack, in High-street, and in a few days felt easier, and after taking three bottles more I was completely cured and have had no pain since. I never felt better than I do now. " Yours truly,
" ISABELLA LIDDELL McEwmg,

" 78, Fisherrow, Musselburgh, near Edin burgh, September 17th, 1891," We congratulate Mrs. McEwan on her recovery, and there are thousands who will do the same. Four months of acute indigestion and dyspepsia is enough, though many suffer for years because they either never heard of or won't use, the remedy that cured her. And to; enlighten them she wants us to publish this little history. Now she will remember April as well 93 December.

div.head: WHERE ARE THEY.
div.p: WHERE ARE THEY.

Oh where are they whom we have loved, Whom now we never see; Who shared our hopes of future joy Which then we thought might be. They lived and died, and still we live Without them day by day. , Death cast his shadow o'er their form, And took their life away. In grief we followed to the tomb Affection's broken tie; And still we mourn a vacant place— For the beloved we sigh. The world pursues its wonted course, Progressive in the strife, Amid the ever changing scenes Of man's imperfect life. While nature bounds in glory yet Upon her endless way, And with eternal harmony Rides on from day to day. But were are they whom we have loved, Whom now we cannot see; Who shared the hope of future joy That once we thought might be.
Warrington, January, 1893.
S. KENYON.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held on 'Tuesday, there being present : Mr. J. Knowles, chairman, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. E. Aaron, Jas. Parr, J. M. Williams, W. Whitlow, W. Turner, J. Whitlow, T. Baxter, C.C., T. Lewis, Jno. Baguley, Joseph Bagulev, J. Stokes J. Weir, P. Hall, J. Brandreth, J. Wilkinson, E. jack- son, T. Taylor, T. Lea, A. R. Norman. J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk.) THE REPRESENTATION OF RUNCORN. The Local G .vernment Board, writing on January 14th, forwarded for the consideration of the Guardians a copy of a communication received from the overseers of the township of Runcorn, relating to representation of that township upon the Board. They requested to be furnished with the observations of the Guardians, upon the communication. The enclosure stated that at a duly convened vestry meeting of the township of Run- corn the following resolution was unanimously carried : —" That in the opinion of this meeting it is desirable that the township have a larger representation on the Board of Guardians of this Union, and the over- seers are hereby requested to bring the matter before the Local Government Board " The overseers submitted that since 1858 the township had doubled in population and more than doubled in rateable value, the figures in 1858 being, estimated population 10.000 and rateable value £28,455 The population at the census 1891, numbered 20,050, and the present rateable value stood at £58,413. The meeting on these grounds thought that they could reasonably ask for a larger representA- tion on the Board of Guardians. It was pointed out that Runcorn had a population of nearly half of that of the whole union, and its rateable value was over one fourth of its total value, while the number of its repre- sentatives on the Board was less than one eighth of the whole. They showed that the following townships : Aston Grange, Bartington, Newton by Daresbury, Newton by Frodsham, and Seven Oaks with a total Population of 588 and a rateable value of £6,997,eujoyed Precisely the same representative as Runcorn. It was felt that having regard to the present and future impor- tance of Runcorn, with its large and daily growing Population, the present number of representatives was quite inadequate to secure the due and proper administration of the relief of the p,or, as it was almost impossible to make that thorough inquiry into the cir- eumstances of the cases which they felt sure their lordships would consider desirable. It was also felt that as in April next a change would be made in the period for which the Guardians served that was, from one to three years' if the application Were acceded to it would be more convenient tor the alteration to come into force prior to the first triennial election.—Mr. Taylor said the members must that Runcorn was not properly represented on the d. Mr. Haywood said if the five Guardians if ,bucorn attended regularly they could understand 'weir wanting more representation, but when they only Saw a pnrtion of them the claim hardly carried the Weight it should do in the eyes of the Board. A short tune ago a relief supervision committee was called for 'Runcorn, and only Mr. Lea, Mr. Brandreth and himself turned up to conduct the business. He must admit that on that occasion Runcorn was not fairly represented (Laughter). Be should be quite willing to vote with Runcorn in getting that place more representation.; ou the figures laid 'before them it was certainly deserved. VMS pointed out that when Appleton and Weston Were each given a second member, and Stockharn and 'Norton were amalgamated,the Local Government Board strongly objected to increasing the number of Guardians beyond 42.—Mr. Whitlow thought the present repre- sentation satisfactory all round.— Mr. Taylor Proposed that a small committee be appointed to consider the question. They talked about the Runcorn Guardians ; there were always some of them Present, and they made a far better attendance than the representatives of some of the small places who did not , even put in an appearance once a year.—Mr. Lea. seconded the motion —Mr. Brandreth said if it were a sluestion of paupers Runcorn ought to hays rather more tePresentation than they had. The paupers in Runcorn formed a serious problem. They cost £2,300 a year.; Since Mr. Cooke was appointed relieving officer the relief had been reduced by £250 a year; but it ought to be reduced still more. It might be reduced as much as £5OO more. He should be glad to support the appeal for a larger number of Guardians if they would only reduce the amount of the relief given in the township.—Mr., Taylor explained with regard to the relief supervision lkommittee of which mention had been made, that he was attending another important meeting.—Mr. Norman said the meeting was on the day following New Year's day and he was away from home. A more suitable time 'Light have been chosen for the meeting.—Asked to aame his committee, Mr. Taylor proposed Messrs. Brandreth, Baxter, Heywood, Baxter, Knowles, Nor- man, Lea and himself.—The motion was carried igitaniinou sly.

div.head: MOISTURE IN BUTTER,
div.p: MOISTURE IN BUTTER,

The Burnley magistrates on Wednesday dismissed a summons which charged the Burnley Co-operative Society with selling better containing too great a per- centage of moisture—namely 20 per cent of water. It as stated that Irish salt butter, such as that to which the summons referred, required 20 per cent of water to keep it in good dondition. It was further asserted that ?decision in the case in favour of the prosecution would If upheld, practically ruin the butter trade of the South 91 Ireland by imposing conditions which it would be luTossible for farmers to comply with.

div.head: BEST PAID PROFESSION.
div.p: THE BEST PAID PROFESSION.

£B,OOO FOR 200 SONGS. Chicago is to be afforded an opportunity of listening to the warblings of Yvett Guilbert, who has been offered b, a music hall there 8,000/ for two hundred songs. All her expenses and those of her maids will be paid. She aho has telegraphed assent, but asks for half in advance before she leaves New York. Yvette Guilbert is very clever, but her style and feeling is that of the " voyou- cratie "of Paris. She is not to be compared to Theresa, 'Who was a woman of genius, and whose diction—for she could have hardly been said to sing—was incompar- able. She was often grandiose, and by the most simple Ineans. Whatever old thing she took up. she put quite a new face on. Her pathetic efforts were sure to draw tears from the eves of the most sceptical French audience and she cou!d be irresistibly droll. Yvette is many Pegs lower in her comic songs,which, as she says herself, when going to sing thena,are not fit for the ears of young ladies.

div.p: MESSRS. CROSFIEID AND THEIR

PLOTES. INAUGURATION OF SOCIAL EVENINGS. On Saturday evening a gran I concert was given in the Mission Room, Bank Quay, Warrington, in inauguration of weekly social evenings for the men employed at Messrs. Crosfield's Soap Works. Mr. A. H. Crosfield presided, and on the platform there stood a magnificent piano, by Schwechten of Berlin, presented by the Chairman, at a cost of be- tween seventy and eighty guineas, for use in con- nection with the social evenings. There was a large attendance, among those present, we noticed, being Messrs. John Crosfield, J. J. Crosfield, Miss A. Crosfield, Miss G.Crosfield, and Dr. Adams. The CHAIIIIILN in opening the proceedings said he supposed it was hardly necessary for him to explain ' why this inaugural meeting of theirs had been delayed ' for a few months. The detestable epidemic was respon- sible for this, as for the loss of GO much pleasure among all sections of the community. He might refer to that also as a sufficient explanation, he thought, of the time this instrument of theirs had been on the way, and which they regarded as the indispensable preliminary of their social evenings. If they did not think that the epidemic was a sufficient excuse, he could only refer them to those principles that he imbibed with his mother's milk those sordid principles of political economy, and Radicalism, which taught one to •buy in the cheapest, and sell In the dearest ma.rket--,(laughter)—and as they were going to have a piano he wanted his funds, so far as they would go, to bring them the best instrument be could get. (Hear, hear. 1 This little reference to politi- cal economy was not intended as any Peg on which to hang a political address. They would have no harangue of that sort from him. For one thing, they would very soon have their fill of politics. They were on the eve of probably one of the stormiest sessions they had had for a long time, and with the prospect in the distance of an unsettled condition of political parties for some time to come, and in the foreground a series of pitched battles, they had a 'picture of stirring times in the political field for probably some years. Viewed simply from the party point of view politics must 'be admitted. even apart from the practical results obtained from them, to have a certain advantage even if they only stimulated public interest and general mental activity. Viewed from another standpoint, as am ()gag the greatest, perhaps the greatest practical example of these forces which with enlightenment, education, and self-discipline must make slowly, probably very slowly, still not less certainly, towards the amelioration of the general condi- tions under which human beings lived, politics had a much higher title to their respect, notwithstanding the drawbacks appertaining to them. Well, that was possibly rather vague, but he was not in the position to speak more distinctly at present, and they must not complain if he did not say anything more definite on political matters, because, in the first place, he told them he had not come there for anything of the kind, and, in the second place, he was not in a position to do so even if he had wanted,although last night he had the advantage of listening to a rising man in the cabinet, and who when a number of enter- prising people in the audience tried to throw light on public affairs, refused to " let on? 'Well, that was all he (Mr. Crosfield) had to say about politics, and it was not very much. There was an old book that told us that man did not live by bread alone, And it was very certain that he could not subsist exclusively on politics ; nut even of the kind they were getting. A certain amount of their leisure they might give up to political life, but nature was net going to be denied, and as the fierceness of competition increased and the strain on the mind's faculties and energies became more intense, they sought to indemnify themselves by finding sources of relaxa- tion and amusement. And this was where amusement stepped in, not, of course, as any novelty, because he supposed it was almost as old as humanity ; but what he meant was this, that the value of music, for instance,as a means of ordinary enjoyment and culture was being constantly recognised by a larger circle in the , country. And not only did the trade for enusic advance, but the quality and the average standard of music throughout the country advanced. Of course, there ' might be a little drawbackto this. There were some people who, because good music was the thing, would , go into ecstacies over classes of music they could not understand. While without intending in any way to emulate these people Who ccin their cheek to smile:, and cry aloud

In worship of an echo, they might still think it very well worth their while to cultivate their taste for music, and to develop their powers in that way. (Applause.) In reference to the evening's programme, he must congra ulate the ladies and gentlemen who had been kind enough to come to help them at this their first meeting of that kind, and on the most suitable selection they had chosen—(ap- plause)—in which there was good music. (Renewed applause.) The following performances then followed :—Duet, piano and violin, " Luci di Lammermoor," Messrs. M. Rosetti and Pearson, encored ; song, " Comin' through the rye," Miss Bottomley ; pianoforte performance, "La Joyeuse," Miss G. Crosfield, encored ; recitation, Mr. I Greener ; song, "Lead to battle," Mr. M. Levien ; piano-1 forte, Rubenstein's "Tarantelle," Mr. M. Rosetti ; song, "Andalusian maid," Miss M. Bottomley, encored ; reci- tation the skating scene from " Pickwick," Mr.Grsener, encored ; "The nocturnal sketch," by Tern Hood.

ADDRESS BY THE SECRETARY. The Secretary to the committee, Mr. J. Willett, said ; perhaps some present, might be aware that last sum- mer they took great interest in getting up bowling com- petitions for Saturday afternoons, and he was very , happy to say that these competitions had been very i highly appreciated by the workmen. They had on one or two occasions Mr. John and Mrs. Crosfirld, and Mr. A. Crosfield present, and Mr. J. J. Cros- field would have been with them too, but he was undergoing that frightful punishment re-vac- cination at the time. (Laughter.) At their last corn- petition when they had taken tea, Mr. Arthur Crosfield and he happened to be chatting together, and he mentioned to Mr. Crosfield that he thought something in the shape of what they had to-night would be benefi- cial for the workmen on Saturday evenings. He told Mr. Crosfield that the only difficulty he could see was this : they could work the entertainments on a very cheap scale, but there was one thing that would fail them, the hire of a piano. " Well ' Mr. Arthur said, " if that is the biggest failing that there is, I will present you with a piano." (Applause.) He was sure they were very much obliged to him for his beautiful present— (hear hear)—and he hoped and trustedthey should meet there Saturday after Saturday night to hear the music coming from the piano. Their first object in calling these meetings was that they might meet together, and try to cultivate one another's minds as regarded music. For his own part he thought some people made a serious mistake as to music. Some went in for one thing some for another, but they always found anywhere that if there were plenty of the comic element in an enter- tainment you could get plenty to go. It was very difficult to get people to come and listen to anything like classical music, music that would really do them good, but if they would only tome and listen to it, and get used to it, they would learn more by it. The second object of the social evenings was that the workmen of Bank quay 'k Soap Works might meet, fraternise, and enjoy them- selves. They wanted every man and woman who came to feel that they were at perfect liberty to enjoy them- selvcs in a rational manner, and the Committee had decided that on no occasion should any song be sung or recitation given, which the men could not bring their wives and sweethearts to hear. He had been asked several times that week what about the finances. The Lancashire people generally wanted a good deal for their money. The Committee decided that the money they took out of the concerts should go to form a benefit and contingent fund; and if it so happened that any one of the workmen had the misfortune te meet with an accident, or be laid up with sickness, they might be able to make him a grant, and they all knew that five or six shillings a week under such circumstances would be very accept- able. THE COMMITTEE

had laeen elected from every or nearly every department of the works, and consisted as follows :—President, Mr. John Crosfield. Vice-presidents, Messrs. A. 11. Crosfield and J. J. Crosfield, Dr. Markel, Messrs. W. H. Robinson, It. Proud, Studer, and Newall. Committee: Messrs. T. Randalls, jun., P. Gleave, Joseph Massey, G. Gleave, T. Bridson, John Rigby. John Wilcock, James Lawton, Thomas Dykes, William Brobbin, J. Dimelow, John Atherton, William Welsby (treasurer), and J. Willett (secretary). They purposed carrying on the concerts every Saturday night. There would be a certain amount of labour in getting them up. He had made up his mind that he would sacrifice his time if he could be of any ser- vice to them. He wanted to try to make his fellow-men happy, and he did not think they could do better than meet there as that night and have song and recitation which would take away from them the care that they had had to pass through during the week. They would get into closer communion one with another, and chat matters over on Saturday nights, and be happy. They were very much obliged to Mr. Arthur Crosfield for his kindness in getting up that conccrt. They had had nothing to do but arrange the performances. He had provided the ladies and gentlemen who had .so kindly come forward that night. The Committee did not in- tend to advertise the concerts but wanted the men to do this themselves, and to bring their friends. There were some 18 to 20 ladies and gentlemen who had kindly volunteered their services for the concerts. After an interval the programme was continued as follows: Duet, " William Tell," Messrs. Pearson and Rosetti, this being encored but the Chairman excusing the artistes from compliance with the request on ac- count of the lateness of the hour. Song, " Because I love thee," Mr. Mewburn Levien pianoforte, "Im- promptu," (Schubert) Mr. Rosetti ; recitation, Mr. Greener , song, " Tit for Tat," Miss M. Bottomley, Pianoforte, Listz's Grand Wedding March, Mr. Rosetti. A vote of thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had taken part and to the chairman was accorded on the motion of Mr. Willett, seconded by Mr. Benjamin, to which the chairman responded, on behalf of the recipi- ents: and the proceedings thea concluded.
