div.head: TB E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 1893.
div.p: TB E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 1893.
DEBATE AT WIDNES LIBERAL CLt.B.

POLITICS AND MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. On Monday night a good audience assembled in the Lecture Hall of the Widnes Liberal Club to hear a debate on the question " Ought municipal elec- tions to be fought politically." Mr. S. Deacon occupied the chair. Mr. Hartland opened the debate in the affirmative. He remarked that upon this question differences of opinion existed, hot they felt that it was of the highest importance that this ques- tion should be settled before the next municipal election, which would be fought in November. After most seri- ous consideration he was most decidedly in favour of fighting municipal elections politically. The House of Commons was the legislative machine, where measures were passed into law, and the local authorities were formed to administer these Acts of Parliament. There were now no fewer than 650 acts to be administered by by local bodies, and he understood that they were being added to at the rate of 60 per year. If Liberals are the best to pass Acts of Parliament, why should they not be the best to see that they are administered ? (Hear, hear.) And within the ranks of the Liberal party there were many able men who could' serve the people if they had the time at their disposal. There was nothing to prevent the meetings of Town Councils being held in the evening, •when the working classes of the county could have representatives of their own working in their inter- ests. (Hear, hear.) He did not believe in fighting election seat against seat, or in fighting Englishmen against Irishmen ; or in electing a man because he was wealthy. The fairest, the best, and the simplest way was to fight these local contests on the broad ground of political opisdon. There was no such thing as an inde- pendent, and aso called independent was not to be trusted. (Applause.) Alderman Timmis expressed his pleasure in having an opportunity to take part in that academical debate. He had consulted public men in other places with a view to obtaining the fullest information on the subject, and he had also looked out for books of reference, but in both instances he had been unable to obtain anything bearing upon the subject. He argued that they should have the best possible men, men who would do their best for the town, to govern a municipality. It was immaterial to which political party they belonged if they were the right men. No party had a monopoly of good men ; there were good men on both sides; and if one party was much stronger than the other; it would carry all seats, to the extinction of good men on the other side. A Town Council had to administer Acts of rarliament, by what- ever party passed, independent of politics, and therefore he saw no need why politics should be introduced. He contended-that Mr. Hartland had made no case ()et whatever.—Mr. E. Carey supported the affirmative. Government by party was supposed to be the best form of Government on the whole for the coun- try,and it would be very much better for municipalities than the happy family arrangement ley which there was no really effective opposition. He did not agree with Mr. Timmis that their great aim should be to get the best men. They might have a most excellent man. They might have an angel, but supposing that angel always voted on the wrong side, he would rather have somebody a little inferior to that angel. (Laughter and ap- plause.) .Lord Beaconsfield once said" lam on the side of the angels," unfortunately he was on the side of the Tories. (Laughter.) Mr. Carey argued that Govern- I merit by party would not lead to factious opposition ; he believed that both parties would join together for the good of the town when such a subject was brought for- ward. He had never seen that to be the case.—Mr. F. J. Poole supported Alderman Timmis. Because a man was sound on Home Rule or the disestablishment of the Welsh Church, it was no guarantee that he had any knowledge of sanitary matters or the other important business of a corporation.- r. P. Whelan supported the affirmative and Mr. S. Jackson took an opposite view. The latter said they did not want politicans on a Town Council, but men of sound business capacity, men of ability, and men whom the people could trust and hon- our.—Mr. Paton held similar views. Messrs. Carey, jun., and Mr. J. Morrison and Mr. F. Lawrinson sup- ported Mr. Hartland. Mr. Morrison said he had made up his mind to take an active part in municipal or imperial elections, but he thought this was a question upon which he might have an opinion. He contended that they wolud get the best men by using their party organisations. For a time they would have a great number of candidates coming forward, but these would find that it di 4 not pay to be on a Corporation, and ultimately men who had not the time or the ability would fall away, and the best men would come to the front. If elections were not fought on party lines they would have men who said they were independent, and secured the votes of their party as well as of other people whom they could influence. Alderman Timmis and Mr. Hartland having summed up, a vote was taken, with the result that the affirmative was carried by 19 votes to 14. A vote of thanks to the Chairman was carried on the motion of Mr. E. Carey, seconded by Mr. Rowe. A smoking concert was afterwards held and a very plea- sant evening was spent.

PRESENT TO THE SCHOOLS. The Master of Padgate schools reported the receipt of a parcel of sweets from Miss Lythgoe, Sankey-street, for the school children. HOUSE COMMITTEM—DISMISSAL OF THE BAKER. The House Committee's minutes were read, which recommended, among other things that Mr. Cliffe, the cook and baker,be dismissed.—MriaTcoven moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Davin seconded.—Mr. Slum moved an amendment that the matter be referred back to the Committee. He said it was brought before the committee last Friday. At the time the subject was discussed Ilit was not a party to the proposition, and informed the committee that he should bring the matter before the Board. He said now as he said then that he considered the committee were adopting a rather unwise comae in giving a man a week's notice, considering that he had been under the Board en the last occasion for 14 years, and it was about 25 years since he came into the employ of the Union. He had served the Union well and it had only cropped up within the last few weeks that the man had simply spoilt a few batches of bread, in fact the matter now appeared to resolve itself into one case in which the bread had been spoiled. His salary was about 275. a week, and his work was excessive. Mr. Shaw detailed the duties Mr. Cliffe had to perform, and said bethought it was only right to give the man a fair chance. There had been, a question asked in com- mittee as to whether he was doing his duty, and the master said there was no further complaint.—Mr. Debson seconded the anaendinent.—Mr. GILL said he knew nothing of tie circumstances except what he had heard from Mr. Shaw, but thought the committee were taking a very harsh step indeed in proposing to discharge at a week's notice a man who had been with them 25 years. They had only had one complaint against him. Any baker might at any time spoil a batch of flour as Cliffe had done. If they had been getting this man for 275. a week to work there from early morning to do their baking, their cooking, and provide their beef tea and porridge, it looked to him very much like sweating. It would be a very hard thing to dis- charge the man at a week's notice for such a trifling offence.—Mr. RATCLIFFI said for the last three years there had been continual complaints about the food. About a fortnight ago the committee informed Cliffe that they would be compelled to give him a week's notice unless he improved in baking and cooking. He asked whether there had been any complaints during last week, and the previous day's baking was brought in, and said it could be rolled up like marbles, and the soup had been so bad that it had to be given to the pigs. The House Committee felt very reluctant to dis- charge the man, but had no alternative.—Mr. HILL said the step was not taken in consequence of one particular complaint,but on account of the general neglect of duty. —Mr. HILL was proceeding, when the Chairman ruled him out of order in speaking at this stage of the discus- sion, he also ruled Mr. Muir out of order, the former gentleman disputing his ruling.—Mr. &taw desired to speak again, but he, too, was declared out of order.—On a division, four voted for the amendment, and all the other Guardians for the original motion.—lt was re- solved that a new baker should be advertised for ; the terms to be fixed by the House Committee. CHILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT. The School Committee recommended that the offer of the Master of the Padgate National Schools to give an entertainment to the children be accepted,and of this the Board approved. HR. *WRIGHT'S RESIGNATION. There was a letter from the Local Government Board accepting this, and stating that they would issue orders for an election to fill his seat. •

SMALLPDX. IN LIVERPOOL-ROAD. A letter was read from Dr. Sephton asking that as smallpox had extended from the borough into the extra municipal portion of Liverpool-road, the Board would grant increased facilities for vaccination and re-vacci- nation to meet this emergency.—lt was decided that Dr. Gornall be requested to attend to the matter. RELIEF OF FEB UNEMPLOYED. A letter was read from Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, stating that during the recent frosty weather outdoor employment had been almost entirely suspended, and In consequence of the many applications by able-bodied men for relief he had found it necessary to administer relief in the form of goods in seven cases.—The CLERK pointed out that these were cases in which the relief was not legally administered, but read a provision ac- cording to which Guardians could in their discretion depart from the regulation and make such allowance, but must obtain the consent of the Local Government Board within 21 days. During-six weeks ended January 20th, in Mr. Garnett's district alone—he had no report from Mr. Wallace. though he had expected oae-78 families had been relieved with food at a cost of £27 Hs. dd., and 30 pairs of clogs had been allowed, the total amount paid for relief within the period named being £225 4s. 9d., or an average of £37 14s. lid. per week. The average number of persons relieved each week was 542. In addition to that, there was the re- lief of•the seven cases as to which Mr. Garnett now write.—The Crimaimim said the cost of these seven cases was about 50s. He proposed that the Clerk write to the Local Government Board for their sanction to this additional relief.—Mr. RATLIFF'S seconded, and the motion was adopted. The Board then resolved itself into committee to consider a complaint by Mr. Shaw.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mt. H. E. Heywood. There were present the Rev. J. N. W. Tanner, Messrs. E. Aaron, James Parr, J. M. Williams, W. Whitlow, W. Turner, J. Whitlow, T. Baxter, C.C., J. Knowles, T. Lewis,John Baguley, J. Stokes, J. Weir, P. Hall, J.Brandreth, J. Wilkin- son, E. Jackson, J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk). CANAL BOAT INSPECTION. Mr. Farrington submitted his annual report respect- ing canal boats. He stated that be bad inspected 125 canal boats, and that their general condition.as wall as their occupants continued to improve. There had been little or nothing to complain of as regarded any infringe- ment of the Acts or regulations. Ho had met with no instance of overcrowding, had received no notification of infectious disease, and the cleanliness and ventilation were satisfactory.

inn SMALLPDX OUTERSAX. Mr. Williams, chairman of the Infectious Disease Hospital Commiteee, said the committee had met that morning to deal with the smallpox outbreak. The build- ing at Weston they had intended to convert into a hospital, was unsuitable, but the Ship Canal Company had made an offer, which the committee had accepted, and the completion of the hoseital had been left in the hands of Dr. Adams and himmlf.—Dr. Adams said the Ship Canal Company had offered to transport at their own cost, their well built and commodious offices from the Big Fold/Norton, to a site on a disused spoil bank at Moore, for the purpose of an infectious hospital. The site was a most suitable one, and the building would have three wards capable of accommodating twenty patients. He had engaged two nurses from the Liverpool Nurses' Institute, at a fee of £2 21. each per week, which was the lowest fee any institution would let out nurses to take charge of smallpox patients. He had also given orders for fifteen bedsteads and other furniture, and Mr. Wm. Williams had ordered the bedding. The doctor mentioned several sanitary arrangements that would require to be made, and he was requested to carry them out. The outbreak, so far, had resulted in fourteen cases and three deaths. There were now several other cases of which he had rot yet had notification. At Lower Walton the disease had broken out, and he had taken action tinder the 128th Section of the Public Health Act, and the place was now closed. He draw attention to the delay that had arisen in notifying from Weston a number of cases of continued fever, which in nine cases out of ten was unrecognised typhoid fever ; and also in notifying a case of smallpox from Walton. It was resolved that the Clerk write to the Runcorn doctor having charge of the Weston cases, ask- ing for an explanation of the delay, and the Clerk was also instructed to communicate with the medical gentle- men in the district, drawing their attention to the necessity of immediate notification of infec- tious disease. —At the meeting of the Board of Guardians later, a letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that the medical officer • had reported to them a case of smallpox which had occurred at the Workhouse. They asked what steps had been taken for preventing the spread of the disease and especially for the vaccination and re-vaccination of the inmates. It should also be stated what provision had been made for nursing the patient. Dr. Robinson, Frodsham' with reference to the case said the sufferer was admitted on Saturday, January 14th, from Run- corn, witla a certificate from the district medical officer, suffering from a cold. There was nothing unusual in his appearance until Monday morning, when spots were observed on his face. The man was at once isolated and placed in the infectious ward at the hospital. Disin- fectants were freely used, and the patient was placed in charge of a male inmate, who had suffered from the dis- ease and previously nursed such cases. All the officers were re-vaccinated two months ago. He intended to re-vaccinate the whole of the inmates of the House as soon as possible.

div.head: SCENE AT WOODSIDE LAIRAGE.
div.p: SCENE AT WOODSIDE LAIRAGE.

A HORSE GORED TO DEATH BY A BULL. A scene of the wildest excitement occurred at the Woodside Lairage, Birkenhead, on Tuesday, when a young Colorado bull broke loose from the,rnen who were taking it from one of the pens. The beast charged about the place in a most savage manner, and but for the 'fact that everyone fled incontinently, injury to limb would have inevitably ensued. Finding no man left, the bull charged a valuable horse which was at- tached to a railway lorry, and gored it so terribly that thespoor beast died almost immediately. Ultimately the bull was captured, and so treated that he is not likely to trouble the lairage employes any more. While the scene lasted there was the greatest excitement, for a Colorado bull "on the loose" is no joke for the pluckiest man to encounter.

div.head: LABOUR COMMISSION.
div.p: THE LABOUR COMMISSION.
MR. GIFFEN ON STRIKES AND WAGES.

Mr. R. Giffen, C. 8., Assistant Secretary to the Board of Trade, gave evicence before the Labour Com- mission on Tuesday. Ile gave some interesting statistics as to the numbers of men, women, and children em- ployed in trades in the whole country, and the wages earned by them. He said the aggregate income in a populati.n of 24 millions fifty years ago was not more than 550 millions sterling, while at the present time the aggregate income in a population of 37 milliona was was from 1,400 to 1,500 millions sterling and the work- ing class share had increased from 200 millions to 630 millions. The average price of commodities was not higher now than it was fifty years ago. Questioned about the effect of strikes, the witness said the losses from this cause only amounted to a fifth or a quarter of 1 per eent. on the whole wages fund of the country. In his opinion the serious effects of the strikes were not so much felt in the direction of a loss of wages as in the destruction of particular branches of trade. He did not think that in the long run the immigration ef aliens into this country caused any substantial reduction of wages; in fact he doubted whether any reduction at all could be traced to that cause. Facts showed that there was a general tendency to shorten the hours of labour, and he considered that an eight-hour day was likely to come of itself in most trades without any legislative in- terference.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY ACTIONS OF A YOUTH.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY ACTIONS OF A YOUTH.

Before the Borough Bench, Alderman Chandley in the chair, on Thursday, a youth named Lionel John Smith, of Padgate, son of Quartermaster Smith, was charged with stealing seven safe keys, from the shop of Messrs. J. C. Sutton, iron mer- chants, Market Buildings. The evidence given was to this effect: The prisoner, who was 14 years of age, went to Messrs. J. C. Sutton with a note pur- porting to come from the Rev. J. Langham, of Pad- gate, whose son he said be was. The note asked that several keys and locks should be sent with the prisoner (described as the son), and the account , sent to the Vicarage at Padgate. The articles were given to the youth. This was on the 10th. On Thursday the 12th, the youth cams again with aaother note for some more keys. The keys were given to him, but when he had gone Mr. Sutton missed two locks and some keys from near where the prisoner had been standing. On the 17th the boy went to the shop again, and ordered a safe to be sent to the Vicarage, for he said his father wanted one to keep the church plate in. Mr. Sutton, who suspected. the boy of having stolen the missing keys, asked him about them, but got no satisfactory answer. Something occurred by which the police got to hear of the affair, and Detective Monaghan went to look for the boy. He found him going to a jeweller's shop with the following note in his hand :—" The Vicarage, Padgate. Dear Sir,—Kindly examine the bearer's watch, and see what's the matter with it. Fix it up for him, and send the account to me.—Yours truly, J. J. Longhorn." The boy tried to destroy the note when the detective caught him. Monaghan afterwards went to the lad's home, 99, Pad- gate-lane, and the keys and locks were found hidden there. The Rev. J. J. Longhorn, who appeared in court, said he did not know the boy. He had only seen him once, and that was when he came to his house and said he ' had formerly been to the Parish Church Sunday Schools; but he had left now, and the Rector of War- rington, the Rev. W. F. Willis, wanted to know if he (Mr. Longhorn) would take the youth to his school. Witness thought this was strange, but he told the youth he should be pleased to see him at the school any time. But the boy never came near the school. The Chairman: What kind of an intellect did the youth strike you as possessing? The Rev. J. J. Langham : He seemed to me to possess the intelligence, and shrewdness of speech of a person ten years his senior. Mr. Sutton next gave evidence, and then the prisoner's mother, a very respectable lady, who seemed much distressed stated that her son appeared to be much addicted to thefts of that charact r. She did not know how to account for it. They had done all they could for him; he had been brought up well, and was a very clever scholar. They were going away to Birmingham on the 31st, and if the Bench would treat the case leniently they would put the boy to a trade. The Chief Constable at this junction produced a rope, some yards lone, which the boy carried about with him. Alderman Sutton, who was on the Bench, thereupon remarked that the boy seemed td be a modern Jack Shepherd, and would have to be looked well after. The Bench spent some time in considering the case, and then inflicted a fine of 20s. and costs or 14 days. The boy was admonished well, and the parents were warned that if they did not see after the youth closely he was likely to get into serious trouble, and bring dis- grace and endless trouble on them. THE AGITATION AGAINST RAILWAY

RATES. The agitation against the new railway rates has caused one big company at least to beat a hasty retreat from a position which, soon or late. it was bound to find untenable. On Monday Mr. Holland Ribbed, a director ef the London and North-Western Railway Co., announced that the old rates for the carriage of milk on that line would be restored this week,and morsover,that the extra amount which has been paid since the beginn- ing of the Hertfordshire County Council, will gladden the hearts of tke dairy-farmers who have to use the London and North-Western line. But hundreds of similar concessions are demanded by over-charged traders and agriculturalists, and there is as yet no indication that the surrender of the railway companies to the force of public opinion will be sufficiently wholesale to be satis- factory.

A meeting in connection with the Lancashire and Cheshire Conference on Railway Rates and Charges was held in the Manchester Town Hall on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Marshall). Representatives were present from Liverpool, Oldham, Bolton, Preston, and many other towns. A resolution was passed expressing regret that the railway companies after giving positive assurances to the contrary at the Board of Trade inquiry, had in a large number of in- stances imposed their maximum rates. It was further resolved to appeal to Parliament in the matter, and to request the Prime Minister to receive a deputation of traders at the earliest possible moment.

-- Mr. Mundella, replying on Wednesday to a deputation of agriculturists and traders in opposition to the pro- posed new railway rates, said the Board of Trade was in constant communication with the railway companies, who, given a little time, hoped to come to a satisfactory arrangement with the traders. He had that morning received a letter from the London and North-Western Railway Company stating with regard to the convey- ance of milk that it had been resolved to revert to the rates enforced prior to the recent revision. If any substantial grievance existed after the companies had had timie to readjust their rates, the Board of Trade would not hesitate to represent the matter to Parliament The Liverpool Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday passed a series of strongly condemnatory resolutions re- garding the action of the railway companies.

Several Radical members have announced their in- tention of blocking all Railway Bills, unless the com- panies consent to modify the new rates for the carriage of goods. SCENES AT THE BOROUGH COURT. ELIZABETH WELSH'S WHISKEY.

div.head: BASHFUL YOUNG MAN.
div.p: A BASHFUL YOUNG MAN.

------- There were two cases with more than a spice of humour in them at the Borough Police Court on Tlsursday. In the first case to the call of Elizabeth Welsh, an old woman, with a thin gaunt face and staring eyes, appeared. She was ragged in dress; her hair was unkempt and as it straggled about her face only lent effect to her generally wild appearance. A. constable told the Bench that some one came run- ning to him at twelve o'clock the previous night, and said" Say, there's an old woman either dead or drunk near the depot at the end of Winwick-road." Despite the fact that this was out of the boundary, the police- man hurried off, and after searching about in the dark he found the old woman "I couldn't tell whether she was dead or alive at first," continued the officer" she couldn't speak, stand, lie down, get up, walk or any- thing." In not being able to move, the old woman struck him as being dead; but he felt assured this was not the sad case when he found she couldn't lie down. After some consideration the officer procured the drunkard's chariot—a barrow—and wheeled her down. "We arrived at the Police Station near one o'clock" resumed the officer, "and then we set to, to examine the prisoner. We thought she was poisoned at first, and we gave her salt and water, but she didn't vomit. By- and-by we thought she was drunk—we knew she was— 'cause there was an odour about her breath which had a way of seeming to emphasise the fact strongly." Somebody suggested was it "as strongly as onion," and there was laughter, "But how came you to think she was poisoned ? " asked Mr. Chandley-the Chairman. "We found a bottle upon her "said the officer" and we thought it was carbolic acid. We examined it and—" . _ _
"Well, was it carbolic acid ? " "No sir."
"What was it then ? "

"It was a bottle of gin sir." Hitherto the old woman said she couldn't hear any- thing. Now her large eves glittered, she bobbed her head up and in a squeaky voice shouted. " Skuse me. It wasn't:' "It was," retorted the constable.
" It wasn't." There was a momentary dead silence after this con- tradiction. The Chairman peered solemnly over at the old woman and said : _ .

"What was it then ?" A tear trickled down her withered cheek ; she looked the chairman reproachfully in the face, and tearfully whimpered: " It was whisky." Some more details respecting the woman's drinking proclivities were given, and then she was fined ss. and costs. The next case was one in which a respectable looking labourer was charged with being drunk in Queen-st., the previous evening, and lying on his back whilst he kicked his legs in the air. It was stated that he had never been in court before, and this must have account- ed for the unsophisticated simplicity of his actions. The Chairman said" What have you got to say sir ?" Frederick laughed a merry laugh ; then seemed to be a little bit abashed at his boldness. He rubbed himself against the box in a cooing kind of way and snig- ' gyred. " He, be, he, Nowt !" He was also fined ss. and costs.

The Chief Inspector of Penitentiaries in Canada has sent to the Minister of Justice a strong protest against the exportation of English criminals to the Dominion. He protests against the unchecked immigration of cockney sneak-thieves and pickpockets,' who are irreclaimable and become a burden on the Canadian tax- papers. The Inspector's protest has created a great sensation in Canada.

THE SMALLPDX OUTBREAK AT RUNCORN.

A special meeting of Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners was held on Saturday morning for the pur- pose of passing such resolutions as might be neces- sary to deal with the outbreak of smallpox. Mr. F. I Wiswall presided, and there were present Messrs. H. J. Once, S. Taylor, J. W. Lightburn, J. Meadow- croft, T. Lea, B. Bisbrown, 0. W. Hankinson, E. W. Humphreys, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (surveyor), and Dr. MacDougall (medical officer). Mr. Lightburn moved "That the offer of Mr. E. D. Jones, on behalf of the Manchester Ship Canal Company to erect four hurs at the hospital for the sum of £45 be accepted; that the Health Committee be authorised to incur such expense in dealing with the outbreak of smallpox as might be necessary." This extra accomoda- don, explained Mr. Lightburn, was in anticipation of any persons suffering from smallpox that might be im- ported into the town. He also should like to propose that the people of Runcorn be invited to be re, vaccinated. .

Mr. Meadowcroft said it was desirable that they should take up this matter vigorously and deal with it with firmness and resolution. This was an evil, which accord- ing to their medical officer, had been imported; it was not a disease which had sprung from any local insani- tary condition of matters; but it was a disease which,he ' understood, had been imported, and these cases were ; not unlikely to occur again on account of the workmen who were travelling into Runcorn from another quarter which had been infected. He should like the Chairman of the Health Committee to have ample powers given to him to exercise his discretion in these matters without the trouble of calling the Committee together —that he should have full liberty of action to take such. steps as he might deem advisable; and he had no doubt. that by a little energy and combinatiorr they wiyald overcome the evil which had fallen upon them.—Thd Chairman said he had no doubt the Chairman of the Health Committee would be prepared to act in an emer- gency. In the past Mr. Lightburn had consulted him (the Chairman) and he had given him his support and advice and he would continue to do so.—Mr. Bisbrown supported the motion, which was carried. Mr. Meadowcroft then moved that the Health Com- mittee be instructed to consider the advisability of appointing a medical officer as superintendent of the hospital, to carry out such duties as the Committee thought fit.—Mr. Humphreys seconded, and suggested that the Health Committee should meet daily until the disease was stamped out.—Mr. Grice supported the resolution and said as a member of the Board and as a member of the community he thought they had every reason to be satisfied with the exertions that were being used. As to their medical officer, he was equal to any condition that may arise if he had only proper power given to him ; if not it would be a reflection upon the members of the Board, if the public should think he was not fit for it. He quite disagreed with any notion like that, and also with the discussions that were put before the public as to there being any negligence, and their only effect was to make people nervous. The Board were,perfectiv satisfied that the best arrangements were being made that could be made. —Mr. Meadowctoft incorporated Mr. Humphreys's suggestion in his resolu- tion, which was carried.

Mr. flankinson moved that Mr. Grice be a member of the Health Committee.—The Chairman said this could not be done without notiec of motion. He was sure that the Committee would be always glad to see Mr. Grice.

It may be said that the ratepayers want the man who is personally the fittest. But then there is an undesirable vagueness about that distinction. Every candidate who comes out thinks lie is the fittest, and there must needs be a demoralising disregard of modesty, if a man were to be con- tinually harping upon his own superior fitness for the office he was aspiring to. IT seems as though there were to be a veritable erusade against adulteration in the coming session of Parliament. Let us hope that it will have a suc- sessful issue. There is quite a crowd of IVI.P.'s who have undertaken to fight in this good cause. It is said that a considerable part of the " fresh " butter which finds its way to our breakfast and tea tables has never been in the interior of a churn, as a kind of explanation, one authority tells 118 that this country imports a sufficient quantity Of margarine to allow 4lbs. per head of the popula- tion, and that we are producing from imported tallow,—known s " oler " to the initiated,---21bs. Per,head of the population per annum. It is in the highest degree desirable that people should know What they are buying when they lay in their stock of provisions. If their palate has been trained to• 4q)preciate margarine and sophisticated tallow let , them have it ; but at the same time when they ask for, and pay the price of, butter "fresh from the dairy " there should be a reasonable assuranc e that they obtain it. There is a movement, 1.430, in favour of compelling butchers to label the foreign meat they may offer for sale. This is, of course, to enable purchasers ims ascer- ; tain whether the beef which is sold to them has been English-fed, or has formed part of an animal ' that has been nourished on the succulent herbage of the American prairies. Mr. YERBURGII, M.P. , for Chester, has gone so far as to propose that hotel or restaurant keepers should announce to their guests when they had prepared foreign beef , for the table. This seems to be carrying the pro- tection of the lio:ne article to an unnecessary and vexatious extent. The fines which the St. Helens magistrates on leesclay imposed upon Dr. DONNELLAN wore a signi- b.?". nt reminder to medical men of their responsi- d! Itiee in connection with the notification of , isease• The St. Helens Corporation had laid four charges against Dr. DONNELLAN of having neglected to notify cases of smallpox, and in regard to each Charge the magistrates imposed the full fine of two pounds and costs, amounting in all, it is said, to twenty-five pounds. There was no denial of I the allegations of the Corporation, but for the I defence it was contended that Dr. DONNELLAN had been influenced by "mistaken notions of kindness;'' toWards the relatives of the sufferers, whose : business as milk-dealers would have been endanger- hail the cases been reported. There can be no . deubt that the notification of disease often leads to serious, and at times to irreparable, losses to People engaged in business, and it is easy to Understand how it is that a sympathetic doctor may !eel disposed to shield a patient. But,after all,the Public good should be the supreme law in this as in either respects. It is next to impossible to success- cope with infectious disease unless the 131.0rept isolation of patients can be secured, and that cannot be obtained without an immediate notification of an outbreak to the Sanitary Auth- °titY• The St. Helens magistrates took this view ef their duties, and their action should have a sMutary effect.

At the Runcorn Police Court, before Messrs. div.p: SAD END OF A RIM:CORN WOMAN.

_ On Sunday the body of a woman was found floating in the Alexandra Dock, Bootle. and was removed to the mortuary attached to the Bootle Hospital, where it was identified. The deceased was Martha Thornhill,the wife of a flat master, who resides at Runcorn. On Friday morning the flat Loire, of which Thornhill was ma wter, was in the Alexandra Dock, and Mrs. Thornhill left for the purpose of purchasing some articles in town. She did not return, and on Saturday morning her basket was found floating in the dock. It is believed that as she was returning to the flat she fell accidentally into the water. Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on the body, on Wednesday. A verdict of "Found drowned," was returned. Go to PRITCHARD'S for the best five guinea watch a work- ingman can have.—Advt. THE LATE DR. MCCIAMERIDGE, OF WIDNES.

Before commencing the debate at Widnes Liberal Club on Monday evening, the chairman (Mr. S. Deacon) paid a high tribute to the character and abilities of the late Dr. McCambridge, and proposed the following resolu- tion :—" rhat the members of the Liberal Club take the opportunity of expressing our deep regret at the irrepar- able loss which has been occasioned to the inhabitants of the town generally, and the Liberals in particular, through the death of Dr. McCambridge. Further we desire to convey to the relatives of the deceased this expression of our heartfelt sympathy with them in their affliction.—Mr. Joseph Morrison seconded the resolution in a highly appreciative speech. The town of Widn es, he said, had lost a very able and good citizen, and the Liberals and members of that club had lost a warm- hearted and sincere friend.—The resolution was carried in solemn silence.

- JOSEPH PRITCHARD has the best stock of ladies' silver and gold watches in the town.—Advt. Sunning DEATH OF A SAILOR AT WESTON POINT. On Monday morning, at 7.45, Henry Gatevog, aged 43 years, seaman and cook on the brigantine Perilla, now lying in the Weston Point Dock, was found dead in his bunk.—James Reynolds, captain, stated that he had known the deceased for five years. He was a Nor- wegian, and had a family living at Limerick. He had been healthy, and on Sunday night, at nine o'clock, was apparently well. He had not been ashore. He slept in the forecastle with William Houston, who noticed him come into his bunk at 10.10, and did not hear anything further of him during the night. The mate—Philip Breslin—finding that he was not up at the time stated above, went into the forecastle and found him in his bunk dead. On Thursday, Mr. J. E. Worsley held an in- quest on the body. Dr. McDougall deposed that he had made a post mortens,and gave the opinion that death was due to suffocation. The condition of the left arm and leg rather pointed to a fit. A verdict that death re- sulted from suffocation was returned. JOSEPH PRITCHARD'S sale shop is 81,Hign-st., nis workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Advt. WIDNES BOYS SENT TO A REFORMATORY.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thurs-da-Y, before Messrs. H. Gaskell, jun., and H. Wade Deacon, three boys, named John Fitzsimons aged fifteen ; Charles Smith, sixteen years of age ; and Samuel Starratt, aged sixteen ; were charged with stealing a quantity of timber from Craig's Works, Widnes Marsh, on Monday night last. 'The prisoners all pleaded guilty, and had been previously convicted,Fitzsimons no fewer than four I times. They were each fined 103. with the alternative of seven days' imprisonment.—Two lads named Patrick Daly, aged -fourteen, and John Donnelly, aged thirteen, were brought up charged with Isreaking and entering the shop of William Palin, grocer, Dugsdate, and stealing goods to the value of 145., on Monday night last. They were also charged with breaking and entering the plumbers' shop at Pilkington's works, and stealing a number of tools therefroni, on the same night. There was a further charge against them of stealing two nip- pers from a cupboard in a shed at Pilkington's works, the goods of two workmen, also on Monday night last. The boys pleaded guilty to the three charges. Both prisoners had been prevously convicted for felony, and they were now committed to gaol for ten days, and be followed by four years' detention in a reformatory.

_ If you want a lucky wedding ring go to 51, litou-sx.,where you will zeta present with it.—Advt. 1 THE EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A BOATMAN AT RUNCORN. 1 Mr. J. E. Worsley held an inquest at the Seamen's Institute, Runcorn, on Saturday, on the body of James , Kershaw, a boatman, 47 years of age, who met with his 1 death under extraordinary circumstances on the pre- 1 vious Thursday. Supt. Atherton was present on behalf ; of the police.—Emma Kershaw, widow, said her husband had suffered from inflammation of the lungs. On Thurs- day afternoon he was under the influence of drink.— P.C. Proctor said he had the summons for the deceased charging him with being drunk and refusing to quit the Stanley Arms. About a quarter to four he found 1 the deceased on the towing path of the Bridgewater Canal at lop Locks. The deceased refused to receive the summons, and witness put it inside his waistcoat. Witness turned round and had walked a few yards, when he heard a splash and some men shouted " He's in the canal." Witness and some byestanders pulled the deceased out after he had sunk once. Deceased was not in the water more than a minute, and he was carried to the cabin of his boat. Witness tried artificial restoration for nearly half-an-hour. Deceased was only out of the water five minutes before he was taken to the fire of the cabin.—Richard Walker, boatman, deposed that after the constable had served the summons upon the deceased the latter staggered back and fell into the canal. It was not until ten minutes after he was rescued that deceased was taken to the fire of his cabin.—Other evidence to a like effect was given.—The Coroner said the constable and others appeared to have done the best they could for the deceased, and to his mind the only verdict they could return was that the deceased died from shock after accidentally falling into the canal.—The jury returned a verdict to that effect. - - -

The funeral took place on Wednesday, at St. Bartho- I lomew's Church, Rainhill, of the Rev. Father Henry r O'Connor. S.J. priest in charge of the mission attached to the colleoe at Ditton Hall, Ditton, near Widnes. The deceased was born at Cashel, in Ireland, on the let of January, 1851. His father was a contractor, and rail- way work took him to Germany. Consequently young O'Connor was educated in that country. He returned to England and entered the ministry of the Catholic Church, being ordained at Ditto., in 1881. He was first appointed to the charge of St. Edward's Church, Bed- ford Leigh, and about eight years ago he was appointed to the mission which was commenced in connection with Ditton Hall. During the time he spent at Ditton, Father O'Connor was much esteemed by the entire population, of all religious beliefs, for his arduous work in connec- tion with educational matters in the township, and with all matters connected with the welfare of the people. He tounded day schools at Ditton, and these have always been looked upon as the best conducted schools in the district. Father O'Connor was secPetary of the Ditton Technical Instruction Committee, and was also a mem- ber of the Ditton Educational Committee. On Wednes- day of last week Father O'Connor caught a severe chill, and congestion of the lungs supervened, and he died at a few minutes past midnight on Sunday. A requiem mass was celebrated at Ditton Church, on Wednesday, before the funeral procession left for Rainhill, and this was attended by the Catholic Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. O'Reilly) and the clergy from Bedford Leigh, TyldesleY, Widnes, Appleton, Warrington, St. Helens, St. Francis Xavier's, Liverpool, Preston, &c. The Rev. C. M. Wool!, _ . .
MA., the Reef-,Or of Ditton Parish Church, was also pre- sent at the service, which was attended by a very large number of tbe laity.

AN BY OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The Rev. J. T. Evans, who has recently been ap- pointed curate of Farnworth Parish Church,besides being a preacher of more than average ability, is a brilliant pianist and composer. About eight months ago he issued his first composition, entitled "The fairy's song to the water babies," dedicated to Mrs. W. H. Barlow, the Vicarage, Islington. The words are from Kingsley's "Water Babies," and are set to a plaintive and pretty melody. Madame Adelina Patti has frequently sung the composition. The latest song of the rev, gentleman is of quite a diffe- rent style, and is entitled "Wind and Wave." The words were written by the Rev. Norman Bardsley. Mr. Evans is a native of South Wales,and previous to his ordination last Advent, he wai a student and chapel organist at the London College of Divinity.

Considering the position of affairs at the recent municipal election at Widnes, the debate at the Liberal Club on the question of the desirability of introducing politics into these local conflicts will doubtless serve a good purpose. Experience would seem to show that politics cannot be kept out of municipal matters, and there is not a Corporation where the Town Council is not broken up into two great camps of Liberal and Conservative. If it is good that Liberals should frame the laws, it is surely just as important that they should administer them. A good and beneficent law may become of ' no avail through weak or negligent administration. Who are the more likely to carry out reforms in a thorough spirit, those who have advocated them for years, or those who have opposed them by every means in their power? The value of administration is seen in several Government departments at the present time. The president of the "Education Department is dealing with the Assisted Education Act and education generally in a far more effective manner than did his predecessor, and the .same re- mark applies to the President of the Local Govern- mentßoard in his administration of the Factory Acts. Reforms are far more likely to be fully and effec- tively carried out by reformers who are the Liberals, than by the leave-things-as-they-are party, the Conservatives. Hence it is good that in municipal matters the Liberal phr.y should use their organisa- tion to secure control of the administration of lucal affairs. It should be remembered in regard to independent candidates that there is an old saying "Scratch an independent and you will find a Tory, and its truthfulness is often demonstrated.

Mr. Asquith, the Home secretary, in a speech at Liverpool last week, showed the importance of administration. In September of last year, he said, it became the duty of the Education Department, under the Act for the establishment of free educa- tion, upon a representation' that in any school dis- trict there was an insufficient supply of free places, to direct the deficiency to be made good. It may be surprising to know that at that day, until three months ago, out of 19,500 elementary schools in England and Wales there were nearly 4,000, nearly one-fifth, which still charged fees. Out ot 5,000,000 children upon the hooks of those schools there were no fewer than 1,125,050, or nearly one-fourth, who were paying fees of from a penny to ninepence a week. It depended entirely upon the spirit in which the department construed its duties under the Act, and the manner in which it carried that duty into effect, whether and how far this state of things should be remedied, and free education became not a sham but a reality. The parents over large parts of the country were wholly ignorant of their rights. In many schools they were told that fees might be abolished if they desired it ; but that the quality of the instruction given would be pro- portionately lower. (Applause.) In other schools only the lower standards were free, with the result had it been allowed to continue—a result,which would have been fatal to popular education—that the parents would be put under the strongest possi- ble inducements to withdraw their children.from school, just after they were beginning to reap the advantages of early study.

In others again—and I fancy something of this kind has happened not 100 miles from Liverpool— fees continued to be charged from indirect motives, and parents were practically told that they could only have free education upon condition that they submitted to a poverty test. A mere hateful form of class distinction it is impossible to conceive. Mr. Arthur Acland,who understands the ins and outs of our educational system as well as any man in Great Britain, has struck a series of blows at those ex- pedients for withholding and fettering the greatest boon which the last House Of Commons conferred upon the country. He has taken care that the rights of the parents shall be clearly explained in plain language, and that that explanation shall be widely diffused and circulated throughout the coun- try. He has insisted that the education given shall be really free, without distinctions of standards, without discrimination of classes, without indirect means in the shape of payment for books or of dues for irregular attendance, whereby the parent would be prevented from enjoying to the full the privilege of the legislation as given. The result is that throughout the length and breadth of the land free education is being brought home to the people. Will the progressive members on the School Boards of Runcorn and Widnes justify their position by talc- ing:action,which clearly they ought to do, in regard to tbe;fees charged in both towns?

The smallpox epidemic in Runcorn, and in the surrounding rural district, is gradually extending instead of dying away. It is satisfactory to find that the Runcorn Commissioners are determined to leave no effort untried in their endeavours to stamp out the disease, and the Rural Authority have also acted with promptitude and determination. The action of the Ship Canal Company in providing temporary hospitals will be a considerable saving to the ratepayers, who, however, will not feel in- clined to grumble at expense if the authorities will ' rid them of the repulsive scourge quickly and effectually. There is such a horror of smallpox, that people will not, unless absolutely compelled, , visit a locality where it is in existence, and this is a serious matter for the shopkeepers. Runcorn Hospital, it would appear from the report of the Commissioners' meeting on Saturday last,has so far been without a superintendent, a most grave on- mission, and it is pleasing to know that such an- official is. now appointed. From rumours that one cannot altogether shut his ears to, there would not seem to he that promptitude in isolating patients that Is desirable ; and the suggestion that the Health Committee should meet daily ought to be carried into effect.

He believed they would hold the same strong position in the future, and he had no doubt that if they worked harmoniously they would benefit not only the Liberal party in the town, but the com- munity at large. In his opinion they ought not only to use this influence in Parliamentary affairs, but also in municipal affairs. They ought to take an interest in all that was going on around them,'and in that way they could do a great deal for the community. In conclusion lie impressed upon the members the necessity of always being ready for a fight, because they had Every Radical Government in power, and when they brought in some of their Radical reforms, an. appeal to the sountry might become necessary. He mentioned that in the past the menibers had not cultivated the literary side and educational side of politics as they might have done, but he hoped when they got settled in suitable premises there would be a new departure taken in this direction.

PRITCHARD'S have now stood the test tor 50 years, andquality and fmt-class workmanship are still guaranteed.--Aidvt. A FARMER'S DISPUTE Kr RUNCORN. At the Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, William Watkifi, farmer, Halton, sued Peter Flodgkinson, also a farmer, of Widnes, for £4 10s., the price of a plough. Plaintiff stated that defendant agreed to purchase the nlough in question, but seven weeks after it had been received he said he would not have it, and wanted plaintiff to take it back, lie ref uqed to do so, as no objection had been made sooner. Defendant contended it was the wrong kind of plough and did not suit him. His Honour, ii giving judgment against the defendant, said any article that was bought and retained in the purchaser's posses- sion for some time without complaint, the law implied that the article was accepted by the purchaser. If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen, take it to PRITCHARD'S.—Advt. WOMEN THIEVES AT WIDNES. _ . _

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Messrs. H. Gaskell and H. Wade Deacon, a married woman named Catherine Tarlton was charged on re- mand with stealing a shawl from the shop of Ann Jamieson, pawnbroker, Anne•st., Widnes, on Saturday night last. The prisoner said she must have been drunk and she did not know what she had done. There was a second charge against the prisoner of stenling several articles of clothing from the pawnshop of Mary unison, Waterloo-road, also on Saturday night. There were three previous convictions against her, and she was fined 20s. in each case, or fourteen days' imprisonment in default.—A young woman named Elizabeth Bushell, was charged with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of James Heys, Widnes, on Saturday last. She pleaded guilty, and was fined 20s. and costs, or fourteen days' hard labour in default.

Jos FM PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to suit all sights from a shilling a pair.--Adrt. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The annual meeting of the teachers of the above school was held in the large vestry, Greenway-road Chapel, on Monday night. The Rev. C. Finch presided. The report read by the secretary showed that on the roll book there were 40 teachers, with an average attendance of nine in the morning and 24 in the afternoon ; 293 scholars, with an average attendance of 55 in the morn- ing and 159 In the afternoon. It was also found that in addition to the ordinary income, which amounted to £6B 13s. 7d., £4O had been raised in the school specially for the building fund of the new premises, making a total of £lOB 13s. 7d. The expenditure was £B2 15s. id. leaving a balance in hand of £25 18s. 6d. The result of the year's working spiritually was fairly satisfactory, but not all that could be desired. After the adoption of the report, Mr. James Sayle was unanimously re-elected superintendent, with Messrs. R. Billidge and T. Booth, assistants. Mr. John Fleet was also re-elected secretary, with Mr. H. Woodward assistant. Mr. Aston was re-elected to the office of treasurer. It is expected that the new school will be ready for opening in June next. ALL HOUSEHOLD LINEN, hemmed and marked, free of charge.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-et.—Advt.

div.head: CHESHIRE LIBERAL UNIONIST ASSOCIATION.
div.p: CHESHIRE LIBERAL UNIONIST ASSOCIATION.

The Duke of Westminster presided at Chester on Satur- day over the annual meeting of the Cheshire Liberal Unionist Association. There was a very meagre attend- ance, only 13 members being present. The statement of accounts showed a balance on the right side of £4l. The annual report stated that the members "might look back with satisfaction," but did not give the members much encouragement, as while it had not a Single victory to chronicle, it was cotstrained to deplore the loss of a seat at Stockport, the increase of the tiladst?n- ian majcrity at Crewe and Northwich, and the reduction of the Unionist majority in Eddif,bury. In moving a resolution in favour of the association embracing the whole of Cheshire, instead of being mainly confined to Mid and West Cheshire, the Duke of Westminster said that the Government had a very difficult job on hand, inasmuch as its majority embraced very conflicting opinions. Great Britain was against Home Rule, and England was very decidedly so, but it was necessary for the Unionists to continue their organisation on the same lines as hitherto, or even on better lines.—The resolution was seconded by Mr. J. Naylor (Beeston) and adopted, 55 was also the following resolution :—" That in the opin- ion of this meeting it is desireable that the operations of the Cheshire Liberal Unionist Associations shall be extended and enlarged so as to include the whole of tue county of Chester, and that other Liberal Unionist Associations within the county be invited to federate with the proposed county associations, which shall henceforth be styled the Cheshire County Liberal Union- ist Association." The Duke of Westminster was elected president of the new association.

div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of Runcorn Liberal Club was held in the Billiard-room. Bank Chambers, on Wednesday night. Mr. A. R. Norman presided and there was a good attendance. Mr. A. Riley, the secretary, read the annual report, which showed that the year had been a prosperous one, and the number of members had been increased by 20. There were now 240 members. With regard to the financial position there was a balance in hand of £45 12s. 11d.—The Chairman in moving the adoption of the report, said they hoped that something would transpire that would enable the club to have more suitable pre- mises, and premises that would be more productive of comfort for the members. Since the last annual meet- ing, they had had a General Election, and they could congratulate themselves that they in Runcorn did their share in producing the magnificent result of the election in Northwich Division. (Applause.) They knew the high position the Liberalism of Runcorn held, and the stand they took in the Northwich Division, and he was certain that the existence of the club tended to strengthen them in an election campaign. He never saw the ' Liberals in the town, and the members of the Club Ilespecially, put their shoulders to the wheel like they did lat the last election. There was tie doubt about it they worked very well indeed, and for the magnificent majority obtained by their member Mr. 13runner, they could without any qualms of conscience take a considerable part of the credit. (Hear, hear.) They I had had a change of Government. Lord Bartington had a stated that if any gentleman had not actually known eif the change otherwise than by the things that had taken place he would not have been aware of it. He (Mr. Norman) did not agree with that. All people who had had their eyes open had had string evi- dence that they had a change of Government, not only in name, but in action. In all Government depart- ments there had been a stirring of dry bones, and the Government were showing that they had net made any promise they did not intend to fulfil, and that they were keeping good faith with the country, and would strive to carry out the wishes of the electorate. (Applause.) He hoped the members of the Club would keep together, and that the club would flourish in the future as it had done in the past, and that it would continue to be a tower of strength to Liberalism in Runcorn, and through Runcorn in the Northwich Division. (Applause.) They were looked upon as the backbone of the Northwich Division and other parts of the division expected a great deal from the town, and he did not think that hitherto they had

div.head: CORPORATION MODEL LODGINGHOUSES FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: CORPORATION MODEL LODGING- HOUSES FOR WARRINGTON.

The Warrington Corporation. is considering the advisability of erecting a model lodging-house in the town after the plan of those in several large towns. A deputation consisting of Mr. Whittle, Town Clerk, Dr. Gornall and others visited Liver- pool yesterday, and investigated the Corporation "models "there. It is acknowledged that Warrington is in need of such institutions for certain sections of the labouring classes. Besides providing poor people with comfortable and healthy accommodation at low prices, the establishment of these Corporation houses, which would be under corporation supervision, would strike at the root of one of the worst features of this town, and that is slum property. The Corporation have full power to launch into the matter, and as the "models " would provide a weekly turnover the outlay in thei erection would not be much felt.

At the invitation of the London County Council, a number of ladies and gentlemen on Wednesday after- noon visited Parker-st., Drury-lane, where an experi- mental "municipal lodging-house" has been erected by the Public Health and Housing Committee of the Council. The establishment has been prepared to ac- commodate 328 men with lodgings. They will be housed in separate compartments. which are Bfl. high, 7ft. long, and 4ft. wide. The roof], are lit by elec- tricity. The house also contains a large general room, a kitchen, a library, a shop for the sale of cheap provisions, and a lavatory fitted with baths. The work of erecting the building was put out to tender, and the cost had been kept within the amount of the contract-214,300. The furnishing had cost £1,250, and with the addition of £3,700, the value of the site, ' and £l,lOO for architects' commission, a total of £20,350 was reached. To secure a return of three per cent. on this, and such a sinking fund as would ordi- narily be required to replace the cost of building in eighty years, a yearly gross income of £2,450 was re- quired. To meet this the Council had fixed the charge for a bed at sth a night. He concluded by defending the erection of the house, and traversing the objections which bad been raised against it.

EARLESTOWN HARRIERS. The Second meet of the season took place en Saturday afternoon from the Wargrave Inn, under favourable circumstances The meet was not quite so large as the previous week, but a most enjoyable run was experienced. The route taken lay over several ploughed fields across country, through Newton and part of Hayclock, round by , the racecourse, along the canal bank and home, J. Twist finishing first. The distance coveted was about five mile, and the time occupied 42 minutes, which is a creditable programme considering the heavy going. A paper chase has been arranged for Saturday. div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. J. E. BIRTLES.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. J. E. BIRTLES.

On Thursday at the Ebenezer Baptist Chapel, Bacilli, the marriage of Mr. John Edward Birtles, eldest son of Mr. Thomas Birtles, photographer, Legh House, Warrington, was celebrated. The bride was Miss Alice Shepherd, third daughter of Alderman George Shepherd, J.P., late mayor of Bacup. The bridesmaids were Miss Florence Birtles, sister of the bridegroom, and Miss Annie Shepherd, sister of the bride. The best man was Mr. Reginald Birtles, brother of the bridegroom. The bride was attired in white Bengaline silk, trimmed with lace, the bridesmaids wearing cream empire dresses, trimmed with pale green, with hats to match, and carried shower bouquets. On entering the church the choir sang " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," Mr. Law presiding at the organ. The bride was given away by her father. After the ceremony the wedding breakfast was served in the billiard room at Holmes Villa, the residence of the bride's father. Those present were mostly relatives of the bride and bridegroom, there being also a few invited guests. Several toasts were proposed and acknowledged. The bride and bridegroom after- wards left Bacup for London and Brighton where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's presents include set of cutlery and cheque, Alderman Shepherd ; silver tea and coffee service, Mrs. Shepherd ; dinner service, Miss Annie Shepherd ; bed- room suite, oak table, amd clock, Mr. and Mrs. Birtles ; silver dinner cruet, Councillor and Mrs. Law ; china tea service; Councillor and Mrs. Browne (Warrington); case of silver dessert knives and forks, Mr. and Mrs. J. div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.

We are by no means yet quit of the small-pox epidemic. Fourteen cases occured last week in the town, the victims being chiefly persons residing in houses where the disease had previously been. One or two serious eases, however, have been dis- covered. One was an especially serious one, and came from a local lodging-house, where it is said, an attempt was made to conceal the case. The man was in the last stages of the disease when discovered. The affair has created some concern in the town and a summons has teen issued upon the individual concerned in the attempted conceal- ment. It is expected he will be brought before the Borough Bench, on Monday. The question now raised is, will this be right considering the per- son has ben in recent contact with an infected person. Outside the borough the disease is prevalent at Stockton Heath, and as the patients cannot be iso- lated through the lack of hospital accommodation, the residents of tne neighbourhood are by no means feeling comfortable. The infected man who was found walking about in his night-dress one night, was buried on Tuesday; but another dis- tressing case of a victim being at large occurred la,t Saturday night. A Ship Canal man, who was in a pretty advanced stage of the disease came with his wife to Warrington. He was discovered on Sunday and isolated. . -

Thei:e are also some bad cases at Sankey Bridges, outside the Borough. The went of proper hospital accommodation is also preventing proper treatment to these cases, and some indignation is expressed at the action the Rural Sanitary Authority took some time ago, in refusing to participate in the maintenance and use of the Warrington hospital. Stockton Heath is in the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority district, and, of course, removal: to any hospital in Runcorn is practically impossible. div.head: AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AT WARRINGTON.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN

I am sorry to say that there seems to be some danger of the early closing system in Warrington collapsing. On Thursday afternoon all the boot and shoe dealers in the town had their premises open for the first time since the half-holiday closing was adopted. I have observed that several shops in other lines of business that were closed at first on Thursday afternoon are now open. Avarice and instability, I fear, will probably do their work in time,and the pleasant Thursday afternoon move- ment will be at an end.

Smallpox has not yet left us. It seems that there were 14 cases last week and it is said that in every instance it is those who have not been re-vaccinated who are "catching it." With a remedy so simple, so cheap, and as has been I ully established as the result of the experience gained in Warrington, so efficacious, why will some people still continue to neglect their duty in this respect? One cannot help being reminded of "Zarlyle's " brief but emphatic description of the numbers and mental quality of the population of this country.—" Mostly iools,"—when one reflects upon the situation.

It has often struck me that a good deal might be done to improve the appearance of our park. That wooden unpainted partition between the boys' and girls' gymnasia is a very ugly eyesore, I think, and if railings were substituted it would be much better, and I don't suppose the children of the two sexes would be much the worse for being able to catch a sight of each other. The Park Committee seem to have as objection to railings or I fancy they would have preferred these for the bandstand instead of the heavy brick-coloured enclos- ing wall which encircles the musicians when they use the building. I think a few more trees wculd be an advantage in the grounds and do something to cut it off from the outside manufacturing world which impinges so closely and obnoxiously upon it. I must confess that I think his honour Judge Ffoulkes, was decidedly in the wrong the other day, in not allowing Mr. Jenkins to take the oath in the County Court with uplifted hand, without kissing the Testament, according to the formula now permitted by Act of Parliament. Judge Ffoulkes said that a witness could not avail him- self of this form unless he had a religious objection to the oath, and that as Mr. Jenkins desired to re- frain from kissing the book to avoid ali danger of infection with smallpox he could not be permitted to swear in that way. If this were the case the Act would be a dead letter, because it was passed expressly to meet Mr. Ffoulkes's objection, which would have been perfectly valid under previous legislation. Mr. Jenkins had a perfect right to make the demand, and his Honour could have been compelled to comply with it.

Here is a word of warning to local Sunday School superintendents ard managers. At the Padgate Wesleyan Sunday School tea party, held on Thurs- day evening, a dialogue was to have been given by a number ot scholars. This came to the ears of the village magnate—the policeman—and he warned the managers of the school that if they ventured n upon that armless little entertainment, without a theatrical license, they would be brought beioretba justices of the peace. This, I believe, would have been in aczordance with the law. lijelloomewhere I have seen the law described as a " bass.' Maybe it is ; maybe it isn't. But from ray personal know- ledge of the law, I can assure all Sunday School managers who would now submit a dialogue with- out a license, that the law has got the obstinacy of the" hass,rwithout its modifying virtue of patience. For my own part, I should prefer to know of an Act which forbade "Chairman's address," rather than what is usually about the pleasantest part of an entertainment.

So the testimonial to Sir Gilbert Greenall is a "frost "—a " killing frost." The poverty-stricken, attenuated, decimated and utterly forsaken Liberal Association did manage to raise quite a respectable sum—about £l5O —in token of its admiration for Dr. Houston, but the wealthy, aristocratic, purse- proud and blue blooded Consei vative party.who pro- fess such unbounded admiration for " dear Sir Gilbert," have raised such a magnificent sum of money, that it won't even run to a " statue " although something might have been got quite cheap (and good) enough for the purpose. The Testimonial„Committee, finding that the heart of the Tory workingman has not responded sufficiently generously for a " statue," have decided upon a " bust." A" bust "is no uncommon thing at the Emporium of all the Virtues in Sankey-street, and I did hope that on this occasion we should have had a full-sized article. " 414 c transit."

The reputation of Warrington Town Councillors does not improve very much. The St. Helens folk say they (the Warrington Councillors) are a "thirsty lot "and if the rumour is correct that the depute- iion which recently visited St. Helens consumed over .£4 worth of " liquor " then undoubtedly the appellation is fully justified. But then we are a "thirsty town." We keep two big breweries and several little ones agoing, also a host of pubs, beer- houses, and off-licenses. We give " sweeties "to the children on a Sunday so that we may get their parents' custom and altogether we do our level best to keep the " trade " in a flourishing condition. True,one or other of the Dissenting parsons becomes extravagant in his language occasionally as to the enormities committed under the noses of " good " people and which the police seem either unable or unwilling to prevent,but we take no notice of these wild outbursts because nearly all the Church par- sons are dumb on the subject—what matters it to them if the Trade is doing its "devilish and destrue tive work" (vide Lord Randolph), they get money for their churches and schools and are therefore consciously blind. At the same time it would be interesting to know who were the members of the Council that formed the deputation to St. Helens, and isithe statement referred to correct ? I hope some enterprising Town Councilbr will put a ques- sion at the next monthly meeting on the subject.

A funny incident occurred the other day. The Committee, acting under the advice of their medical officer,have erected a barricade at each end ' of the Smallpox Hospital right across the street so as to prevent people passing and re-passing in the immediate neighbourhood of the hospital. Of course the object of this is palpable—to prevent conta- gion. There is a small door to each of these bui- -1 cades to admit the doctors and staff and those per- sons whom duty compels to be in attendance on the victims of this pestilential disease. Will it be ' believed that a member of the Town Council, actu- ally forced his way, through the barricade the other day in spite of the protests of the man in charge, and not being satisfied with that, it is said, he actually brought the matter before the Health Com- mittee a few nights ago as a "grievance l'" It is stated that his reception at the hands of the Com- mittee was a "warm" one,that he was informed that the Committee would not allow even a Town Coun- cillor to jeopardise the public health by such absurd and reckless conduct, and that if he again attempted to pass the barricade he "should be chucked out. The excuse of the sapient indivi- dnal was that he had frequently to go to Longford and could not afford the time to go round Stamford- st. The extra time involved would not be five minutes.

div.head: MERLIN.
div.p: MERLIN.
WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

It is said that several Warrington traders have already begun to derive advantage from the service of steamers between London and Saltport. By using this new means of transport a great caving it effected. An instance of this is to be found in the case of Messrs. John Geddes and Sons, tea merchants, who have now had two large consignments of tea from the bonded warehouse in London by the Manchester Ship Canal. The tea is conveyed to Saltport by the service of steamers mentioned, and then by the river to Howley. Messrs. Geddes by this means effect a saving of about 18s. a ton as compared with the railway charges. In the new railway rates, the carriage of tea is fixed at about 4s. Bd. a ton more than was formerly paid, CO that to have an alternative and a much cheaper means of carriage is a matter of great importance to firms like Messrs. Geddes.

div.head: BEFO RE THE MAWTRATES.
div.p: BEFO RE THE MAWTRATES.
Tot's A-Cou).—AN UNHAPPY NEGRO.

At the Warrington Borough Sessions, on Monday, John Wilson, a negro, a poor harmless-looking man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st. on Sunday afternoon. A constable said he was annoying the driver of the horses of a menagerie passing through the town, with which establishment he had been connected.—The defendant said he was trying to get his money from the proprietor of the menagerie, as he wanted to get to Liverpool with his little sister, aged four, in order to get back to his country, England being too cold for them. Ile was dismissed on promising to go to Liverpool._ THHFT OF A WATCH BY MILITIAMEN.

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Cepeley, a Londoner,Mark Reynolds, and Albert Bennett militiamen, were charged with acting in concert in stealing at the Black Horse Inn, from the person of Henry Shepherd, an army ressrve man, a Waterbury watch, value 17s. 6d.—The Chief • Constable said the three prisoners came from Liverpool, and were stationed at Orford Barracks. The complainant Met them and Wsked them the way to the barracks. Copeley asked him into the inn, and each of the defendants paid for a quart. Then Copeley asked the complainant the time, and when he pulled out his watch snatched it and broke the chain. He handed it to Reynolds, and Reynolds handed it to Bennett. shepherd asked for his watch, and Copeley got up ancisquarea at hini,wanted to fight, and threatened to hit him with a forne. Efe went to P.C. Corcoran, who came back with him to the inn, but the prisoners had gone. He apprehended them at the Rodney, and it was found that they had pawned the watch in Winwick-st.. for 33.—Evidence was given by John Byrne, pawnbrokers-assistant, P.C.' Corcoran,and! the complainant. Copeley said he and the other pri- soners having stood . a quart apiece, Shepherd wanted tnern to pledge the watch that he might stand one. They went out and pawned, it, but spent the money on the way from the pawnbrokers' instead of coming back to the Black Horse. They were sent to jail for a month's hard labour each.

Monnar.—Before the Mayor (Alderman GreenaU) in the chair and Messrs. F. Monks, J. Geddes, J. W. Hay- ward, and S. Wright. DNIINI AND DISORDERLY. —Martin Quinn, labourer, *id Road, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting Catherine Cayley, in the Old Road, Latchford, on Saturday night.—A police sergeant said he ran at the woman and knocked her down, and then continued his abuse of her, and it was all witness could , do to pull him off. The defendant said both the woman and her daughter hit him on the top of the head with a poker, and he could not stand that. 10s.and costs, or 14 days' hard labour.—Thomas Canning, shoemaker, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Baketmuse Yard. It was stated that he had assaulted two boys.— The defendant denied the charge, but was fined ss. in- cluding costs. Mr. Jenkins, by whom the defendant was employed, asked the Bench to forgive the defendant as he had been a hard-working man, and hitherto of irreproachable character.—To pay costs, 7s. 6d.
