THROWING MISSILREI IN THE STRIZETS.—Joseph Leyland, labourer, 28, Orchard-street, was charged with throwing potatoes on the 16th inst., to the danger of passengers, in the Market Place. He was fined h.—Patrick Farring- ton, son of William, 83, Boyle-street. was charged with discharging stones from a catapult to the danger of passengers on the previous Tuesslay morning, in Bath- street. P.C. Robinson having given evidence against the defendant, the latter called a boy as a witness, who said the officer started kicking him.—The constable denied this.—A young lady, living with Mrs. Tunstall, corroborated the lad as to the kicking, and said the officer took him by the scruff of the neck and kicked him very severely. The constable said he spurred the boy with his foot, but did not hurt him.—The Chief Con- stable: The days are gone by for kicking.—P.C. Robin- son : It wasn't a kick.—The Mayor: Better make a note of this for nest Thursday.—Mr. Hunt : I shall have to make a note of it, sir.—The case was dismissed. DRIINRENNESS.—James Birchall, a labourer, was fined for drunkenness on Saturday, and on Wednesday Mrs. Annie Williams, a respectable married woman, of St. Mary's-road, Latchford, was fined for a similar offence.
Farnar.—Before Councillors Fleming (in the chair), and

H. Roberts. STiALING SCRAP—James Dtvereux, ,labourer, Pad- gate, was charged with stealing a quantity of firewood and an axe, the property of the D *Ham Forge Company, on Wednesday evening. It was stated that the prisoner, who was employed in the forge, took the articles from amongst a quantity of " scrap." As he was leaving the forge, Sergeant Lawrence observed the prisoner with the articles beneath his coat. Prisoner, who pleaded guilty was lined 10s. or in default seven

days. DRUNILENNESS.—Sarah Ann Fleming, of Dial-st., was charged with drunkenness the previous night. She was fined 561. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment. DEFRAUDING THE CHESHIRE Li NES COMMITTEE RAILWAY CO.—ThOITIRS HATTOp, a soldier, of Liverpool, was charged with travelling on the 9 30 train, Cheshire Lines Committee, on Thursday nig,ht, without a ticket, and with intent to defraud the company. One of the com- pany's officials stated that when the train arrived in the station he found the defendant asleep in one of the compartments. He awakened him, and prisoner walked on to the platform and sat down. He was asked for his ticket, but denied having travelled on the train. He was given into custody. Fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. Wont") BREAK HIS LITTLE HEART.—Benjamin Jaun- drell, of Warburton-st., and James Riley,also of Warbur- ton-st. ; two boys of about 12 years of age,were charged with stealing a box of sweets from a stall in the market, owned by Mr. Newton. Both boys are in the habit of frequenting the market both day and night. Market In- spector Place, who proved the case, said that when he took the boys into the office, and charged them with the offence, the boy Riley seemed much distressed, He cried bitterly and said " Oh, Master Place, it will brake my fickle heart." The boys were ordered to be detained in the Bridewell for a day, and receive six strokes of the birch rod. A DEFAULTING 'Bus DRIVEL—Joseph Curran, a licensed 'bus driver was charsed with defaulting the bye-laws by refusing to run his vehicle, on Saturday night, at the times arranged by the Watch Committee. Evidence was given by Inspector Bowen and several constables showing that defenlant stopped an unneces- sari, length of time in tho read Opposite the Hop Pole. 1 When remonstrated with the de.T:dant refused to move. He was under the lane-ice of drink, and very noisey.— Fined ss. and costs. AN ECONOMICAL " Busiont."—:t harles Cotterill, Albert- st.,was charged with travelling in! the L.N.W. Railway, on Saturday night between Wigan and Warrington , without a ticket. Detective Osborne stated that the

defendant came by the 11 18 train from Wigan. He loitered about the platform for close upon an hour, and then attempted to get by the ticket collector. When thus discovered he said ha-get his living_ by "busking;" be was poorly off, and thought the company could better afford.to lose a shilling than he could afford to pay one. Fined ss. and costs, or seven days' imprison- ment. ABSENTING AEPRENTICES.—EIIen Barrow, Priestly-st., Margaret Chrimes,Portiand-street,and Mary Ellen Cain, Friars' Green, all apprenticed to Mr. Platt, master fastian cutter were summoned for unlawfully abs'enting themselves froth work. The cases were adjourned for one month.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTON BANGRRS T. BIRKENHEAD Sr. ANNE'S— The return match between these two clubs took place at Lovely-lane on Saturday. St. Anne's losing the toss, commenced operations against the strong wind, the ball going in touch. From the line-out the Rangers broke away and reached the visitors' lines. St. Anne's, how- ever,retaliated,and a fine passing run looked like-scoring when Jackson tackled Finch. The homesters improved their position, and the oval becoming loose Monks got I bold, and smartly handing over to Savage the latter scored a good try, the goal kick hitting the bar and re- bounding into play. From the drop-out St. Anne's strove hard to equalise, but the defence left nothing to be desired, and at half-time the score was—Rangers, one try, one minor; St. Anne's nil. After the interval the game continued to be splendidlv contested, both , ends being attacked in turn. Eventually, the heavy ground began to tell upon the visitors, who relaxed in their endeavours • whilst, on the other hand the home team played with greater dash, and the climax wat reached when Warburton secured in mid-field and sent the ball across to Massey, who kicked, and racing down the open again got possession and ran in a grand try. The visitors now seemed to be over-pl., ved, but with the exception of minors they repelled any further inva- sion, the Rangers winning an interesting game by two tries, three minors, to nil.
WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER.

This return match was played at Wilderspool on Stitur- day. Neither team had indulged in a game since they met on December 26, when after a finely contested game our local club managed to account for the Mancunians, winning by a goal and a try to a penalty goal. The enforced idleness had affected both teams, as, judging from their display on Saturday, although it was a rare exhibition, there were several points which lacked that finish one really expects from first-class organizations. Of course want of practice was the caase, but we hope now that the frost has gone, Warrington will remedy the defects and go on adding victories to their already long list.

There would be a gate of 3,000 when Turner kicked off almost at punctual time, and Woods, aided by a strong wind, found Boscow's return not so effective as usual. Scrimmages ensued, and Bate foiling Mullintux, play varied between the quarter flags. Eventually, Manchester gained a footing well inside the Warrington quarters, Woods being the leading operator. Twice the visitors showed pretty passing, but in both instances Winces, was at fault. Still Manchester pursued the attack, and when they looked like scoring, Turner inter- cepted, and a brilliant run and a decent chance to Webster saw the tall Warrington three-quarter failing to gather. The effort was applauded, realizing as it did the half-way, and then ancther bout of passing by Evans, Heesom, and Lawless saw Warrington's position still further improved. Steel, Smith, Woods. and Jones defended brilliantly, and a spell of attacking by the homesters was succeeded by Jones kicking to half-way, and although Lawless retaliated the city men would not be denied, and Warrington being penalized tile kick culminated in Boscow touching down. Heesonz got out of difficulties with credit, and then Ashton, Jolley, and 1 Nevins dribbled well, being repulsed in the nick of time by Mullineux. Bate dribbled nicely along the reserved touch, whilst Evans lost an opening a moment later, when he parted unselfishly to Webster, who was grassed by Steel. Getting the better of some loose scrimmaging, the visitors forced the oval at the railway end, and when Smith looked almost certain to score Ashton appeared on the scene and a safe tackle upset calcula- tions. lbscow met a kick of Mullineux's, and Coghlan and Smith took play under the home posts. Nevins boldly dribbled away ,and short passing being started by the same player the quarter flag was reached. War- rington' however, could not clear to their liking, and Heesom eesom bad a kick charged matters presented a bad aspect. Louden made his mark and Woods essayed a shot at goal, but it was no go, Webster piloting back to the quarter Bag. Evans intercepted a pass intended for Woods, but the county player grassed his man before he had travelled far. Another pretty piece of com- bined play by Bate, Evans, Heesom, and Lawless reached the Manchester line, but this was Warrington's final visit to this half, for by judicious kicking Jones and Mullin- eux reached Warrington quarters. Boscow now showed something like his proper forra,and an effort deserved all the applause it elicited. Manchester appeared certain scorers when he snapped the oval from their feet and cot out of a difficulty in smart manner. Tharniley, Donohue, Berry, and Ashton were prominent in some tough seri minages, and Woods intercepted a pass from Heesom, the home goal having a narrow escape. Holmes and Berry led up a dribble which partially relieved, and then Woods kicked brilliantly, the second minor bringing about half time with nothing substantial on the score sheet. There now prevailed a consenses of opinion as to what the ultimate result would be, for Warrington had the immense advantage of the wind, and as matters turned out, the prognostications were correct. Cameron's kick off was met by Webster, ard Jolley and Ashton taking up the running Manchester fell hack on their lines direct. Wild passing by the homesters lost them ground, and then a fine piece of play by Steel brought forth a ringing cheer from all parts of the ground. Bate,Evans, Heesom, and Webster passed beautifully, and the game was waged on the verge of the visitors' line, and when Bata got nicely away from a scrimmage a score to that player appeared a certainty, but somehow he lost pos- session, and Jolley being in attendance an easy try fell to that player's credit, while Heesom sent up the first goal of the new year at the first time of asking. Boscow met the restart in fine form, but Wincey was at fault and Manchester were again hard pressed. So determined were Warrington in their attack that minors fell in quick succession. Turner made his mark on one occasion, and, following up, dribbled single-handed to Steel, who re- pulsed the Warringtonians. Mullineux gave Winsey a pass which he failed to utilise, whilst a daring save by Bate spoiled an attempt at relief by Coghlan and Lou- den. Bate and Evans passed repeatedly, and Lawless slipped once when he had cleared opposition. Ashton next took a free kick, but nothing came of it. Steel
,tar...l4ti.) 1.,-.2:nlta
6'l liitY (7,

leffected a fine relief, and the Warringtonians cheered heartily at his performance, but they, had scarcely sub- sided before Smith, Evans. and Nevins exchanged, the last-named testing the Manchester custodian, but this time he was sadly at fault, and Bate ran in a soft try, Heesom hitting the posts in his place. Another minor fell upon an effort, by Jolley, Holmes, and Bate, and on the stroke of time, Webster put in a brilliant run along touch,kicking over Woods'g head,and racing up,regained possession, scoring at the corner. Turner failed. Final : Warrington, 1-2-2; Manchester, 0-0-2. ' Teams :—Warrington; J. Boscow, back; H. Webs- ter, F. Heesom, and P. R. Lawless, three-quarters; John Evans and John Bate, half-backs;' H. Ashton, Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, T. Donohue, W. Berry, J. Holmes, J. T. Thorniley, and H. Teare, forwards. Man- chester : W. B. Steel, back ;D. C. Woods G. P. Win- cey, an C. L. Jones, three-quarters; M. Mullineaux and T. Wilkinson, half backs; G. N. M. Cameron, P. Steel, J. H. Smith, K. P. thrifty, W. G. Hogg, D. C. Hampson, F. Dodson, J. E. Louden, and H. G. Coghian, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. W. Clegg, Wigan. WARRINGTON A T. MANCHESTER A.—At Whalley Range Manchester started against a blustering wind, a dribble by Birley forcing Warrington to defend. Though the visitors had to defend so early they cleverly recovered the lost ground, a couple of beautiful runs by Bate carrfing the warfare to the home quarter flag. Lally and Lawless then took up the running, but Manchester gained relief, when a kick by Ashurst rolled dead. A fine bit of play by Lawless ensued, and after Molyneaux kad almost rushed over, Bate got hold by a pass from Lally, and, dodging his opponents, secured the first try. The home team were then severely pressed, Bate per- forming splendidly. Little, on behalf of Manchester, however, cleared finely,' but Warrington, who were playing four threequarters, showed some delightful pas- sing all along the line of backs, with the result that Potts ran over in vigorous fashion. Manchester then improved their position by dribbling to midfield, where Bate seized posseession,and, after having feinted to pass the leather, dashed away, dodging his opponents splendidly, and gained a brilliant try between the posts, which Barnes converted. The Warrington forwards, who had been playing extremely well, continued to adopt the heeling-out process, and the backs utilising the chances by splendid bouts of passing, quickly pressed their antagonists. Massey gently tapping the ball over an opponent's head, and deftly regaining it, scored a splendid try far out. Still Manchester had little respite, for Davies, Monks, Higham, and Edwards, made their presence felt by.rushing,to the line, a couple of minors accruing, and half-time arrived with War- rington 1-3-3 to nil. Warrington slipped away from the restart, the forwards dribbling into Manchester quarters. and in a short time Davies scored. Matters now took a different turn, a splendid run by Jones transferring the contest to midfield, and Little having the leather passed to him ran in finely, for Harby to place a goal. Then Edwards, Hampson, and Iligham showed up prominently, but danger threatened when Vichoff was seen careering away with the ball, until a grand tackle by Bailey stopped his onward rush. Barnes regained the lost advantage, though it looked as if Little was going to repeat his previous performance until swamped by superior numbers near the line. Some fine play by Achurst, Bailey, Eden, and Davies ensued, and from some lusty forward play Monks al- most ran over. A run by Barnes was followed by some exhilarating work, the rapid manner in which the ball travelled about being very exciting, and then Massey made a splendid run to the line from half way. Hare Bate again hoodwinked his watchful opponents, obtain- ing his third try. Immediately after the restart Jones intercepted a pass, and scudding down the ground got clear away, with Massey in hot pursuit. An exciting race ensued, but Massey grandly overhauled his man when within a few yards; of the coveted rut. Ashurst, Lawless, and Potts speedily cleared the danger, and the sound of the whistle brought ths game to a finish, with Warrington winners by 1-5-4 to 1.0-0.
WARRINGTON JUNIOR LEAGUE COMPETIFION.

LATCHFORD V. STOCKTON BEATH.—Played at Latchford, on Saturday, before about 400 spectators. Deacon kicked off for Latchford against a strong wind, and Stockton Heath failing to return the first scrimmage took place in their 25. Stockton Heath broke away and took the ball well in the Latchford quarters, the good defence of Latchford keeping them from scoring. With a com- bined rush Latchford changed the venue, when some tight scrimmages took place. After some exchange kicking, Broady made his mark, Latchford charging the kick, Stockton Heath saving. After some give and take play. Stockton Heath were granted a free kick, and the ball went in touch at the Latchford 25 flag. Latchford were not to he denied, and with a grand rush invaded Stockton Heath quarters. Hughes. receiving a pass, dropped at goal, the ball just going outside the post. Soon after this the whistle went for half time, neither' Lside having scored. Stockton Heath restarted, and Houghton returning, the ball was soon near the Stockton Heath line. After some exchange kicking Latchford forced a minor. The drop out did not avail Stockton Heath much relief, as the ball was soon back on their line, and from a scramble over the line Houghton scored, Starkey failing at the place. Soon after the drop out Broady received a pass in his own 25, and, dashing through, looked dangeaous,but Starkey proved a stumb- ling-block, tackling him in fine style. Latchford soon had the ball back again on the Stockton Heath line, but the latter' s defence was good. After somegive an take play, Latchford was awarded a free kick, from which starkey made a good bid for goal. Soon after this Hughes received a pass, and dropped a grand goal. Result: Latchford, one goal (dropped), one try ; Stock- ton Heath, nil. Referee, Mr. Frank Turner, Warring- ton F. C., whose decisions gave every satisfaction.

RUNCORN RILITOBAS V. RUNCORN RECS.—This match was played on the Irwell-lane enclosure on Saturday be- fore a goid number of spectators. When the teams faced each other they were as follows :—Rangers, full back, C. H. Cook ; three-quarter, H. Hughes, J. Butterworth, (Captain) and A. Houghton ; half backs, E. Woodward and J. W. Johnson ; forwards' T. Woods, J. Brennan, W. Sutton, W. Russel, W. Hough, E. Chaney, J. Helsby, F. Johnson, and R. Harrison. Recreation, full back, R. Worrall ; three-quarters, S. Brimelow; J. Lightfoot, J. Leathwood ; half backs, W. Nickson and M. Kenwright ; forwards, Summerfield, Darwall, Purslow, Mottram, Pusql, Tickle, Banner, T. Banner, and another. Summerfield losing the toss the Recs. kicked off at 3.15 with strong wind at their backs. Houghton returning well, play settled in midfield fora ' few minutes, when Woodward kicked well into the Recs.' 25, and Worrall being tackled by Russell, before he could return the Rangers got dangerously near the Recs.' use. The Recs. however worked back into the Rangers' quarters, and Lightfoot intercepting a pass from Wood- ward ran nicely until pulled by Hughes. The Recs. pressed, but Cook saved smartly with a kick to touch, Hughes bounding the ball into play, dodged through the Recs.' backs easily, and planted the ball across the line in good position, Butterworth's kick at goal failing. Half time score, Rangers 1 try, Recs. nil. After the restart the Rangers played up finely, and from a good forward rush Harrison crossed the Recs.' line at corner ; the try however was disallowed. After the drop out several scrimmages were carried by the Rangers, the short passing of their halves being quite a treat. Tickle got possession near his line, but his kick being charged down by Johnson, Russell secured, and dash- ing across the line scored close to corner, Cook making a splendid but unsuccessul attempt at goal. The Rangers still continued to press, and a fine dribble by Woods ended in that fleet forward scoring under posts Butter- worth again failing at goal. Nickson dropped well to touch at half way, and from the ensuing line out Brennan got hold and took the leather back, to the Recs. "25." Nixon now got hold and made a good run towards the Rangers' line,and when on the point of being tackled by Houghton,threw to Brimelow,who ran over at the corner, Worrall failing to convert. The Rangers' for- wards now played well together, showing good combina- tion, and Johnson, getting the ball from the scrimmage, got well away, and passed to Butterworth, who evaded Tickle, and scored again for the Rangers, Johnson steer- ing the leather over the bar. The whistle now sounding, the score stood Rangers, 1-3-2 ; Recs., 0-1-1.

RUNCORN OLD EDWARDIANS.-011 Saturday Runcorn journeyed to Birmingham with only an " A " team. Ow- ing to the Cheshire and Yorkshire match, at Halifax, they were short of nine of their usual players. The first meeting, which took place at Runcorn, on November 12th, ended in a win for the Cheshire men by one goal, two tries, to one try. Runcorn on that occasion were fully represented. It will be seen from the following list that Runcorn only played 14 men. Teams :—Run- corn: 0. Dunvaband, full back; Rev. G. H. Kingston, T. Warder, and T. Robinson, three-quarter backs; %V. Evans and J. Faulkner, half-backs ; A. Hampson, J. Davies, J. Evans, J. Stubbs, S. Derbyshire, H. Farmer, G. Moores, and T. Antrobus. Old Edwardians: J. H. Moore, full back ; A. Badger, H. C. Adams, H. D. Hope, and W. P. Nicol, three-quarter backs ; G. F. Goodwin, E. Prosser, half-backs ; J. F. Jordan, F. A. Burges, B.E. Burges, J. Taplin, W. H. Goodwin, J. B. Smith, M. A. Wood, and H. A Slater. Dunvaband with a poor kick let the homesters, in,and,Adams passing wide to Badger, the latter dodged skilfully over, Jordan kicking a goal. Restarting, Runcorn warmed to their work in good earnest, the forwards using their feet to great advan- tage, which caused the Edwardians to defend their lines. Now some exciting passages took place, King- ston making good efforts to get through. Faulkner missed a good chance by hugging the ball too long. Offside tackling by Runcorn gave the home team an advantage, Warder very cleverly staying a dangerous- looking rush. Here a splendid combined rush ,by the " Greens " regained a lot of ground, and a good passing movement between Evans, Faulkner, Warder, and Kingston enabled the latter to sprint cleverly over ; but the try was disallowed on appeal for being passed for- ward. However, the Runcornians were not to be denied, and a spirited attack led up to Faulkner scoring. War- der kicked a fine goal. After this the game was even for some time, until ,Fardan and Burgess with a dribble carried play to the quarter flag. Here Moore's kick came clean into Adam's hand, who on being tackled by Kingston, threw to Badgers, and the latter had an easy I run in. Jordan failed to hick a goal, half time arriving with the score—Old Edwardians, one goal, one try ; Runc9r.u, one goal. Upon resuming it was evident that the visitors meant business, the ball being rushed to the, home lines, Moore saving just in time. Still pressing,

' Runcorn kept the game well within their opponents' quarters, and with ordinary luck should have scored at least a couple of tries. Antrobus next initiated a dribble which ended in Stubbs scoring in a_favourable position. Warder took the place, which just. failed. The restart was well replied to,andosome exchange kicking betwten Adams and Warder ended in Kingston securing , and making a brilliant run along the touch, only being stopped close ro the line. From now to call ef time Runcorn had all the game, 'but' failkt to get through. The game ended :—Runcorn one.goal, One try ; Edsvar7 diang, one goal, one try,

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

RUNCORN ASSOCIATION V. Wrrrost ALBtort.— Played at Northwich on Saturday. The teams were as follows Runcorn : Mainwaring, gsalkeeper ; Hughes and boombes, full backs; Fisher, Richards, and A. Limb, half backs ; Limb, Bate, Pye, Wright, and Blainer, for- wards. Witton Albion : Tytiswell, goalkeeper, Dudley and Preston, fall backs; Cocks, Plant, and Isherwood, half backs ; Perkins, Hornby, Done, Connor, and Lang, forwards. The homestors had somewhat-the best of the game, their centre, Done, scoring two most creditable goals. The visitors, nevertheless, were by no means idle,and gave the borne defence many anxious moments, especially during the last ten minutes, when they fairly bombarded the Immesters' charge, and it was only through the superb play of their. goalkeeper, coupled with the efforts of Dudley, who showed up well, that the visitors had to retire a losing but by no means beaten team. The final score was—Runcorn 0 ; Witton Albion, three. 1 .,„„, vr ARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB v. ECCLES.—These duos , met on the cricket ground on Saturday. The Cricket ' Club kicked off against a strong wind, but Eccles im- mediately began to press, and Forest was soon called on to cave. The Cricket Club backs played a good game. and prevented Eccles from scoring for some time, but at length Whittaker scored the first goal, and soon after- wards the centre forward added another, making the score two to none in favour of Eccles. Thus the score remained till half time. With the wind in their favour, the Cricket Club had much the best of the game, but their shooting was miserable, shot after shot going wide of the mark. At length, however, they managed to score, Hoare kicking what broved tobe their only point. A very pleasant game thus ended in favour of Eccles by two goals to one. LYMM RESERVB v. WARRINGTON RESERVR.—At Lymm. The home team kicked off against the wind and it once attacked, but good kicking by the Warrington backs prevented any score, and the play became very even. The Lymm right again got away, but Wilson's final just went over. The kick-off afforded the visitors no relief, and Wilson soon scored with a good screw shot. Up to half time play was very even,the good play of the backs preventing any scoring on either side. Half-time score Lymm, one goal ; Warrington, nil. After half-time Lymm had mach the best of the play, and from a scrim- mage near the visitors' goal Hinde scored. The visitors now tried hard to break away, but were unsuccessful, and from good centres by Leah and Wilson Broady scored two goals in quick succession. Lymm still con- tinued to have the best of it, but nothing further was scored, the game ending—Lyinin four goals ; Warring- ton, nil.

Y.M.C.A. HARRIERS V. PADGATS INSTITUTE ASSOCIA- TION F.C.—This match was played at Padgate on Satur- day. Padgate retired defeated to the extent of two goals to cne, after a hard and fast game. The brothers Weston were the pick of the home team, while, for the Harriers, Pearson, A. Lengshaw and Jenks played a splendid game.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES BARBER .fIANGS , HIMSELF.
div.p: A SANKEY BRIDGES BARBER .fIANGS , HIMSELF.

At the Blalk Ilorsq Inn, on Tuesday afternoon, Coroner Brighouse conducted an inquest touching the death of James Kelly, a barber, of Liverpool- road, who hanged himself on Sunday. The chief witness was the deceased's wife, who said that her husband was a man of peculiar temprement. He had several times threatened to take both his own life and hers. He had once tried to poison himself. On Sunday night she.ando the children went to bed and left him downstairs. She waited for him some time, and then called downstairs to him. He answered but did not come. She called again, but he did not come, and so she ran downstairs and found him sus- pended from a beam in the back kitchen by a piece of a clothesline. She ran tor Sergeant Devlin and he with another officer cut her husband down. She had been confined but a few days before and the child had died. She thought this had made him show signs of melan- oholy.—Sergeant Devlin give evidence as to cutting the deceased down. The jury returned a verdict of suicide whilst temporarily insane.
WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY A.UTHORIT Y.
THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.

A special meeting of the above-named Authority; was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday afternoon. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, and Messrs. A. Jolley, Smith, Heaton, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, and Humphreys, Mr. El, Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and Mr. Kerfoot (inspector). The CLERK read a letter he had received from the Town Clerk, dated the 19th inst., stating in reply to Mr. Sutton's letter of 'the previous day,that he had laid it be- fore the Health Committee of the Corporation, and they did not see their way to admit smallpox patients from the Authority's district to the borough Smallpox Hospital. The Clerk said the Medical Officer to the Authority had , written to him on the 20th inst., stating that the disease I appeared to be spredding in the Liverpool-road, district of the Authority. Four cases had occurred since Mon- day last. He suggested that it would be well tO call a special meeting of the Authority to consider wbat steps should be taken to arrest the progress of the disease, such as the taking of some house, temporarily as a hospital, since the Warrington Corporation would do nothing for them. He (the Clerk) then summoned that meeting. The CLURIC then read a report from Dr. Sephton, a copy of which had been sent to the Local Government Board. This stated that there was an extension of the smallpox epidemic from the borough of Warrington to the extra-municipal portion of Liverpool-road district. There had been in that locality up to the:present 11 cases since October last, five of them during the last 10 days, also two other cases in different parts, namely, one at Grappenhall, that of a servant in the house of Dr. Gornall, Medical Officer of Health, wto was received to the borough Smallpox Hospital, and another case at Hollins Green. The infection was traced in both cases to Warrington. He (Dr. Sephton) had advised vaccination and re-vaccination ; and isola- tion so far as practicable. The authority had no hospi- tal for such cases, and that in the borough was not full. There were now six cases.—Dr. Seeurom, in answer to a question, said the bnrough hospital was not full, though the eases were on the increase.—The CHAIRMAN : It does not affect the question whether it is full or not. In the course of some conversation that then took place the Chairman asked if there was any cottage likely to be available for the purpose of a kospital.—The SUR- VEYOR said there were the Ship Canal huts.—Dr. SEPHTON suggested that some house or cottage should be obtained, but said he did not know of any that was available or suitable. It was essential that it should be at least 300 yards from any inhabited house.—The CHAIRMAN said there could be no doubt that seeing there had been such an epidemic in Warrington, it was the duty of the Authority to make the necessary provision.—The Medi- cal Officer pointed out that cases in the Authority's part of Liverpool-road district were, except as to one case, confined to Dale-st. They were mild cases, and several were convalescent. Last week there were three cases, this week there were two. It was the mild cases that spread the disease, because people were less cautious as to coming in contact with them and this patients went out before they were thoroughly recovered. Suggestions were made as to various places for a hospital, Penketh Common, and Orford Park,and Bewsey and Winwick Halls even,being mentioned.—A committee was appointed consisting of Messrs.Heaton,W.Houghton, A.Jolley,Warburton, and Smith, was appointed to make enquiries, with the Medical Officer, as to providing tem- porary hospital accommodation.

div.p: RZiENS CORPORATION AND BARLEY BROOK._

The Cmtax said St. Helens Corporation were seeking for powers for extension of their borough, and their ap- plication furnished a good opportunity to bring forward the subject of Sankey Brook. He submitted to the Authority the following resolution he had drawn up -- "That the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Warrington Union, having been informed of the intention of the Corporation of St. Helens to promote a Bill in Parliament for the extension of their municipal boundaries, desire to call attention of the Local Government Board and the County Council of Lancashire; to the disgraceful condition of Sankey Brook, passing through several townships within the district of this Authority, and to ask that before Parliamentary sanction be obtained for such extensions the Corporation of St. Helens be re- quired to adopt steps for the prevention of the pollution of the brook within their municipal borough."—Mr, HEIkTON proposed the resolution and that copies be sent to the Local Government Board and the Lancashire County Council. He mentioned that the Town Clerk of Warrington had to meet Mr. Atherton Selby and some one else with regard to Sankey Brook, with a view to joint action towards having it cleared.—The CttAntmAx Does the brook touch any portion of the borough ? Mr. HEArox : It runs through it for a mile and a quarter. —The resolution was adopted.—This concluded the meeting.

IN 'THE CAUSE OF TEM- . PER A.NCE. BT 34 n. H. W lIITHAM.

If by any means I should happen to say any- thing displeasing to the friends of temperance in my efforts to further the cause, I hope to be for- given. We are not all constituted alike. We do not look at things from the same standpoint, nor, are all our experiences alike. It must happen, therefore, that in giving expression to our opinions wide differences may be apparent. The bond of unity will be in the motive, and in the object aimed at.

An old, and a wise injunction would, I think, do good service if adopted, and acted upon by the teetotal party. aße temperate in all things." In- temperance in methods and language has been the great stumbling-block of the party. lam led to this hard saying through the reading of a number of temperance speeches delivered in various parts cf England during' the past few weeks. Without particularising I may especially refer to, two features I have noticed—a want .of true and kindly sympathy for the poor drunkard, and a somewhat bigoted adherence to what is known as Local Option. In this, and the following article I propose to deal, incidentally it may be, with these two features.

I know of no sadder reading than than of the English papers of the past few weeks ; especially has this been the case with the Warrington papers. Drunkenness in all its worst forme and results, has been the most promi- nent news offered to the public. Couple this sad feature with the "Homes for the People "question, and then take a pride in 19th century progress. When I read of the " back ':o back rabbit hutches reeking with filth " in which the poor workers have to linger through life, I am much disposed ta ask myself as philosophically as possible Bow can such things be ? lam no Chris- tian, and have no desire to be such. As an Agnostic I feel a freer hand to touch, and deal with all things and persons I may come in contact with. No Divine right scruples would hinder me from laying heavy hands on the " " idea which rules the conduct of so many of the • unco guid." see that quite a bright notion has got int* the heads of some few of the Tory party. If the notion should ever materialize it would certainly be known, and pointed to as" The Tories' Folly." I refer, of course, to the wish on the part of a few to raise a statue to Sir G. G. This movement naturally came to my mind while thinking of the hutches reeking with filth. Cause, and effect thought I. Well, I am not one of those who associate drink and poverty together in every case. There is honest poverty, at least I think so, but it is rare to find it in a drunkard's home.

It is an easy, and short step from the custom that con- fers titles on mediocrity to the clergy as also established by law. Beer and the Bible have always been associated together. Happily there are signs that the connection is likely to be severed before long. Several political rea- sons are supposed to (mist for tying the clergy to Con- servatism. I think it possible that these reasons will shortly be swept aside, and then the leisured and cul- tured amongst them may turn to their legitimate work. . .

In the meantime it is well to know how the residuum amongst them conduct themselves. I quote from the "Fall Mall Gazette." From this it appears that between the let of October. 1891, and the Ist of October, 1892, there had occurred among the clergy of the established church 12 suicides, 14 breaches of promise, 17 elope- ments, 18 acts of cruelty to animals, 109 assaults on women (speaking euphernistically),l2o cases of drunken- ness, 254 cases of bankruptcy (the number of fraudulent cases not specified), with 54 other offences not definitely described, the total being 629 in an aggregate of 23,0001 Iclergymen and others joined to the sacred' office. The proportion of the offenders is nearly 3 per cent." If I impeach the clergy, I hope to do it fairly, because I know that in good time the intelligence, and 'learning possessed by their body will have its own weight throws into making a sober, and happy people. But we suffer from the work they are doing now. 1 happen to have by me a speech made in the House of CommonS,immedi- ately after the General Electi3n. The speaker, Mr. O'Connor, unfolded such mean and despicable work on the part of the clergy as must have made many of his hearers tremble for the seats they held, and which the election judges are now shaking up to the dismay of the un-seated. I give one quotation. The speaker said, " a elergyman of the Church of England arranged that "on the polling-day, a cask of beer should be stationed " at or near the polling-station, and that all who would "partake of it should be supplied. The beer was dis- " pensed by a man who was in the service of the clergy- " man, and that clergyman was a Unionist who worked "hard for his party." le justice to my dear old home, I must say that temperance has in its clergy and minis- ters of all denominations, a host of warm, and earnest advocates, and I read the reports of their sayings and doings with interest. I happen to be one of those who believe that a nation can only be free when it is sober. Speaking personally, I should never have joined the teetotallers but that I am persuaded the great majority amongst us weak mortals cannot touch pitch without,somehow, getting smirched. I candidly confess that I like a glass of good beer; and that I could never become a drunkard I am quite cer- tain. Still, there is the example, and more than this, there is the power, the moral power, ene feels in com- plete sobriety, in the work of lifting one's fellow-work- men out of the gutter. Now, let me get back to the temperance party as a working body. I would like to ask,is the work done satis- factorily? Are the methods adopted the best methods ? Is the object aimed at, the complete abolition of the manufacture, and sale of intoxicants, ever likely of ac- complishment? Touching the first question. I have seen it stated several times tecently, that drunkenness is on the increase. I have a heap of figures before me, showing the money spent, and quantities sold in recent years. They are dry figures, dealing .with a wet subject. In order to spare the reader, I will leave them, merely saying, that they, and my own observations, prove conclusively to me, that drunkenness is on the in- crease. The question then is, what other methods shall be adopted ? Right here,l must ask my teetotal friends to follow me calmly, and not to say with the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes, that because a "pecuniary interest would result to every citizen in adopting the Gothenburg or Swedish system, the temperance party would sternly, and unflinchingly oppose it." Mr. Hughes is mistaken in supposing that pecuniary interest is the object aimed at, or that the prosperity of the traffic is a matter hoped for. As to methods, the Prohibitionists, led away by doc- trinaire methods, fail in their work, because they do not make sufficient allowance for the traditions, usages, and habits of the people, as a whole. It is no use wondering, however, people can drink beer. It would be just as reasonable to wonder however De Quincey could eat the quantity of opium he did. The Irish take ether, the French absinthe. How is it ? I have sat and watched the Mexicans drink muscat by the glass- ful, yet I could not swallow a spoonful without gasping. How is it ? Well, I suppose the taste may be cultivated to almost any extent, and in any direction. And, then, have we not inherited a large portion of this drinking habit? Other features to be dealt with further on, are, "the homes we live in," and " the work we do." To the Prohibitionists who are willing to give their influence in favour of sensible measures, I say the Gothenburg plan, or call it the Bishop of Chester's plan, offers the best means,and the only possible way of making a sober people. The temperance reformers must do what is possible. No reason why they should not aim at what is ideally right, but tken the very fact that drunkenness is on the increase, and spreading amongst all classes, proves that their ideal is beyond reach. This plan does not attempt to say that men shall not drink,but it takes away from the whole arrangement of liquor its private interests. It enlists the public in the efforts to mitigate its difficulties, and prevents men from making fortunes 1 out of their brothers' weakness. It is Socialistic in its workings, and whatever gains come from the traffic are returned to the community in the form of benefits which reach the whole body of the people,and this makes the public the interested judges of the efficiency, with which the plan develops. If I understand the bishop right, he suggests that the public-houses shall be purchased at a fair valuation, and shall be managed by the County Couacil. This is the only way, in my opinion, to make a start. The "trade" interest would be quietly shunted on to a side line. In fact, there would be no mat-interest at work, and impe- rial politics, as well as the temperance reformers, would see the greatest curse of the 19th century, that is, the publicans' selfishness, besome a thing of the past. Since I came to this New England town I have seen a little of the working of Local Option. My friends, it is the shallowest farce ever put forth by man. I have beside me a list of towns throughout New England, where it has been tried, and quite a long list it is, and dating back for a number of years, the report reads like a tale of see-saw, one year license, the following year prohibition. During the prohibition year, everyone who wants liquor can get it. Deception and rascality of every description are practised. JR' you had prohibition in Warrington, Liverpool and Manchester would, by hook or crook, supply to its citizens as much liquor as was wanted It would come in in all sorts of disguises. Instead of having public-heuses selling it openly, you would have private houses turned into drink shops, or, as they are called here "Kitchen dives." John Bright said Force is no remedy ; 'the saying applies with most fearful force when used to make men give over taking their glass of beer. Remember, there is the moderate drinker, the man who loves his glass of beer, or spirits, but who is never seen drunk. What will you do with him on the total abstinence question, or rather what will he do for you ? Simply nothing. To make the drunkard an impossibility he will help you ; he believes with the temperance reformer and with Mr. Gladstone that "they should all carry with them, deeply stamped on their hearts and minds, a sense of shame for the great plague of drunkenness which had gone through the land, sapping and undermining charac- ter, breaking up the peace of families, oftentimes choosing for its victims not the men or the women originally the worst, but persons of strong social suscep- tibility, and open in special respects to temptation. This great plague and curse, let them all remember, was a national curse, calamity, and scandal." He believes

all this, but attempt to take away from him his owls sober glass, and he will thwart you at every point. Ascept human nature as it is, and deal with it. I think the correspondents' column of the "Examiner" might be used to advantage in discussing this question, and any further light, gained by experience in this coun- try, I should be pleased to give.

div.p: ”SANTLEY 1"

(A RHAPSODY.) "A country lad from Lancashire,"— One of the "Sacred Harmonic Choir"— To thee would dedicate his lyre, Bentley. My humble muse would sing thy praise, In "soothing, soft, enchanting lays," And laud thee in a hundred ways, Bentley.
Who could interpret Slendelssohn, In every phase, in every tone, With fullest truth but thee alone?
Santley.
"Elijah': rings in accents clear, Now showing vengeance, now a tear— Fit music for a higher sphere, Santley.
Now, in a fierce, tumultuous strain; Now, wrapt in saddening grief and pain; Now, speaking faith and hope again, Santley.
And who in Handel's melody, Could show his grand sublimity, Or girt him justice like to thee?
Santiey.
For thee old Haydn's music bright. And Mozart's fine melodic might, Seem to thy splendid genius light, Santley.

Thou art indeed a monarch high, Thou makest me feel—nor need ask why,— As ,if ev'n Heaven itself were nigh, Santley. Let foreign nations vaunt their skill, And boast their heroes till they're ill— Thou art supreme—thou foremost still— Santley.

In thee thy countrymen rejoice; They say of thee, as with one voice, "O'er O'er all the world thou art our choice," • Bentley. May thou be kept in health, and strong, Thy days with thy admirers long, To be our Emperor of Song
Santley. TUM. 0' PEGS.
Rose Bank, 29/1/893.

div.head: LATE MR. WILLIAM !A.RMITAGE,
div.p: THE LATE MR. WILLIAM !A.RMITAGE,
r. p•
PULPIT REFERENCE BY TUE REV. J. YONGE.

On Sunday evening in Wycliffe Chinch, Warring- ton, the Rev. J. Yonge preached a sermon to young men, Wit h special reference to the late Mr. William Armitage, J.P. There was a good congregation. Mr. Yonge took as his text "The hoary bead is a crown of glory, if it be formed in the way of righteousness,' Proverbs, 16 chap., verse 31.. . . . .

-kr. Yonge said : I chose this (mit immediately the news reached me of the passing away of my old and honoured friend, Mr. Willism Armitage. The man suggested this text and this message to young men. Ile was only remotely known to most of us. But the honour- able position held in our midst for so many years by his eldest son; the occasional occupancy of this pulpit by his second sun ; the recent renovation and decoration of this building by his fourth son, and his own munificent gifts to this church both at its erection and since—all these things have made his name and his reputation to belong in measure to us. Besides and beyond this,the late Mr. Armitage is considerably inwoven in my own personal , history. He had been upwards of 25 years a very im- portant link in the chain of my life. But for his inter- vention in 1865,when I was resident in the Isle of Wight. I might never have been led to Lancashire. During my pastorate at Heywood, Mr. Armitage ' rendered me generous and unstinted service. He also had his " say " in my introduction here. Years ago, I spent happy days under his roof, and in later years it has een my privilege to work by his side in the cause of our churches in this county. I Mr. Armitage's old age has been a striking illustration of ,this text. His hoary head has been a crown of glory, for lit has been formed in the Svay of righteousness. He has lived a long life, v.hich, for its characteristic fa dares, for its conforming and controlling spirit, is a worthy example to young men. Industrious in youth, and throughout his long career, never so happy as when most at work ; intelligent in the use of leisure, in the employment of the ample means which his industry I secured, without professing any special intellectual or literary gifts, ever interested in literature, in art, in science, in politics, surrounding himself from youth with wise and elevating friendships which have been his joy through life until, one after another, death re- moved them from his ken ; ever seeking out lines of Un- selfish service, whereby he could benefit his fellows, and advanee the cause of his master and throughout j,iving in the fear and love of God. He has been considerably succeesful in life; and the glory of it is that he hag reached his success in such a way that few names are more honoured in Lancashire commerce than his; ' His escutcheon bears no stain. His home his ever been known as one of the purest and brighteatChristiari type, and in it he has ever been, not only the mere prOsolder of its comfort, and regulator of its order, but the very sunshine of its joy. I have known in the course of my life many Christian men, and not a few wealthy ones. I have occasionally sojourned under many of theieroofs, but I am free to state that I never found myself in a home se bright, so pure, so elevating, so Christian, as that of Towafield. Nor have I ever known a brighter or more joyous christian than Mr. Armitage. The influ- ence of his brightness, of his unconquerable optimism, of his quenchless gladness in God, has poured sunshine upon many a darkened heart, and made many a sad one ready to sing for joy. Ido not ,wonder at the joyous reverence his family ever paid him. Nor do I wonder that when he was carried to his sepulchre, so large-an d varied a company were gathered together. ; Both rich and poor were there Churchman and Dissenter, Conservative and Liberal, and, not the least interested, some of the blind children from the asylum, over which ha presided for many years. Specially would I allude to the fidelity with which throughout his life he clung. to the church of his youth. Born in Manchester, from his infancy he was identified with the Roby Independent Church, in whose service, as Deacon and Treasurer, he died at the age of 77. There were not many men in these days of changes of whom such a record is possible! It Is getting to be common now for even Christian men to recognize no special bond, save that of convenience, to a church. But Mr. Armitage was a man of strong attach- ments, and great persistency of purpose ; therefore amid all changes' as often as possible, he would be in his old spot, and he officiated as Deacon at Roby Chapel, so recently as last month's communion. He was, more- over, a staunch and faithful Nonconformist. Rising in the world, with him did not mean courting social favour by abandoning Nonconformity and going over to the Establishment. Never a bigot, never a partizan, never i narrow, he was clear, firm, and thorough n his dissent from a State church and in his adhesion to the free church in which he was born. And he has been a generous man. Very rarely did he refuse to help a needy and deserving cause. In this, it is only right to say that Mr. Armitage was one of a considerable com- pany of Manchester men who have set a fine example of Christian stewardship ; but who now, alas, have nearly all passed away ; and some of them unlike our friend, leaving no successors. Ido not say they have not left sons ; but sons are not always willing to walk in the footsteps of fathers. Not a few old honourable Noncon- formist names in Manchester have died out of Noncon- formist associations. But the name of Armitage surely is an indefeasible inheritance of our congregational churches, and the influence and example of such a life as that just ended are not likely to be lost upon the men he has left to bear his name.
A MENDICANT CLERK'S SAD END IN

THE WORKHOUSE. A man named James Joseph Baguley, aged 40, died at the Warrington Workhouse on Saturday under sad cir- cumstances. Deceased was found late on Thursday night in Buttermarket-st. by P.C. Evans in a stooping position. He complained of feeling ill, and stated that he was a clerk out of employment, and had been tramp- ing the country for two or three years. He appeared to be suffering from chronic bronchitis and asthma. The officer took him to Mr. Gallop's lodging-house, where he was treated kindly by Mr. Gallop. He could not par- take of any food, as he said he had had very little for some time, having taken nothing but spirits. On Friday he was taken to the Workhouse Hospital, and was found to be suffering from consumption. On Saturday Dr. spinks was sent for, but he died before the doctor's ar- rival. The circumstances were reported to the Coroner but no inquest was held.

IMPORTANT ANNOUNCEMENTS.

Home Secretary on Tuesday received a number of ttions from the Women's Liberal Federation, the nentary Committee of the Trades Unions Con- the Women's Trades Union Association, the Trades Council, and other bodies, who urged Ina the necessary of appointing additional inspec- Including women, of factories, workshops, mines, ,Miss Balgarnie, Lady Aberdeen, Mr. Fenwick, M.P., EL Wilson, M.P., and others having spoken, the Secretary, in reply, said it was impossible te 'rate the importance of the subjects brought before They concerned the life, health, and well-being of eat mass of their fellow-citizens. The proposal of ilsory registration of all places where work was Would require a change in the law, and he deeply :ted that the Factory Act of 1891 did not include )rovision. With regard to the enlargement of the Of inspected trades, if he found there was urgent Lnd a genuine demand for it he would do what he give effect to it. With regard to employers' the Government had prepared a bill which he

would meet the demand; ofthe working classes,. Vect to the administratian of the existing law, there was a strong prima-fade case in favour of the services of women in the work of inspec- far, at any rate, as women and children in and workshops were concerned. He intended , of experiment to appoint two women inspectors, London and one for Glasgow. As to the ques- If the inadequacy of the existing staff of inspectors, `sed to increase the staff by appointing fifteen ' assistants, and to erect in three of the large )fficers which he hoped would be a gathering if useful information in connection with labour 4ustrial disputes. THE SHIP 'CANAL.
SHOCKING ACCIDENT ON THE CANAL. A WARRINGTON BOY TORN TO PIECES.

On Saturday morning an accident shocking in its details occurred on the Ship Canal at a point near to the , Latchford Viaduct. From the evidence given at an in- quest opened by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, at the Latch- ford Hospital on Monday afternoon, it appears that a youth named Frank Caldwell, aged 19, had been engaged 1 as a fireman on a steam navvy for about nine months, under the superintendence of a middle-aged man named Belter, and was literally torn to pieces by the chains of a 1 steam navvy in the full view of two men who were powerless to assist him. As to the accident exactly occurred no one could speak authoritatively, but the 1 shocking death is accounted for in the following manner. , At about half-past eleven the steam navvy on which the deceased had been engaged was stopped for a time, in , order that a set of rails might be laid up to the face of the cutting where operations were to be carried on. After oiling the steam navvy the man in charge, Beater, went to the foreman of the section, to inquire when the engine of the navvy would be supplied with water, as the stock was running low. Before going Beater told the deceased to take a rest for an hour, as he would not be expected to work. When he left the deceased began to clean a lamp. Hardly had the driver of the navvy departed about 40 yards when he was startled to hear a dreadful shriek. He next saw a man standing on the navvy, beckoning to him as if demanding his immediate return. Then the steam navvy began to move, and the chain of the bucket rapidly wound in. Rushing back, the driver saw a portion of the deceased's body en- tangled among the chain on the drum of the engine, which was being rapidly wound in. Beater was, ac- cording to his own statement, transfixed with horror and fright, and for a few seconds lie stood gazing at the rapidly turning drum, which,at every fresh revolution crushed and mangled the poor youth. Then realizing the lad's awful position he shut off the steam and put on the brakes. But the deceased was beyond all human aid, and to complete the sad story Baster said that he thought he saw, but was not sure "because he was dazed," that before he stopped the steam navvy one of the lad's arms was torn out and fell on to the ground beneath.

Another man named Arnold gave his story to the Coroner, and it was to to the effect that while passing the scene of the sad accident he heard a piercing shriek from among the machinery of the steam navvy, but as the footplate of the engine was some distance irom the ground, and he being a small man, he could not see dis- tinctly what was the matter at tide moment. On clam- bering on to the engine he saw the deceased entangled among the chains on the drum of the steam navvy. The drum was revolving rapidly. and at each turn the chains crushed some fresh portion of his body. For the moment the witness was paralysed with fear, and hardly knew what to do. From the confused huddled heap and above the rattle of the machinery, he heard the boy cry faintly " Shut the clutcher, shut the. clutcher Suddenly regaining his composure, he shouted and waved his arms for assistance. To his intense relief, nester's attention was immediately drawn, and he came I back and stopped the engine from further mutilating the I poor victim. Witness did net understand the method of •&fatting off steam, and consequently he was powerless 'to help the deceased. He had heard the term " clutcher," but he was not aware what particular func- tion that instrument bad on the control of the engine. Cester then gave his theory as to how the deceased came bp his dreadful death. In spite of the fact that witness had oiled the engine, and told the deceased to rest him- self for an hour or so, he had every reason to believe that the deceased took it on himself to oil the machin- ery. His assertion was grounded on the fact of the presence of a piece of wood that usually lay on the f oot- I board of the steam navvy on the cross bar that strengthened the arm of the engine, and which extended lacross from the boiler over the drum. On that piece of wood there lay an oil can, that had been taken from the place where he had laid it. He supposed that after placing the wood in question in position, the deceased slipped on a greasy cog-wheel, and sliding down the splashboard of the engine; he fell over on to the drum, not, before, however, he had in some way knocked back the lever, regulating the flow of steam, and this had instantly caused the engine to start in motion before the deceased youth had time to extricate himself, and so occurred one of the most dreadful accidents that has happened on the Ship Canal from probably its commence- ment. The jury returned a Verdict of accidental death. '

THE CANAL AND THE FOREIGN CATTLE TRADE. A Liverpool correspondent telegraphs that the cattle importers at Liverpool, whose business centres at the lairages at Woodside, will, by arrangement with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, proceed up the Ship Canal,with a view of deciding upon a site suitable for a new lairage and slaughter-houses. It is understood that the imports of cattle from Canada during next season will be largely increased. The Dominion Government as desirous of encouraging the trade, and their Liverpool agent is furthering their views.

L'2.000,000 FRESH CAPITAL. The Examiner on Standing Orders (Mr. Campion) had before him on Monday the Bill of the Manchester Ship Canal Company authorising them to raise further capi- tal to the extent of £2,000,000 for the completion of their works. The company have already expended or incurred liabilitiesto the amount of nearly £12,000,000 in connection with the undertaking. The amount of share capital authorized in the original Bill was £8,000,000, the cost of the works being then estimated at less than that sum. The Examiner certified that the standing orders had been complied with.

div.p: "KING SOLOMON'S" SECT. ALLEGED ACCKING DEPRAVITY.

At the South-Western Police Court, London, on Satur- day. Mrs. Fercival Smith, the wife of the vicar of St. Stephen's, Battersea, attended the court with a respect- able-looking woman, and made the following disclosures to Mr. Denman, whose help and assistance she sought to obtain. She stated that the husband of the woman who accompanied her had been at different times during life a shoemaker, a greengrocer, and a local preacher among Wesleyans, ultimately joining a '.religious sect known as King Solomon's sect, a body which created no small amount of notoriety at Brighton a short time since, the police interfering to suppress some alleged acts of immorality. The husband was now at Woodford, in ' Essex, one of the headquarters of the sect, and when he left his wife two years ago;he told her that he had received &Divine message commanding him to live with a woman whom lie had introduced to his wife, telling her also that her wants should be supplied as the Lord directed. Shortly afterwards the wife was inter- viewed by a member of the same sect, a perfect stranger to her who told her that he had received a Divine mes- sage directing him to live with her. She indignantly refused to recognise the Divine message.. She had received from her husband at irregular intervals_ sums of money, he stating that they were the Lord's freewill offerings.—Mr. Denman observed that the applicant was entitled to a summons. for a maintenance order and
_ this she accented.—The wife gave the name of Sarah Turner, and an address in Balfern-st., Battersea.

div.head: COLLAPSE OF A PO ttTION OF CHESTER
div.p: COLLAPSE OF A PO ttTION OF CHESTER
WALLS.

On Monday afternoon, an ancient historical landmark known as Pemberton's Parlour, situated on the north side of Chester city walls, collapsed with a great crash, the only portion of the tower remaining being the arch and west corner with the inscribed panel over the centre. Experts attribute the collapse to the recent frost and thaw,combined with vibrations caused by the passing of heavy luggage trains on the Chester and Holyhead and Shrewsbury railways, contiguous to the walls. The tower stood upon a decliyitous rock, on the right side of which is a plantation owned by the Municipal Charity Trustees, and it has a history connected with it,partica- laxly about the time of the Civil War. When the city was besieged by Cromwellians, it is recorded that the vicinity of the wrecked tower was the scene of the fierest part of the siege, which was directed against what was considered the most vulnerable point. In 1702 the tower was restored by the aldermen and others of the Corpora- tion, and an inscribed panel was placed on it to the , effect that bortions of the restoration took place in the reign of Queen Anne. It received the name of Pember- ton's Parlour, owing, It is believed, to the fact that. John Pemberton, the then Mayor, used to sit-in the semi-cir- cular chamber, and watch his men at work in a rope- walk beneath. There is no hope of restoring the tower, but efforts are being made by the city surveyor (Mr. J. M. Jones) to preserve the remaining portion of the e structure, which is now supported by woodwork.

POSTAL FACILITIES AT HAY DOCK.

Sir,—With your permission. I should like to draw at- tention, through the medium of your valuable paper, to tke inadequate condition of the postal arrangements in Haydock. lam sure it would be a great boon to the inhabitants, to have a later dispatch than 6 p.m., and I feel sure if they would bring themselves together, and lay the matter before the postal authorities, they would be only too willing to meet their wishes, as they must be quite alive to the fact, that, considering how Hay- dock has grown this last 16 years, the present arrange- ments cannot ho convenient. If lam informed aright, bath Sutton. Gerard's Bridge, and St. Ann's districts kave all a dispatch about 9 p.m., and about four de- liveries ; yet a rising place like Haydock, has only two, and the last dispatch at 6 p.m. Letters have to be posted very early for both Manchester and Liverpool, to get delivered the same day. Cannot some our of influential citizens take the matter up, and present to the postal authorities, and see if there could not not be deliveries, say about 6 p m., and the last despatch, say about 8 p.m ?—Yours Sze., Haydock, Jan. 25, 1893.
PROGRESS.

A WARRINGTON SOLICITOR AND THE OATH. Sir,—l shall be pleased if you will allow me to call the attention of the public to the erroneous impression en- tertained by his Honour Judge Floulkes on the " kissing of the book," in courts of justice. On Thursday last Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, was called as a witness at the Warrington County Court, and said he preferred to be sworn with uplifted hand instead of by " kissing the book," when his Honour ruled that as it was not against Mr. Jenkins's religious belief he must be sworn in the usual way. Permit me, sir, to point out that the very reasonable objection entertained by many to kiss- ing the greasy cover of the Bible placed in their hands when the oath is administered in the usual form in the pence courts and courts of justice is met and provided for by Clause 5 of the Oaths Act, 1383, chapter 46,w hich runs as follows :—" If any person to whom an oath is administered &sires to swear with uplifted hand in the form and manner in which an oath is usually adminis- tered in Scotland he shall be permitted so to do, and the oath shall be administered to him in such form and manner without further question."—Yours, L. S. A.

div.head: SABBATH NUISANCES.
div.p: SABBATH NUISANCES.

Sir,—l was pleased to see in your last issue, the notes by Merlin, describing the curfew bell, rung at Trinity Church, as a nuisance, a.nel an unnecessary item of ex- penditure to the town. It is a nuisance, and I, as a resident wish to corroborate " Merlin's " statement to the effect that in the near vicinity the bell is a nuisance to the inhabitants. But there are other annoyances which I sheuld like to allude to, and they may be des- cribed as Sabbath nuisances. I live in the neighbour- hood of Bold-st., and am but one of a large number of persons who are compelled week by week to endure some of the most painful inflictions of confusing and distressing "rows" imaginable. The real nuisance cemmPnces at six o'clock on the Sunday evenings, by the clanging of the mournful sounding bells of Trinity Church, the Reformed Church, and St. James Church. Between them those three bells send forth a conglome- ration ot sounds which are quits as depressing as a funeral. and what earthly reason is there for this? The primary object of a Church bell was to warn wor- shippers of the time of service ; but to toll such crack- pot kind of instruments for such an object now is as absurd as would be the revival of some of the long- since dead old barbarous customs which were in vogue when the ringing of the Church bell did serve a purpose, and that is a long time since. The Nonconformist places of worship can get along without inch ridiculous and childish things, why can't the Church of England. But there is another nuisance I have to complain of and that is the open air prayer meetings held on a Sunday evening in Bold-st., by the Wesleyans. Within ear-shot of all that goes on at those meetings reside people of all kinds of religious beliefs,to many of whom such loud chantings of God's name are exceedingly hurtful. Besides that, we people of that neighbourhood are compelled to pay high rents to enjoy the privileges of a quiet neighbourhood ; if rowdy roughs annoyed us with their shoutings, I think the police would soon get complaints made to them. Yet, religious bodies are allowed to hurt our religious scruples and break our peace without interference, despite the fact that there is a bye-law forbidding them, or anyone else, to sing either hymns or comic songs to the annoy- ance of residents.—Yours, &c. L. B.

div.head: BRITISH FILE STILL THE BEST.
div.p: THE BRITISH FILE STILL THE BEST.

An American who decries the trade of his native coun- try in the newspapers has not long to wait for a reply I from someone who believes that he knows more about the matter than does the disparager. This is not the way these things are ordered in Great Britain. A nervous Englishman may go into hysterics in the journals, fre- quently without an atom of cause, over " the markets we are losing to our competitors" But the average clear- headed manufacturing son of Albion takes no notice of him—he is too busy either executing orders or endea- vouring to secure them. A United States citizen, Mr. Albert D. Pentz, has been writing slightingly of Ameri- can files. The Swiss Grobet article will, he sap, outcut and outwear four Yankee files, while the English Stubbs product is worth two American rasps, but it is " not so evenly cut as the Swiss." The Helvetian and British files are, moreover, better finished than the Transatiantic tool. " Now what," asks Mr. Pentz, "is the matter with American files P Our steel is good ; we have the mechanical ability, and we have the market, for we use more Swiss files than all the rest of the world ; and I I am of opinion that we consume more Stubbs files than the whole of the British Empire. Americans need not be ashamed of many kinds of native metalwork, but our files are below com- parison." The foregoing is the denunciation. Mark the response of Mr. J. D. Foot, of New York, "a large manufacturer of American files." This gentlemen says, in effect, " Take care of the Pentz and our rasps will look after themselves." The fact is, Mr. Foot asserts, and we shall not gainsay him, that " the Stubbs files are considered by nearly all file manufacturers, and by nine out of ten consumers, to be of better wearing quality than the Grobet make." He admits, further, that Mr. Stubbs uses a superior class of steel te that generally worked by American, or. for the matter of that other English manufacturers. Now and then in the United States, Mr. Foot continues, one will meet with " a few machinists who still think that they must have a Grobet file to finish with, a Stubbs paper saw-file to improve the cutting qualities of a very hard saw, and an English file for general machine-shop work." To such terribly unpatriotic artificers he endeavours to prove that not only is the American rasp ousting the British tool from the Canadian and ether British Eoloniat !markets, but that it is also becoming in Great Britaia itself a " formidable competitor of the best Brands of English files, the Stubbs article not excepted I" What says Mr. Pentz to this P—lron,.

div.head: WOMEN'S LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: THE WOMEN'S LIBERAL FEDERATION.

At last welt's important conference of the “ :Women's Liberal Federation," held in connection with the great meetings of the "National Liberal Federation" at Liyerpool,which were attended by so many representative M.P.' s from all over the British Isles,and bythe Home Secretary,Mr.Asquith,the following ladies were present as delegates from the "Warrington Women's Liberal Association" W. Piernoint, Marlfield ; Mrs. Garnett, Penketh ; Mrs. Clay, Warring- ton ; Mrs. Holford, yarrington ; Miss B. Dutton, hen. sec. of the Association. The meetings included confer- ences at the hall of the Free Library and Hope Hall, a mon etre gathering at the Philharmonic Hall, and a conversazione at St. George's Hall. They were addressed by Lady Carlisle, Lady 11. Somerset, Misses Wynford, Phillips, Stewart Brown, &c., and by Miss Willard., the renowned president of the World's " Women's Christian Temperance Union." The President of the Warrington Association, Mrs. Armitage, and the Hon. Treasurer, Mrs. H. Roberts, were unfortunately prevented by bereavement and sickness from attending.

NOTES ON GAMES AND

FOOTBALL. A considerable "gate" awaited the performance at at Wilderspoel on Saturday. It was a boon and a bless- ing to get a first team match, and more especially when Manchester were to be the visitors. I thought to have seen our home team a little rusty after their long rest. But it was not so. The whole team appeared to be suffering from a suppressed eagerness which is wont to associate itself with spirited horses, which have been confined in a loose box too long. Of course this is not meant as a comparison. It is merely one of my—l was going to say rude, but I mean crude analogies. The players were all exceedingly fresh.

Starting with the wind the Manchester men had all the best of the game during the first half. But the home team held them at bay, thanks to the activity of Webster, Lawless, Bate, Evans, and Boscow. Nothing, accordingly, but minors fell to the lot of the visitors, and at the end of the first half they had two of those not very useful apologies for scores on their boards. But mark the anticipated contrast. No sooner had the first half of the game expired than one half of the " field " began to thrutch and push for places right at the visitors west end of the field. They thus showed where they expected the game would chiefly rage.

The snectators were not mistaken in their anticipa- tions. Scarcely once from the restart did the leather ever cross into the Warrington domain. The game became rather vigorous, there were scrimmages in galore, and some bleeding noses, and tempers were lost, mostly amongst the visitors. One of the latter, who stood over four feet, became indignant with " Fair" Turner in consequence of the way he shoved in the scrimmages. Fair heeded not the simple remonstrance of the fair youth. The latter pushed his arm out at our tall Champion, possibly intending it as a challenge to combat. The audience yelled in a most enthusiastic way at this. But" Fair" would not fight ;he simply cast a withering look at the irate youth and it must have affected him in the bosom because he calmly subsided.

The scoring was however, only made by Warrington; and the tries were scored very rapidly by Webster,Jolly and Bate. Only one of those tries was turned to account and the game ended by the hornesters having the respectable show of one goal and two tries against two minors. A few words of commendation, however, are due to some of the individual players in both teams.

There were two pieces of individual play which struck me as being a kind of two divided parts ot a perfect player. I allude to the play of Boscow, and the play of Steel, Manchester full back. As a smart kicker and runner Boscow seemed all that could be required ; whilst Steel at the other end of the field showed a talent for dodging with the ball through a crush, and a natural alertness, seldom seen at Wilderspool. What a good thing it would be if Steel could add to his abilities those of Boscow, or say, if Boscow could become possessed of Steel's particular qualities.

The A teams of both clubs also had the pleasure of meeting at Manchester, and Warrington again had the pleasure of being the victors by a large some. The champion of the Warrington team this time was " Smack " Bate, who had a veritable omnipresence on the field. lam glad to say that the forwards—in- deed the whole pack—played with a unity and compact- ness, which bids well to banish the fatal individual play which I have sometimes alluded to lately.

The return match between Wigan and St. Helens created more than ordinary interest, owing to the fact that the representatives from the glass-blowing town have only been defeated once this season, and that was in their opening encounter, when Wigan were the visi- tors. The sides were as strong as they could be, and after a very tight tussle of seventy minutes dura.tion,the result was a draw, not even a minor being scored.

A correspondent wants to know " flow has " Smack "Bate acquired the cognomen of Smack, Ste. Myself and others are interested." I'm sure 1 can't answer the question. Probably some of my readers who knew the popular player better than I do would tell. Well ; but I surmise—mind, only surmise—that the famous halfback came by the cognomen " Smack "in consequence of his disposition to have a smack in at scoring whenever he saw the slightest chance.
