div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

I have some sad ne-W-s-t-oCo—n-v-e-it.o those of my readers who are interested in the Association game. Last week were published some verse by" C.," re3pecting the War- rington Association team, and the numbers of the verse were attuned to a song of encouragement for the mem- bers to cheer up, take their licking in the cup competi- tion philosophically, and go on "playing up." Well, since then lam told the team have "chucked up," which is quite a different thing. Two reasons are given for this sudden abandonment of the team, and they are that the members have become scattered and the funds have become low. I am sorry to hear this, but I cannot account for it. There vre many admirers of the association game in Warrington, and I am fully satisfied that if the War- rington Association would go about the thing in a proper way there is no such word as" fail" for them. There are many sources from whence they might obtain subscriptions if they would only leek for them. And as II for the membership falling off, why, I must say with a friend of mine" Pooh ! Pooh !"

Unity is strength in football clubs as much as any- where else. Let the Warrington Association members take heart ; unite and be courageous, and go in for compiling a substantial subscription and hon. member- ship list. There is a club of 40 of them now, and if they can't make the thing " go," it doesn't speak much for their energy. By the way, I hear that Mr. J. W. Isherwood, of the Cricket Club Association, and Mr. E. Connor, who are both students at Owens College, Manchester, have qaalified for the West Manchester Association team.

div.head: "GYM."
div.p: THE "GYM."

I am glad to see that now the members of the Gym. have overcome the effects of vaccination, they are going to revive the Saturday night displays which were so attractive last year. Next Saturday night they will meet the Manchester Simpson " Gym " team in a com- petition, at the "house" in Palmyra Square. I hope they will have a reception which will encourage them to continue the entertainments.

div.head: MR. BRIUHOUSE AND THE S'S EA.RING
div.p: MR. BRIUHOUSE AND THE S'S EA.RING
OF JURORS.

A WARRINGTON SOLICITOR AND THE OATH. At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, who was called as a witness fer the plaintiff, said he preferred to be sworn with uplifted hand instead of kissing the book. In answer to the Judge, " Is it against your religious belief to kiss the book ?" Mr. Jenkins replied, "No, but in face of the prevailing epidemic I prefer to be sworn with uplifted hand." "Then," said his Honour, "I am afraid if it is not against your religious belief you must kiss the book."

Addressing the jury previous to holding an inquest at the Bootle Coroner's Court on Saturday, Mr. S. Brig- house, county coroner, said he had no doubt they were aware by section 5 of the Oaths Act, 1888, they were entitled to have the oath administered by uplifting their hand. The section read as follows :—" If any person before an oath is administered desires to swear with up- lifted hand in the formal manner in which an oath is usually administered in Scotland, he shall be permitted so to do, and the oath shall be administered to him in such form and manner without further question." Continu- ing, the Coroner said they would notice that the initial step was to be taken by the jurors. He could only say that if such a request was made to him he would most readily consent to it, as he considered this mode of ad- ministering the oath as effiacinus as the other now in existance, and it was decidedly far more cleanly. He mentioned the matter because he saw that morninc, ac- cording to the newspapers that a brother solicitor, Mr. Jenkins, of Warrington, in giving evidence before a County Bourt judge desired to be sworn with unlifted hand, and the Judge declined to accede to his request on the ground that the present mode was not against Mr. Jenkins' religious belief. That was a wrong interpreta- tien of the section as he (Mr. Brighouse) understood it, as the oath was bound to be administered in that way to anyone so desiring it. On Monday Mr. Brighouse held another inquest at Bootle, and in swearing the jury he asked if any juror desired to have the oath administered with the uplifted band. About half the jury asked to be sworn in that fashion.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1893. WARRING-To )N NAY TIES ) COLLISION ON TIIE SHIP CANAL RAILANALYSED. I WAY. HOW TO TELL I•REAL ONE
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 28, 1893. WARRING-To )N NAY TIES ) COLLISION ON TIIE SHIP CANAL RAIL- ANALYSED. I WAY. HOW TO TELL I•REAL ONE
BY LUKE BLUNT.

He is a free, wandering child of nature. He wanders chiefly in his conversation. But I wish to do him credit, for I am fond of the legitimate navvy, and hate his impersonator. Corner-men and navvies are in one sense related, but in others they differ widely. Yet the less discriminating persons i of Warrington confound them—yes confound them! —and much to the legitimate navvy's disgust, class the corner man navvy, who labours for him, as a member of his fraternity. Now nothing pains or distresses, or is more calculated to draw tears from the well-travelled, ;thorough-bred spade wielder than being considered but the equal of the men who have hitherto propped up houses at the corners of , street; and were never out of Warrington in their lives, except, may be, to go for militia training, or another kind of training at Strangeways jail. To one who knows the real genuine navvy it is im- possible to fall into this error. First of all, as you see him at work on the canal, you percuice an aspect and characteristic about him which says " I, and no other, am the real and legitimate spade wielder." First, you notice that his bared arms, like his face and neck, are a aeep brown colour, almost like the clay he is delving, and full of sinew and unmistakable strength.

He wheels his barrow or delves the earth with a dogged, systematic air. His boots are always stout and well repaired, and his trousers and vest are al- ways of thick moleskin. He generally speaks with a pleasant accent, and when he swears his oaths are unplPasantly long and original. He generally turns out to his work in good time and works hard whilst he is at it. When he feels idle or wants a "spree," he just tells the "ganger" he's off, and stalks away with dignified independence. Now, he holds the corner-man in the greatest contempt, and although they are both labourers, he won't deign to associate with him. On the other hand, when the corner- man becomes engaged on the Ship Canal, it is the pride of his existence to be mistaken for a bold rov- ing navvy. But it is only those who don't know him who are deceived. Unlike the legitimate spade wielder, he doesn't boast a brawny arm and well- tanned face. His features are not bronzed and definitely formed like those of the travelled man. They are colourless, or dirty, and inexpressive of anything but fourpenny beer, cunning, and often brutality. His boots are not stout and well-repaired. Sometimes they are odd ones—a woman's elastic side one, and a militia blucher—and they are gener- ally out at toes and down at heels. It is a charac- teristic of a corner-man to be down on eels, when he can get them. That is a joke. His trousers and vest arra mole- skin. They are generally stolen, borrowed, or " cadged " castoffs, and are only worn because ot the behests ,of fashion. In his general state of civilization the corner-man is far removed from the line of clothes—or the clothes line. That accounts for his dislike to clothing. His pants are generally suspended by one brace, and in more or less cases where the seat of his trousers ought to be located his shirt is to be seen.

When he does happen to be seen wheeling a barrow or using a spade, it is unsystematically, and in a painful and distressed way. He reminds me of a small boy trying to wheel a truck of coal up a bridge. When you speak to him, he is generally unable to express himself in an intelligible man- , ner, and qualities all his statements with the word 6, like," as for instance 66 he's gone along there with the brimmer 'like." His voice usually has not a pleasant accent, but is thick and guttural—very gutter—al, in fact. /le can't swear a round oath upon an emergency, like a navvy But his conver- sation is always interspersed with nasty language, such as the navvy would not resort to, when com- piling one of his longest swears. There is one thing which the corner-man won't try to imitate the navvy in,and that is going to tell the " ganger " that he is going off for a spree. It isn't because he never feels idle, or doesn't want a spree. Ile is never known to be anything but idle,and will always have a spree when anyone will pay for it. The reason why he doesn't show this independence is because he dosen't possess it. He will always leave his work whenever he can do so without being de- tected. As a rule he dare not tackle real navvying, but works as a common hack to the navvy.

The greatest contrast comes in when you see the two men about town on Saturday nights. The I navvy then turns out with his best suit of thick (, blue serge, except for the waistcoat, which is mole- skin, bedecked with large bone buttons. He gen- erally boasts two or three silver rings. Ile wears a collar to his shirt, through which he runs a neck- chief. He first visits the shops he fancies, and buys in his Sunday " tommy," and spends the even- ing in walking stolidly about town. He is not a , teetotaller by any means ' • but he isn't an habitual , drunkard. He generally drinks pints of beer, and, if he is an average navvy he can consume three, or maybe four, pints, in five minutes, and keep it up for about an hour. Then he can walk along a chalk line without. faltering. This is his strong point— not pint. There are black sheep amongst them, but the generality of them are quiet in drink. He seldom "sponges," and on the whole is very good- natured. The corner-man navvy doesn't turn out in a best suit, because he hasn't got one. And he never boasts silver rings, for the same simple reason. He generally frequents the lowest public-houses, until he has spent what little money he has had energy enough to make. Then he is turned out, and glides into Bridge-street, and Buttermarket-street, where he becomes exceedingly obstreperous and noisy. Owing to his clothes being bespattered with clay, hels mistaken for a navvy, and people say" Oh, what an awful lot these Ship Canal people are." It is the corner-man navvy whom you generally find in the Borough Court on Monday morning; but he is there described simply as a navvy, and it is from that fact that the public get erroneous ideas of the character of the real navvy. As a rule, the corner-man navvy, is a disreputable scamp, while the generality of the legitimate navvies are well travelled, respectable, and intelligent manly fellows. The explanation is a necessary one, and if the reader is unable to distin- guish the reil article from the imitation by the con- trasting details set forth here, there is yet another method. I have tried it myself. H you are not sure the man is a real navvy, go to him with a bland smile and say you believe what is beneath his hat is not ahead. Say you think it is a lump, but assure him that it will come to a head as the inflammation grows. If he is a real navvy he will use a kind of masonic sign which will soon settle the doubt—and probably you, too. If he is not a ' real one be will not show any signs of observing the point in the joke. His intellect is cloudy.

A CAPTAIN KILLED. A few minutes before eight o'clock on Friday night a collision occurred on the Ship Gaud rail- way between Runcorn and Weston Point. It appears that an engine and waggon, known as the " " conveying between 30 and 40 men to Salt- port to take a night shift in loading and unloading vessels, started from the old quay shortly after half-past seven. On the engine called the Hafod was Nicol Bain, captain of the steamship Cragg, engaged on the London trade from Saltport. When the mail had reached Walker's junction at the bottom of Percival-lane, the driver Wm. Morton, perceived a train consisting of ten trucks of gravel drawn by the engine Mersey, approach- ing him on the same line of metals. Both drivers per- ceived their perilous position, and they whistled, shut off steam, and reversed their engines, but they were too close to each other to avoid a collision, and the concus- sion was very severe. The waggon containing the men fortunately became unhooked and rebounded along the line, or the results might have been more serious. As it was, many of the men were thrown out, and others ' were " banged " about the truck and against each other. 'rhe drivers escaped by leaping from the engines, but , Captain Bain was afterwards found on the Hafod, with his neck broken, death having apparently been instantaneous. John Nicholls,of Welsh-row,had evidently I been run over after being thrown from the wagon ; his arm was terribly crushed, and he was conveyed to Latchford Hospital, where it was found necessary to amputate the limb. A large number sustained injuries to the back, kc., and all were more or less bruised and shaken. Dr.MacDougall and Dr. Robinson attended to the men as soon as possible, and the body of Captain Bain was removed to the mortuary by Inspector Cooper and P.C. Beckett. The buffers of the engines were smashed, but otherwise no damage to the rolling stock was done. It is stated that the trains were not travel- ling more than 4 miles an hour. The driver of the Mersey was Tom Knox, of Ice. At the point of collision there is a very sharp curve. Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, on Saturday, opened an inquest on the body of Captain Bain, William John Milli rieton, ship broker, gave evidence of identification. It appeared that the deceased, who was 45 years of age, belonged to South Shields, where he had a wife and family. When he was killed he was on his way to his vessel which was moored at Saltport and chartered for Messrs.Fisher,Renwick,and Co., of London and Manchester.—The inquest was I adjourned until Thursday. THE INQUEST. Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, resumed the inquest on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Supt. Atherton was present , for the police, Mr. Newman (Grundy Kershaw and Co.), appeared for the Ship Canal Co., and Mr. J. Burton re- presented the relatives of the deceased. Mr. E. D. Jones, agent for the construction department of the Runcorn section' was also present.—Win. Morton, said he was an engine driver for the Ship Canal Co. He had been an engine driver for about 12 years. He had been in the employ ol the Ship Canal Co., for three or four years. He had only had charge of the engine Hafod on that day because the usual driver was ill. He started from the Dock offices about half-past seven with one truck containing a gang of about 33 men, who were to work all night at Saltport. It was called the " mail " train. Just as the train was started the de- ceased got on the engine, and witness thought he was a foreman. He did not know who he was, and had not time to ask. It was a darkish night. The rope runner told witness that he had informed " Slasher " that the train was coming. They had signals to work by. There was a signal at Duke's Sidine,whence they started, and there was a watchman at Percival-lane crossing, who showed a light " all right.' Shortly afterwards they met the other train. There was a signal beyond the cross- ing, but it was dark on this night. There ought to have been a light there " by rights.' They whistled for the .road where there was no signal. When there were lights they went by them.—The Coroner : Am I to understand I that this is a matter of indifference whether there is a signal or not P—Witness : When the signalmen have gone home we trust to whistling. He should say he had ' brought sixty trains through that route,and he knew the way. Lights were generally there, but there had been odd times when the signals had been dark. When the I signal was dark, they whistled and kept on their way and kept a good look out. Mr. Newman pointed out that the signal was not used when there was no work going on for the construction department, and the witness was on this occasion act- ing as an emergency man for the traffic department.— Continuing, witness said he had not passed the dark signal, for, when he saw the eneine Mersey ap- proaching with a train of waggons, he reversed the engine,and put off the steam, and was going backwards, when the Mersey collided with the Hafod. The deceased was thrown forward against the engine. He did not know whether it was through the collision or the revers- ing of the engine. Witness and the roperunner had hold of the machinery and so were saved from being thrown about. The men in the truck were thrown among one another, and one had his arm taken off. The deceased was lying on the footpath, and when they got time to look round they examined him and thought he was only stunned. They at once conveyed him to Runcorn.— By the Coroner : Had there been a light in the signal at Percival's Lane, he supposed the accident would not have happened.—By Mr. Boyle (juryman) : He never heard the other engine whistle, but he expected they were both whistling at the same time.—By another juryman : There were notices that no strangers had to ride on the engine, but the foreman rode on this.—An- other juryman said it ws s customary for captains and agents to ride down to Saltport on the engines. Walter Henry Smith, described as material traffic manager, said this mail train was taking men down to Sehnert to discharge and load ships. It had been run- ning down since Saltport came into existence, in July last, on an average two or three times a week. The running of the train depended upon the exigencies of the trade. It was the duty of the roperunner on the train when it was coming from Saltport in the evening, to give notice to the "Slasher," who was a kind of ganger that the train was coming back again. It was then ter the " slasher " to do what he thought was necessary to safeguard the train back. The " Slasher" was not under his charge and he had no authority over him. Mr. E. D. Jones said he had better clear up j the con- fusion which must be in the minds of the jury with reference to the two departments which worked over this line. The lines were laid for the purpose of the construction of the Ship Canal, but since Saltport had been in existence another department, managed from Manchester and having nothing to do with the construc- tion of the canal, utilized this line for the purpose of temporarily developing Saltport. The line was manned entirely by men in the construction department,and the traffic department in using the line was subject to the regulations in force for the construction department. In the day time the entire " overland route "was man- aged by signals, but he did not consider it necessary to have the signalmen at work at night unless there was more than one engine out. Up to October, when the construction department was working; day and night, the signalmen were employed in the nighttime. There was a slasher on duty at Weston Point until 9 p.m., and if the special mail was coming down it was his place to give warning to any train coming up.—The Coroner asked a qaestion which Mr. Jones said belonged to the traffic department and he did not know anything about it.—The Coroner : I don't think you do. I think your management is se bad that you don't know anything about it.—Mr. Jones said the coroner had misunder- stood him. If the " Slasher' was sending a train in the direction in which he expected a train he would tell the roperunner or driver of the engine to keep a look out.—The Coroner : And that in face of there being a sharp curve where a driver can- not look out more than half a dozen yards. I have the fullest information with regard to the evidence. I wish you would be candid with me.—Mr. Jones : I am can- did.—The Coroner : I don't think you are.—Mr. Jones : I think you misunderstand me. He added that his in- struction was that the overland route was to be manned during the day time and not at night.—The Coroner : His train is going down with a freight of men and surely it ought to be protected.—Mr. Jones : Nothing but giving the engine driver a caution.—The Coroner : Had there been signalmen on duty as they are in the day thine, would this accident have happened Mr. Jones : I think not. It was not the duty of the slasher to see the signalmen on the line. The slasher had discharged his duty when he warned the driver of the engines.—Mr. Boyle (a juryman) : You think it is quite sufficient to let two trains meet on the same line without signalmen being there.—Mr.Jones : I would not go so far as to say that. I think it quite sufficient in that way, but on a temporary work of this kind it is almsst impossible to light every signal, the work is so varied. For their temporary purposes I think the arrange- ments might be worked with perfect safety. In the day time there are 40 trains passing along; in the night time there are rarely more than one or perhaps two trains along. Alfred Bullough, roperunner of the engine Hafod, said he had been a roperunner eight years. He had had charge of the mail train for six months. When he brought up the mail from Saltport, if the mail was re- turning to Saltport, he told the slasher. He had never been told to do this, but he did it " for their own bene- fit," The slasher gave instructions tO the signalmen. Witness corroborated the driver with regard to the dark signal, and said he could not remember a time when there had not been signals for the mail train.—By Mr. Newman: It was not much of a collision. Tom Knox, driver of the engine Mersey, of No. Hut, Ince, said he left Saltport at 8 50 with ten trucks of gravel. All went well until they reached Percival Crossing. When he got to Walker's Junction the signal man Teesdale gave the line clear,but after the engine had passed over the points he shouted to him to sound his whistle, as there might be something coming in the opposite direction. Be sounded his whistle twice, and was about to do so a third time when the collision occurred. Immediately he saw the train approaching he reversed his engine,but it was too late. Ile had seen a light at the box on the curve on previous occasions— half-a-dozen—when he travelled at night. On this occa- sian there was no light. Had there been a signal there the accident could not have happened.—By a juror: He could not say that he had run on the line at night since
October, except on the occasion on which the collision happened._ _

niut.l Ward, 38 Hut. Frodsham Marsh, roperunner, said that the slasher at Weston Point told him to beware of the Hilod coming down, as he did not know whether she would or would not have a mail with her. Ho kept a look out. The signalman at Walker's Junction told him to be careful, as he expected the mail. Be had travelled along the line since October, but had not seen a light at the curve. He should see a light when traffic was running, but although this was so, on Friday night there was no light. Thomas Poulson, the slasher, said he had no authority to keep signalmen out at night. He did not know whether the Hafod was coming back light or bringing the mail. When he knew the mail was coining back he put other engines in a siding, as near as possible to the time that he knew it would be coming. When he allowed the Mersey to go in the opposite direction, he did not know but that he would get to Runcorn. The Cheadle came first, and shunted into a siding to get water, and thus the Mersey got past her. Wm. Johnson, 15, Cartwright-st., labourer, said he sustained injury to his right leg and foot. He had been down the road on previous occasions, and on some nights saw lights at the signal boxes. He had seen trains stopped by a red light. He saw Griffiths, th e signalman, at Percival-lane, who asked if the mail was going to run. Witness answered yes. He then told him to tell Bullock that the Cheadle was working round the curve, and he must be careful. He delivered the mes- sage. _
'Thomas Dixon, Sea-lane, Runcorn, a passenger in the :ruck, gave corroborative evidence.

Joseph Griffiths, the signalman of the Percival-lane signal, said up to some months ago Mr. Smith, who had charge of the work, always gave his orders when the Mail was coming ;he (witness) had to risk it now. If the driver or roperunner said they were coming back, he stopped for the train ; if they did not do so, he went , home. He went home on this night at a quarter to sevan. Mr. Hicks had taken Mr. Smith's place.—At 1 this point the inquiry was adjourned, and the Coroner gave instructions for the attendance of Mr. Hicks.
The inquest was resumed yesterday morning. Mr. Newman said he had seen Mr. Marshall Stevens, the

manager of the traffic department, Manchester, to see if he could throw any light upon this matter, but he found that he could not help them in any way. He put in orders issued to the drivers on the overland route and
also locally.—The Coroner after reading them said they contained nothing affecting the inquiry except a regula- tion forbidding engine drivers to take any person on . . . . . .
their en.: me un—der Pain of instant dismissal.' a Joseph Griffiths continued his evidence, said he had not received instructiens from Mr. Hicks as he had used

to get from Mr. Smith.—The Coroner : In giving your evidence to the police, I believe you said, one never knows now what is going to happen P—No, I didn't say that.—Did you say so to Johnson P—Nol3 .—y a juryman: He knocked off when he had seen the last engine in. He had no proper hours. Be looked upon " Slasher " Goul- son as his master.—Robert Wilson, signalman at Duke's offices, where the mail picked up the men, said he re- seived instructions to stay on duty from Will Taylor the ' " Slasher" at No Man's Land. The only information he would get as to the mail going back to Saltport,would be the men shouting. If he did not hear the men shout he went home. There was no one to look to for instruc- tion about the mail.

Thomes Wilson, signalman at Percival-lane siding, on the top of the curve, said he received his order from this Joseph Griffiths. He had never had any instrue- tiont as to.signalling the mail train. He had signalled the mail on one or two occasions. There had been otner traffic, and the mail had happened to come through at the same time. George Teasdale, signalman at Walker's Junction, Weston Point, said if be knew the mail train was going to Saltport, he should not allow anything to pass him for Runcorn. He had no instructions as to signalling " Slasher" Poulson was the man who ought to tell him when the mail was coining, and he had no other means ' of finding out, unless the men shouted as they passed by. On the night of the accident he did not know that the mail was coining down, but he thought it was, and he cautioned the engine driver of the Mersey. He thought the mail was coming because he thought he heard a whisle, but the Mersey was then past his cabin and he could do nothing more. . .

Ford Hicks, clerk-in-charge at Saltport called and asked if he succeed Mr. Smith, said he believed Mr. Smith was at Saltport before him. He had nothing to do with the mail at all, nor with the signalling.—The Coroner : Who would have to do with the engine ? The foreman in charge of the engine when it is at Saltport--Who is that ? Daniel Price. Mr. Smith recalled said he did not know who was responsible for the traffic of the mail trains. He was was not. Mr. Jones recalled was asked by the Coroner: Whom do you consider responsible for the management of this traffic? I am, lam responsible for the whole working of the line.—Do you consider yourself respon- sible for the mail train? No. Who is responsible for that ? Primarily the general manager of the canal, Mr. Marshall Steven, who was his representatives here, Mr. Smith and Mr. Hick. Of all the traffic that runs upon the line within my knowledge, I issue all instruc- tions. The construction traffic, the mail trains, and the geods traffic of Mr. Marshall Stevens were subject to his regulations. He had everything to do with ordering mail trains and he was not aware the mail train under enquiry was running. The Coroner in summing up said there was no doubt the deceased met his death through the collision. The next question was, who was responsible or was anyone responsible, or was any blame attachable for the death. The truck attached to the Hafod contained over 30 men and it appeared to him that they were not only holding an inquest upon one, but upon a much larger number of men. He was satisfied that the evidence was truth. On the previous day he had made a remark that the management of this line was bad. That remark was true. They were actually seriously told that it was safe for engines to proceed to meet one another, merely whistl- ing to warn each other of their approach. In trying to decide who was responsible they were told one man got his instructions from the driver, another from the rope runner, another from the slasher, another had no orders at all and another got their because be heard someone shouting. Be did not think the wonder was' that they had this accident ; the wonder was that the traffic had gone on at all. That was the secret of that accident. If the jury believed anyone responsible far this state of things they had to consider whether he was responsible within the degree of manslaughter. He did not think so. He thought the control was so distributed and the orders given distributed amongst the officials its such a way that it would be almost impossible to single out any one man. they might say that Mr. Jones who had the , management of the section, and who had in a ' straight forward manner had said he was respon- sible for the trains that ran over the lines, was responsible and ought to be made to suffer for what had occurred. Mr. Jones in the manage- ment of the constructive traffic appeared to have done everything that was right and proper and which it was his duty to do in safeguarding the constructive traffic, but when they came to the mail trains, they found there was a dual control. Mr. Janes did not consider that the sending down of men to unload boats at Salt- port formed part of his duty to look after. That duty was looked after by a gentleman in Manchester. Two other gentlemen who were on the spot were supposed to make arrangements for the mail traffic, which they distinctly said they did not. He did not believe any single one was responsible within the degree of man- slaughter. He believed the secret of this accident was the system of general and universal mismanagement. If the jury differed from him and thought they could affix the charge of manslaughter, the verdict was theirs and they must do so. He did not forget that they were dealing not with an established railway, but with work which had often times to be carried on under great difficulty. The jury after deliberating for twenty minutes returned a verdict of that the deceased met with his death through two engines colliding, and in their opinion the collision occurred owing to the very bad management of the Ship Canal Company.—The Coroner said he entirely agreed with verdict,and he concluded by that verdict they meant to censure the Company. (A Juryman : That is so.) The censure conveyed in the verdict was the best eensure he could give. Be expressed his thanks to Superintendent Atherton and Inspector ' Cooper, for the very great care they had taken in elucidating and following up the evidence. He had no doubt there would be an amendment in the manage- ment of the traffic now.—Mr. Newman said the respon- sible officials with the information in their possession would see that a similar accident did not occur in the future.—The members of the jury were exempted from serving on juries during the present year.
THE HOURS OF CHEMICAL WORKERS.
A WARRINGTONIAN IN THE FAB WEST.
LETTZRS FROM MR. JAMES WINSTANLET.
This week we give more extracts from the letters of Mr. J. Winstanley, of Salem, Oregon, U. S., but formerly of W arriugton.
TEE ELECTION OVER.

On November 13th, Mr. Winstauley writes : " The election of President is now decided and become a fact in history. The Democrats have again elected Cleve- land. I hope it will be the best for this country and the old country. Ido not believe in the Republician party wanting to keep out all the products of other nations by tariffs, and still depend upon other countries buying the produce of this country. Out here, in Oregon, the election is a great disappointment. This is a great Republician State, and has never been known to go Democratic. But the people are awakening to the fact that there is too much protection for the Trusts and Syndicates and no advantage to the work- ingman except in the way of providing saloons for drinking purpose,. The election out here passed over without any fuss, the saloons being closed till after six o'clock. On* of the most wealthy men we have here is a Democrat, and he bought over 150 large tin horns and gave them to the youths of the place who then made night hideous with their discordant noises. I voted for the Prohibition party so as to help to shut down the liquor traffic, and I firmly believe that neither of the old parties will be elected again. There is a third party, called the People's party, and there seems a chance of them and the" Prohibs" going together. If they do they will be able to win the presidency.

TUB HOURS OF THU FBOFIA. Writing on November 29th, Mr. Winstanley referred to some articles on the hQmes of the people in Warring- ton. After alluding to the crowded state of the houses, he adds" Here the poorest cottage has a lot to itself so that there is plenty of air space, and nearly all the houses have the finest kind of gardens. If they were in Warrington they would be thought something grand I can assure you. They have roses blooming every month of the year, and yesterday I saw the loveliest lot of nas- turtiums and chrysanthemums. Of course it is cold just now, and the rains are heavy, but still it is not so bad as the old country for fogs and east wipids ; in fact I have never known it to blow from the east since I came here.

div.head: -•-- PADGATE WESLEYAN TEA PARTY.
div.p: -•-- PADGATE WESLEYAN TEA PARTY.

In the school rooms, on Thursday evening, the congregational tea party in connection with the Padgate Wesleyan Chapel was held. More than 200 persons participated in the tea, the trays being provided by Mesdames Evans, Houghton, Harris, Hall, Steel, Richardson, Roysten, Yates, Hunt, J. Smith, Harrington, London, H. Thornton, E. Thornton, White, Taylor, Holly, Egerton, Ward, arid Miss James, Miss Hanky, and Messrs. Young, Jack- son. J. E. Richardson, and H. Hatton. At the meeting held subsequent to the tea, the Rev. A. Freeman pre- sided, and he was supported by Messrs. Richardson and Bennett. The report of the secretary, Mr. White, was first submitted. It showed that there had been many general beneficial results to the endeavours of the super- intendents and teachers. Many of the scholars, especially those in the elder classes, had noticeably received much christian elevation from the teachings- The number of scholars on the books for the plat year was : 76 girls, and 85 boys, making a total of 161. That was an increase of 17 upon the previous year. The attendance had been creditably maintained, the aver- ages being 77 in the morning and 120 in the afternoon. This was only a slight increase upon the previous year, but that was accounted for by the prevalence of sick- ness. There were seven male and 12 female teachers, but it was felt that the school was not adequately equipped with mate teachers. Financially the school was in a good condition; the teachers had done good work in assisting in the promotion of funds for the additions to the chapels; but after all expenses had been met a small balance was left in , hand. The Echool would be under considerable expense next year however, in contributing to the purchase of saveral essentials. There were at present 297 books in the free library, and several new books had been added during the year. The sum of £43 6s. 6d. had been paid into the clothing club and distributed during the year. The officers elected for the year are :—Messrs. H. Ward and F. Wright, superintendeats ; Mr. F. Harris, trea- surer ; Mr. J. F. White, sec.—Short addresses were de- livered during the evening, by the Rev. A. Freeman,Mr. E. Ford, and others ; and glees were rendered by a num- ber of the younger female scholars. Miss Bessie Dutton, who was also present at the meeting gave enjoyable recitations.

div.head: LETTER FROM THE HOME OFFICE.
div.p: LETTER FROM THE HOME OFFICE.

The Chemical and Copper Workers' Union having passed a resolution in favour of limiting their hours of work to eight per day, Mr. P. J. King, of St. Helens, has communicated with the Home Secretary, and in reply the following letter has been received : Whitehall, 22st January, 1893. Sir,—With reference to your letter of the sth inst., calling attention on behalf of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union to the necessity of rules being settled in respect of chemical works which may at an early date be proposed to the occupiers of such works, pursuant to: the:notice of the Secretary of State, dated 24th Dec. last, and issued by him under the powers given by him , in that behalf by section 8 (1) of the Factory and Work- shops Act, 1891, certifying that in his opinion the processes carried on in chemical works among other works mentioned, are dangerous and injurious to health. I am directed by Mr. Secretary Asquith to acquaint you for the information of your union that no special rules have as yet been prepared under such notice, but that when prepared a copy shall be for- warded tD them for their remarks thereon.-1 am, sir, your obedient servant,
GODFREY LIISRINOTON. Mr. P. J. King, President of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, St. Helens.

div.head: BURIAL CIISTOMS.
div.p: BURIAL CIISTOMS.

Having caught a cold at a funeral, Mr. Winstanley adds ; " You can form no idea of how fussy people are out here over the dead. They dress them up in their best clothes and put them into an expensive " shell " coffin. They put a large square box in the ground and lower the coffin into this. They sit with the corpse in a most outrageous fashion in my opinion, and they expect everydody in the neighbourhood to go and sit with them. Fancy sitting in a room with a man who has died from fever or smallpox. They sent down to our place at one o'clock in the morning for my nephew, Walter. He had just been two hours in bed but he had to get up and go , or be talked about."

div.head: CHRISTMAS IN TRH FAR WEST.
div.p: CHRISTMAS IN TRH FAR WEST.

Christmas Day : " Another Christmas Day in the Far West. This is the fourth we have spent out here. It looks very like Christmas too, for the snow is a foot deep on the ground. We have had a kind of snow blizzard, and we had the greatest diffi- culty in getting to town for flour. It was well we went when we did, as it began to freeze soon , after, and soon made the roads impassible, for the horses break through the hard surface and cut their legs so much that they can hardly haul even an empty wagon. The storm seems to have been general and about 100 miles north they have five feet of snow. We had quite a lively time in getting our cows and calves sheltered from the storm, as they got into the wood and would scarcely stir, yet to leave them there would Ix", to lose them. We went out yesterday to try to shoot a goose for our Christmas dinner. I only went to the bottom of the field and saw three large fellows lazily floating round, but they kept a little out of range, and were lost. It was too hard travelling to follow them up the river where they located themselves, so I came back and killed a couple of roosters, which would do for our Christmas turkey.

div.head: CHESHIRE STANDING JOINT
div.p: CHESHIRE STANDING JOINT
COMMITTEE.
DRUNKEN RUNCORN AGAIN.

A quarterly mteting of this committee was held at Chester Castle on Saturday under the presidency of Colonel France Hayhurst. The Chief Constable's quarterly report (already published) having been submitted, Mr. James Smith (Hoylake) remarked that, proportionately, there was at Runcorn three times the amount of drunkenness that existed in other parts of the county.—The Chief Constable (Colonel Hamersley) said the disproportion was in a large measure due to the Ship Canal works.—Mr. M. T. Graveson (Liscard) replied that whereas in Wirral there were two public-houses for every conviction for drunkenness, in Runcorn there were Is 4 convictions to 138 licensed houses. There must be something radically wrong at Runcorn.—Mr. P. Speakman (Runcorn) claimed that Runcorn was as moral a little town as any in England, and the number of convictions for drunkenness was due to the extraneous labour employed.—Dr. Hodgson (Crewe) sug,gesten that possibly there ought to be greater activity on the part of the Runcorn police.—A resolution to augment the police force of the county by two inspectors, five sergeants, and 14 constables was carried, after a protest had been made against an increase of the police in face cf a diminution of crime.—The Chief Constable slid the decrease of crime was not so great as was generally supposed.—Mr. James Tomkinson asked how it was then that the jails were comparatively empty ?—Sir Horatio Lloyd remarked that the decrease in the prison population was due to the operation of the First Offen- ders Act and to various other agencies.—Mr.Tomkinson notwithstanding this explanation, regarded the proposed increase of the police force as alarming, and pointed out that in Staffordshire and Shropshire there were at least 200 inhabitants more to each p.-,liceman than in Cheshire. Eventually, however, the resolution was carried, as already statel.—Plans were adopted for the erection of a courthouse at Frodsham at a cost of £925. —On the motion of Mr. C. Lister, the Clerk was instructed" to take the opinion of an eminent counsel as to the powers of the police to lay information and carry on prosecutions for offences against the Town Police Clauses Act, without reference to the urban auth- ority within whose district the offence may have been committed, and to incur such expense in coanection therewith as may be necessary."

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
COLLAPSE OF A WALL.
MARVELLOUS ESCAPE OF TWO BOYS.

On Thursday evening some school children were play- ing in an empty house at Coins, when one of them noticed a wall giving way. Ile raised an alarm and made his escape, followed by several of the children, but the wall and root fell, and two boys were buried beneath the ruins. With difficulty they were estricated and it was found that they had been so protected by the fallen matter as to escape death, but one was severely injured.

div.head: LIBERATOR SMASH.
div.p: THE LIBERATOR SMASH.

SAD CASES OF LOSS AT MOLD. Two workingmen living at Mold have lost, one £BOO, and the other £5OO, the savings of a lifetime by the failure of the Liberator Society. To aggravate their condition both melt are confined to bed suffering acutely from shock following upon the disaster.
FLIGHT OF A STARR-BOWKETT SECRETARY.
The Leatherhead and Dorking Starr-Bowkett Society's accounts show a deficiency of £BOO. The secretary has absconded.
THE QUEEN'S SPEECH:

AN AMENDMENT. Sir Frederick Milner will move an amendment to the Address on the Queen's Speech, to the effect that the House regrets the clemency shown to the criminals sen- tenced for dynamite outrages.
THE MORLEY ACTION.
JUDGMENT.

Mr. Justice Wright, delivered judgment yesterday in the case of Morley v. Loughnan. The learned judge held that the money was obtained by the defendants by the exercise of personal influence and the ascendency estab- lished and maintained for that very purpose, under the colour of religion. Judgment would therefore be for the plaintiffs. The Judge reviewed the case at length before giving judgment, and said the principal defendant, W. fl. Loughnan, could not complain if most unfavourable inferences were drawn from his conduct, which con- stituted an abuse of personal influence and ascendency under the cloak of religion. Plaintiffs, who he believed were not influenced by personal motives, were entitled to recover the £50,000 remaining, and inquiry would be made regarding the mcney that had disappeared. He gave costr, against the princ!pal defendant only.
PARR'S BANKING COMPANY AND TIIE ALLIANCE BANK, LIMITED.

ANNUAL MEETING OF THE SHAREHOLDERS. The twenty-eighth annual ordinary meeting of this - company was held on Thursday in the Cannon-st. Hotel, London, The report stated that the balance for the year available for dividend amounted to £177,484. 0,0 of this the directors recommended the payment of a half year's dividend of 19 per cent., payable on the Ist February, leaving a balance of £79,984-. Out of this the directors recommended a further dividend at the rate of 19 per cent, per annum for the quarter ending 31st March next, absorbing £47,500, the sum of £32,484 to be carried forward. The directors proposed to continue ' in future payment of dividends quarterly. Mr. I'l• 11' Fowler M.P., had retired from the board in consequen°. of his becoming a member of the new Ministry, and Mr. J. Charlton Parr had retired through inability to attend the meetings of the board. Mr. Alfred Turner presided, and in moving the ador tion of the report and accounts, said it was gratify!ng to the directors to feel that on this, the first occasion they were meeting in London, they were able to present so satisfactory a report. The past six months had riot been a good half-year for bankers, but notwithstanding the obstacles they had had to encounter, they hi.(l;in the half-year earned a net profit of £97,600. This wal! the highest profit they had yet reached. (Hear, bean) The figures showed that the bank was now in a very strong position. (Hear, hear.) The funds invested were put down at the very lowest value. (Hear hear.) The proposal to pay a quarterly dividend was no idea on the part of Parr's Bank, for it had been 1 fre— mnage! • ' at Warrington. They had never had a better pros Pee quently mooted by their able and experienced a of establishing the practice than at present, and he ' hoped they would be able to maintain it. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to say that the boon had been received with satisfaction by all their shareholders. The incress? in the current accounts since they had amalgamated with the Alliance Bank had been very encouraging. Mr. C. F. Parr seconded the motion. Mr. W. B. Jefferies, of Ipswich, said that as a share" holder of the Alliance Bank he had every reason to he... satisfied with the successful management of their excellent business. (Hear, hear.) The report was unanimously adopted. Mr. W. Dunn, at r. , moved that the dividend of the company be payable quarterly. This was the iir9. occasion on which such a step was taken on the part et a bank. The motion was adopted. Lord Playfair moved the re-election of Sir Greenall, Sir Thomas Frost, Mr. Peter Stubs, C010')8s Gamble, Sir Andrew Walker, and Mr. John Dun a, directors, and the motion was adopted. Messrs. Stem". , Taylor, and Stead, of Liverpool, were re-appointed auditors. Gilbert,

COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONSAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 & 1886. SWINE FEVER. NOTICE IN HEREBY GIVEN, that at a Meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on• Wednesday, the 18th day of January, 1893. IT WAS ORDERED that the Regulations of the Exe- cutive Committee of the said Local Authority, as to the movement of Swine into the District of this Local Authority then in force, SHALL AS FROM THE FIRST DAY OF FEBRUARY, 1893, BE, AND THE SAME ARE HEREBY REVOKED. AND rr WAS FURTHER ORDERED by the said Executive Committee of the said Authority, that from and after the said first day of February,lB93, the move- ment of swine into the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, from the counties er places hereinafter mentioned, shall (with the exception and for the purpose hereinafter mentioned) BE ABSOLUTELY PROHIBITED until this order is revoked, that is to say, from the counties of Bedford Northampton Cambridge Suffolk Essex Surrey Gloucester Sussex Hants West Riding of York Kent Wilts Norfolk and from the District of any separate Local Authority situate within any of such Counties cr Places. Pro- vided always that, notwithstanding the foregoing pro- hibition, SWINE to be used for breeding purposes only may be moved into the district of the Local Authority of this County, from the Counties or places hereinbefore mentioned, subject to the following regulations, that is to say.:- 1. On obtaining a License from an Inspector of the Local Authority ot this County, which License will only be granted on the following conditions: (a) On a declaration of the Owner of the Swine from whom they are purchased or his Agent, that the Animals have been on the premises of such owner during the 28 days immediately preceding their removal therefrom, and that there has been no Swine fever on such premises during the /aid period of 28 days. (1.1 On a.certificate of a Veterinary Inspector of the County of Chester, or a Veterinary Inspector appointed by the Local Authority of the district from which the Swine are to be moved, that such Swine are free from disease. 2. That all Swine brought into the said district under these regulations, shall not be moved from the premises of sugh Owner to which they are first brought for 28 days from their arrival thereat. 3. That Swine which have been removed from any of the prohibited Counties, or places named therein, or from the district of any separate Local Authority, situ- ate within any of such Counties or places, into the dis- trict of any separate Local Authority, situate within this County, or into any other County, shall not be snared into the district of this Local Authority, except supon a Licence granted under the following condition that is to say : On a declaration made by the Owner of the Swine or his Agent that such Swine have been on the pre- mises from which they are to be moved for 28 days immediately preceding the date thereof, and that Swine Fever has not existed on such premises dur- ing the said period of 28 days, and also that the swine intended to be moved have not been exposed to the infection of Swine Fever during such period. 4. That Swine moved into the district of this Local Authority under the foregoing License be at once isolated by the Owner thereof in this County, and kept isorated from any other Swine for a period of 28 days, and shall not be moved from the premises of such Owner to which they are first moved for a period of 28 days from their arrival thereat. 5. That LICENSES. Declarations, and Veterinary Surgeons' Certificates shall accompany the Animals therein mentioned whilst being moved, an be delivered up to the Police Officer of the County of Chester nearest to the place of their destination by the owner or his Agent within 48 hours after their arrival thereat. REGINALD POTTS. Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 27th January, 1893. The foregoing regulations do not restrict the move- ment of Animals by Railway through the District of the Local Authority of this County, without untrucking,. Any offence against the above Regulations is deemed an offence against the Act of 1878, which renders the offender liable to a penalty of not exceeding Twenty Pounds.

DEPARTURE OF THE BLACK WATCH FROM LIMERICK. 'FRIENDLY ',DEMONSTRATION. The second battalion of the Royal Highlanders (Black Watch) Regiment on Saturday left the quarters at Limerick which they have occupied for two years, for , Glasgow. The battalion was very warmly cheered while marching to the railway station, the populace turning dutin thousands, lining the thoroughfares and vociferously cheering the Highlanders. The troops cheered in return, and the band played " Auld Lang Syne" as the train steamed away. The Manchester Regiment will selieve the Highlanders.
